incidents.place: Nayarit

narrative.html: Jesús Alejandro Márquez Jiménez was the founder and editor of the news website Orión Informativo and a former reporter for the local newspaper Crítica in Tepic, Nayarit.50 According to the ONU-DH, his journalistic work focused on politics and current affairs.51 RSF reported that Orión Informativo had published criticism concerning alleged links between organised crime and local politicians in Nayarit, and that municipal officials in a neighbouring municipality had filed a defamation complaint against Márquez Jiménez approximately six months before his death.52
narrative.text: Jesús Alejandro Márquez Jiménez was the founder and editor of the news website Orión Informativo and a former reporter for the local newspaper Crítica in Tepic, Nayarit. According to the ONU-DH, his journalistic work focused on politics and current affairs. RSF reported that Orión Informativo had published criticism concerning alleged links between organised crime and local politicians in Nayarit, and that municipal officials in a neighbouring municipality had filed a defamation complaint against Márquez Jiménez approximately six months before his death.

narrative.html: Márquez Jiménez was last seen alive on 30 November 2018 after receiving a telephone call while eating with his family, whereupon he left his home on a motorcycle.53 His body was found the following morning — the day of President López Obrador’s inauguration — in a ditch near the Tepic airport. Anonymous sources cited by Crítica reported that the body bore at least four bullet wounds and signs of a beating.54
narrative.text: Márquez Jiménez was last seen alive on 30 November 2018 after receiving a telephone call while eating with his family, whereupon he left his home on a motorcycle. His body was found the following morning — the day of President López Obrador’s inauguration — in a ditch near the Tepic airport. Anonymous sources cited by Crítica reported that the body bore at least four bullet wounds and signs of a beating.

narrative.html: FEADLE opened an investigation into the killing.55 ONU-DH called on authorities to conduct a prompt investigation, ensure those responsible are brought to justice, and emphasised the importance of ending impunity in cases of violence against journalists.56 The State Attorney General’s Office subsequently issued arrest warrants against three state government officials for the murder, including the Director General of Transit of Nayarit. The latter pleaded guilty to encubrimiento (cover-up), but two other Transit Department officials were charged as the alleged material authors of the killing and held in pretrial detention, but no conviction for Marquez’s kidnapping and murder has been recorded.

incidents.heading: Rafael Murúa Manríquez — Killed, 20 January 2019, Baja California Sur
incidents.place: near an expressway approximately 40 kilometres north of Santa Rosalía
incidents.identity: Rafael Murúa Manríquez was a community radio journalist and the founding director of Radio Kashana (93.3 FM), a community radio station affiliated with AMARC México in Santa Rosalía, Baja California Sur.

narrative.html: Rafael Murúa Manríquez was a community radio journalist and the founding director of Radio Kashana (93.3 FM), a community radio station affiliated with AMARC México in Santa Rosalía, Baja California Sur.57 He also collaborated with several other outlets, including Peninsular Digital, El Sur Californiano, BCS Noticias, and the Colectivo Pericú.58 He addressed cultural and political topics and was also recognised as a human rights defender and activist by the Organisation of American States.59
narrative.text: Rafael Murúa Manríquez was a community radio journalist and the founding director of Radio Kashana (93.3 FM), a community radio station affiliated with AMARC México in Santa Rosalía, Baja California Sur. He also collaborated with several other outlets, including Peninsular Digital, El Sur Californiano, BCS Noticias, and the Colectivo Pericú. He addressed cultural and political topics and was also recognised as a human rights defender and activist by the Organisation of American States.

narrative.html: Murúa had reported experiencing threats and harassment for several years prior to his killing. He was incorporated into Mexico’s federal Protection Mechanism in June 2017, after receiving threatening messages from an alleged member of a criminal gang.60 Despite being incorporated into the Mechanism, Murúa’s family noted that the home infrastructure measures and emergency button he was promised were never fully installed.61 Since November 2018, he had publicly denounced multiple incidents—including death threats, an attempted arbitrary detention, and a gunshot fired at his home—following reporting and opinions critical of Mulegé Mayor Felipe Prado Bautista’s administration.62 In a first-person account republished by Periodistas de a Pie, Murúa described a crowd pounding on his home’s gate, a bullet breaking an upstairs window, and a municipal police commander arriving at his newsroom seeking to detain him in circumstances he characterised as extrajudicial.63
narrative.text: Murúa had reported experiencing threats and harassment for several years prior to his killing. He was incorporated into Mexico’s federal Protection Mechanism in June 2017, after receiving threatening messages from an alleged member of a criminal gang. Despite being incorporated into the Mechanism, Murúa’s family noted that the home infrastructure measures and emergency button he was promised were never fully installed. Since November 2018, he had publicly denounced multiple incidents—including death threats, an attempted arbitrary detention, and a gunshot fired at his home—following reporting and opinions critical of Mulegé Mayor Felipe Prado Bautista’s administration. In a first-person account republished by Periodistas de a Pie, Murúa described a crowd pounding on his home’s gate, a bullet breaking an upstairs window, and a municipal police commander arriving at his newsroom seeking to detain him in circumstances he characterised as extrajudicial.

narrative.html: Murúa was reported missing on 19 January 2019 and his body was found the following day near an expressway approximately 40 kilometres north of Santa Rosalía.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:64">64</sup> Forensic reports indicated that he suffered a stab wound that perforated the heart and left lung, as well as cranial trauma from a bullet impact.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:65">65</sup> The State Attorney General’s Office announced that investigators found packages believed to contain marijuana at the scene—a fact condemned by ARTICLE 19 and AMARC México as an apparent attempt to blame the victim and deflect attention from the perpetrators.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:66">66</sup>
narrative.text: Murúa was reported missing on 19 January 2019 and his body was found the following day near an expressway approximately 40 kilometres north of Santa Rosalía. Forensic reports indicated that he suffered a stab wound that perforated the heart and left lung, as well as cranial trauma from a bullet impact. The State Attorney General’s Office announced that investigators found packages believed to contain marijuana at the scene—a fact condemned by ARTICLE 19 and AMARC México as an apparent attempt to blame the victim and deflect attention from the perpetrators.

narrative.html: On 27 January 2020, the State Attorney General’s Office announced that three suspects had been found guilty of carrying out Murúa’s murder and sentenced to 43 years and 9 months in prison.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:67">67</sup> ARTICLE 19 and AMARC México continued to highlight alleged investigative shortcomings and the fundamental failure of the Mechanism to protect a journalist who was a registered beneficiary at the time of his murder.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:68">68</sup> UNESCO’s Director-General also condemned the murder and emphasised the importance of protecting community media for freedom of expression and access to information.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:69">69</sup>

UNESCO’s Director-General also condemned the murder and emphasised the importance of protecting community media for freedom of expression and access to information.

narrative.html: Martín Valtierra García was the editor and founder of the news website Contrastes de Comondú, which covered news throughout Baja California Sur, including municipal payroll spending, nepotism within the municipal administration, and water shortages in several neighbourhoods.70 On 8 January 2019, he published a column71 critical of Comondú Mayor José Walter Valenzuela. Although he had not received direct threats, a colleague warned him in November 2018 that his reporting had angered officials in the municipal government.72 At the time of the attack, Valtierra was in the process of being incorporated into the federal Protection Mechanism.73
narrative.text: Martín Valtierra García was the editor and founder of the news website Contrastes de Comondú, which covered news throughout Baja California Sur, including municipal payroll spending, nepotism within the municipal administration, and water shortages in several neighbourhoods. On 8 January 2019, he published a column critical of Comondú Mayor José Walter Valenzuela. Although he had not received direct threats, a colleague warned him in November 2018 that his reporting had angered officials in the municipal government. At the time of the attack, Valtierra was in the process of being incorporated into the federal Protection Mechanism.

narrative.html: On 29 January 2019, two unknown assailants attacked Valtierra with baseball bats outside his home in Ciudad Constitución. Security-camera footage<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:74">74</sup> confirmed by Valtierra showed two men exiting a vehicle, approaching him, striking him repeatedly, and then fleeing. He suffered a head wound requiring 12 stitches and a fractured right ulna, and was scheduled for surgery to repair the fracture.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:75">75</sup>

Security-camera footage confirmed by Valtierra showed two men exiting a vehicle, approaching him, striking him repeatedly, and then fleeing. He suffered a head wound requiring 12 stitches and a fractured right ulna, and was scheduled for surgery to repair the fracture.

narrative.html: Baja California Sur Governor Carlos Mendoza condemned<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:76">76</sup> the attack and promised that the state prosecutor’s office would open an investigation. In May 2019, authorities detained a suspect identified as Fidel “N,” described as a Comondú municipal government employee and the owner of the vehicle in which the attackers travelled.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:77">77</sup> Valtierra subsequently died in an unrelated traffic collision on 21 January 2024.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:78">78</sup>

incidents.place: Hotel Ramos in Emiliano Zapata
incidents.identity: Jesús Eugenio Ramos Rodríguez, known as “Chuchín,” was a veteran radio journalist who had worked for approximately 20 years at radio station Oye 99.9 FM in Emiliano Zapata, Tabasco, where he hosted the popular news programme Nuestra Región Hoy.

narrative.html: Jesús Eugenio Ramos Rodríguez, known as “Chuchín,” was a veteran radio journalist who had worked for approximately 20 years at radio station Oye 99.9 FM in Emiliano Zapata, Tabasco, where he hosted the popular news programme Nuestra Región Hoy.79 According to his brother, the programme had become increasingly controversial in the wake of recent municipal elections, and Ramos Rodríguez had criticised local politicians on the programme.80
narrative.text: Jesús Eugenio Ramos Rodríguez, known as “Chuchín,” was a veteran radio journalist who had worked for approximately 20 years at radio station Oye 99.9 FM in Emiliano Zapata, Tabasco, where he hosted the popular news programme Nuestra Región Hoy. According to his brother, the programme had become increasingly controversial in the wake of recent municipal elections, and Ramos Rodríguez had criticised local politicians on the programme.

narrative.html: On the morning of 9 February 2019, while Ramos Rodríguez was having breakfast at Hotel Ramos in Emiliano Zapata with several other individuals, a lone gunman entered the restaurant and shot him at close range. He died later that morning at the municipal hospital.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:81">81</sup> The Tabasco State Prosecutor’s Office opened an investigation and dispatched investigative and forensic personnel. The Tabasco prosecutor also requested that FEADLE join the investigation.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:82">82</sup> ONU-DH called on authorities to investigate effectively, including the victim’s journalistic activity as a line of investigation, and to adopt effective protection measures for his family and colleagues.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:83">83</sup> As of July 2019, RSF and CPJ reported that there had been no conviction in the case. In December 2020, a Tabasco police officer described as a presumed killer of Ramos Rodríguez was arrested, but for extortion, not for the journalist’s murder. To date, no conviction for the killing has been reported.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:84">84</sup>
narrative.text: On the morning of 9 February 2019, while Ramos Rodríguez was having breakfast at Hotel Ramos in Emiliano Zapata with several other individuals, a lone gunman entered the restaurant and shot him at close range. He died later that morning at the municipal hospital. The Tabasco State Prosecutor’s Office opened an investigation and dispatched investigative and forensic personnel. The Tabasco prosecutor also requested that FEADLE join the investigation. ONU-DH called on authorities to investigate effectively, including the victim’s journalistic activity as a line of investigation, and to adopt effective protection measures for his family and colleagues. As of July 2019, RSF and CPJ reported that there had been no conviction in the case. In December 2020, a Tabasco police officer described as a presumed killer of Ramos Rodríguez was arrested, but for extortion, not for the journalist’s murder. To date, no conviction for the killing has been reported.

incidents.title: Samir Flores Soberanes
incidents.heading: Samir Flores Soberanes — Killed, 20 February 2019
incidents.place: outside his home in Amilcingo
incidents.identity: Samir Flores Soberanes, an Indigenous Nahua community radio journalist and human rights defender, was shot and killed outside his home in Amilcingo in the state of Morelos

persons.outcomeQuote: was shot and killed outside his home in Amilcingo in the state of Morelos

narrative.html: On 20 February 2019, at approximately 5:30 a.m., Samir Flores Soberanes, an Indigenous Nahua community radio journalist and human rights defender, was shot and killed outside his home in Amilcingo in the state of Morelos.92 According to a joint statement issued by several CSOs, armed assailants arrived in two vehicles, knocked on his door, and shot him four times as he emerged, including two bullets to the head.93 He died shortly afterwards. Flores Soberanes was the co-founder and producer of Radio Amiltzinko (100.7 FM).94 His reporting and organising focused on environmental and Indigenous land-rights issues, including opposition to the Proyecto Integral Morelos, a federal energy megaproject comprising two thermoelectric plants in Huexca, an approximately 160-kilometre natural gas pipeline traversing the states of Tlaxcala, Puebla, and Morelos, an aqueduct drawing from the Cuautla River, and an electric transmission line; opponents argued the project would contaminate water supplies relied upon by Indigenous communities.95
narrative.text: On 20 February 2019, at approximately 5:30 a.m., Samir Flores Soberanes, an Indigenous Nahua community radio journalist and human rights defender, was shot and killed outside his home in Amilcingo in the state of Morelos. According to a joint statement issued by several CSOs, armed assailants arrived in two vehicles, knocked on his door, and shot him four times as he emerged, including two bullets to the head. He died shortly afterwards. Flores Soberanes was the co-founder and producer of Radio Amiltzinko (100.7 FM). His reporting and organising focused on environmental and Indigenous land-rights issues, including opposition to the Proyecto Integral Morelos, a federal energy megaproject comprising two thermoelectric plants in Huexca, an approximately 160-kilometre natural gas pipeline traversing the states of Tlaxcala, Puebla, and Morelos, an aqueduct drawing from the Cuautla River, and an electric transmission line; opponents argued the project would contaminate water supplies relied upon by Indigenous communities.

narrative.html: The killing occurred the morning after Flores Soberanes had attended a government-organised informational forum in Jonacatepec at which he publicly challenged the federal delegate Hugo Erik Flores Cervantes regarding the project, and three days before a federally scheduled public consultation on the project.96 According to the People's Front in Defence of Land and Water, Flores Soberanes had received repeated death threats in connection with his land-defence work since 2012, and had been subject to defamation and online harassment.97 Within hours of the killing, the Morelos State Attorney General, Uriel Carmona Gándara, publicly stated that the murder appeared linked to organised crime and asserted that there was no element connecting it to the thermoelectric project.98 A handwritten cardboard sign attributed to “Comando Tlahuica,” an organised crime group, was reportedly left at the scene of the killing, bearing a narcomanta or narcomensaje reading, "X you fucking gossip, you reported [denounced] Abraham Ocampo and you keep on, you Michoacano with your fucking gang. Sincerely, Tlahuica Command.”99 The cardboard was lost by investigators in the course of the investigation.100 The lawyer for the Flores Soberanes family, together with the CNI, publicly stated that they did not trust the Morelos Attorney General's Office to conduct an impartial investigation, and called for the case to be transferred to federal jurisdiction.101 By late 2021, arrest warrants had been issued for three suspects. One, Azael Martínez, was dead at the time of issue; another, Salvador Aparicio, was missing; and the last, Javier Rosendo Pareja, was incarcerated at the time of the murder.102 Pareja was put on trial for Flores Soberante’s murder in February 2026, in a decision described by his neighbor and fellow activist Samantha Cesar as “a set-up.”103 He was acquitted in March 2026, after a trial rife with irregularities that included two of the prosecution’s key witnesses being killed and its evidence being found implausible or illegally obtained.104 On 6 June 2026, alleged leader of the Comando Tlahuica criminal group Homero Figueroa Meza “La Tripa” was arrested by federal agents in connection to the murder of Flores Soberante.105 Sandra León Varo was also arrested in the same operation.106

narrative.html: Santiago Barroso Alfaro, aged 47, was a journalist, radio host, and director of the news portal Red 653 in San Luis Río Colorado, Sonora. He hosted the radio programme San Luis Hoy on 91.1 FM Río Digital and was a contributor to the weekly publication Contraseña.109 The IFJ reported that Barroso had denounced the presence of individuals linked to human trafficking and drug trafficking in Sonora the day before he was killed.110
narrative.text: Santiago Barroso Alfaro, aged 47, was a journalist, radio host, and director of the news portal Red 653 in San Luis Río Colorado, Sonora. He hosted the radio programme San Luis Hoy on 91.1 FM Río Digital and was a contributor to the weekly publication Contraseña. The IFJ reported that Barroso had denounced the presence of individuals linked to human trafficking and drug trafficking in Sonora the day before he was killed.

narrative.html: On the night of 15 March 2019, a gunman shot Barroso at the entrance of his home. He was able to call an ambulance but died at a local hospital around 11:00 p.m.111 Sonora state authorities subsequently characterised the killing as a crimen pasional (crime of passion) and arrested the suspected perpetrator within one week.112 However, fellow journalist Rafael Cano Franco publicly stated that Barroso’s killing was linked to his journalistic work, and PEN America urged authorities to conduct a thorough investigation including possible links to Barroso’s professional activities.113 A court sentenced Omar “N” to 22 years in prison for qualified homicide through an abbreviated procedure.114

narrative.html: Telésforo Santiago Enríquez was an Indigenous community radio journalist and education teacher based in San Agustín Loxicha, Oaxaca. He was the founder and director of the community radio station El Cafetal (Estéreo Cafetal 98.7 FM — “La Voz Zapoteca”), through which he promoted Indigenous rights and Zapotec culture and language.115 He was also a teacher affiliated with Section 22 of the teachers’ union.116 He often criticised local authorities in his radio programmes; the day before he was killed, he had taken calls from listeners on the topic of local politicians and embezzlement.117

He was the founder and director of the community radio station El Cafetal (Estéreo Cafetal 98.7 FM — “La Voz Zapoteca”), through which he promoted Indigenous rights and Zapotec culture and language. He was also a teacher affiliated with Section 22 of the teachers’ union. He often criticised local authorities in his radio programmes; the day before he was killed, he had taken calls from listeners on the topic of local politicians and embezzlement.

narrative.html: Santiago Enríquez had received death threats in February 2019, which he and individuals close to him believed originated from the brother of San Agustín Loxicha Mayor Pedro Vázquez.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:118">118</sup> His niece confirmed that he had been threatened during an on-air call to his live programme.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:119">119</sup> On 2 May 2019, Santiago Enríquez was ambushed and shot while driving to host his afternoon newscast in the neighbourhood of Ampliación de las Tres Cruces in San Agustín Loxicha. His body, bearing gunshot wounds, was found inside his vehicle.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:120">120</sup> The Oaxaca state prosecutor’s office opened an investigation for qualified homicide.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:121">121</sup> UNESCO’s Director-General condemned the murder and emphasised the importance of community media. The Washington Post noted that he was killed on the eve of World Press Freedom Day. As of the most recent available reporting, the case remains unresolved.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:122">122</sup>

On 2 May 2019, Santiago Enríquez was ambushed and shot while driving to host his afternoon newscast in the neighbourhood of Ampliación de las Tres Cruces in San Agustín Loxicha. His body, bearing gunshot wounds, was found inside his vehicle. The Oaxaca state prosecutor’s office opened an investigation for qualified homicide. UNESCO’s Director-General condemned the murder and emphasised the importance of community media. The Washington Post noted that he was killed on the eve of World Press Freedom Day. As of the most recent available reporting, the case remains unresolved.

narrative.html: Francisco Romero Díaz, known as “Ñaca Ñaca,” was a citizen journalist in Solidaridad, Quintana Roo, who founded the Facebook-based media outlet Ocurrió Aquí. He began his career by live-streaming local crime scenes and was mentored by Rubén Pat, alongside whom he co-founded the weekly newspaper Playa News in 2016. Pat was himself killed in 2018.123 After the death of his mentor, Romero was transferred out of Quintana Roo for several months due to safety concerns.124 Romero was known for live broadcasts from crime scenes, often being the first journalist to arrive, and worked alongside colleagues who shared scoops to avoid putting any single reporter at further risk.125
narrative.text: Francisco Romero Díaz, known as “Ñaca Ñaca,” was a citizen journalist in Solidaridad, Quintana Roo, who founded the Facebook-based media outlet Ocurrió Aquí. He began his career by live-streaming local crime scenes and was mentored by Rubén Pat, alongside whom he co-founded the weekly newspaper Playa News in 2016. Pat was himself killed in 2018. After the death of his mentor, Romero was transferred out of Quintana Roo for several months due to safety concerns. Romero was known for live broadcasts from crime scenes, often being the first journalist to arrive, and worked alongside colleagues who shared scoops to avoid putting any single reporter at further risk.

narrative.html: Romero was threatened for his journalistic work on at least five occasions. In early March 2019, he was arbitrarily detained by municipal police while covering a traffic accident and subsequently threatened by a municipal police commander.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:126">126</sup> In April 2019, he was kidnapped by three individuals while covering another accident, blindfolded, tied up, beaten, and abandoned.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:127">127</sup> He filed a complaint with the state prosecutor’s office and released a video holding Solidaridad Mayor Laura Beristaín responsible for whatever might happen to him.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:128">128</sup> ARTICLE 19 contacted the Mechanism the same month, which granted him a panic button and two bodyguards as protective measures.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:129">129</sup> On 7 May 2019, he received death threats against him and his family via private Facebook message.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:130">130</sup>

In early March 2019, he was arbitrarily detained by municipal police while covering a traffic accident and subsequently threatened by a municipal police commander. In April 2019, he was kidnapped by three individuals while covering another accident, blindfolded, tied up, beaten, and abandoned. He filed a complaint with the state prosecutor’s office and released a video holding Solidaridad Mayor Laura Beristaín responsible for whatever might happen to him. ARTICLE 19 contacted the Mechanism the same month, which granted him a panic button and two bodyguards as protective measures. On 7 May 2019, he received death threats against him and his family via private Facebook message.

narrative.html: On 16 May 2019, Romero’s body was found next to his motorcycle in the parking lot of a bar, three blocks from the state police base in Solidaridad.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:131">131</sup> He had been shot by unknown assailants. By 17 May, a suspect had been detained who confessed to receiving telephone instructions to carry out the killing.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:132">132</sup> The state attorney general stated that investigators were probing a network of hired gunmen who received orders and payment by telephone.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:133">133</sup> The suspect indicated the callers claimed affiliation with the CJNG, though prosecutors believed they were likely a local group.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:134">134</sup> Romero was the fourth journalist murdered in Mexico despite having been granted protective measures by the Mechanism.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:135">135</sup>
narrative.text: On 16 May 2019, Romero’s body was found next to his motorcycle in the parking lot of a bar, three blocks from the state police base in Solidaridad. He had been shot by unknown assailants. By 17 May, a suspect had been detained who confessed to receiving telephone instructions to carry out the killing. The state attorney general stated that investigators were probing a network of hired gunmen who received orders and payment by telephone. The suspect indicated the callers claimed affiliation with the CJNG, though prosecutors believed they were likely a local group. Romero was the fourth journalist murdered in Mexico despite having been granted protective measures by the Mechanism.

narrative.html: José Luis Álvarez Flores, known as “Tío Guato” or “Don José,” was an environmentalist leader and founder of the conservation organisation UMA Saraguato, which he established in 2012 to protect a 345-hectare area in Chablé, Tabasco, where he conserved howler monkeys native to southeastern Mexico. He had been threatened with death multiple times—including as recently as the week before his killing—for reporting complaints against a criminal gang’s illegal extraction of sand from the Usumacinta River.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:136">136</sup> Despite multiple requests for protection from the state, authorities never responded to his requests.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:137">137</sup>
narrative.text: José Luis Álvarez Flores, known as “Tío Guato” or “Don José,” was an environmentalist leader and founder of the conservation organisation UMA Saraguato, which he established in 2012 to protect a 345-hectare area in Chablé, Tabasco, where he conserved howler monkeys native to southeastern Mexico. He had been threatened with death multiple times—including as recently as the week before his killing—for reporting complaints against a criminal gang’s illegal extraction of sand from the Usumacinta River. Despite multiple requests for protection from the state, authorities never responded to his requests.

narrative.html: His bullet-ridden body was found on the side of a highway between Tabasco and Chiapas near the Calatraba ejido, along with a series of cardboard signs containing threatening messages against his family and his top collaborators.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:138">138</sup> The Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources publicly expressed outrage over his murder. His case remains unresolved.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:139">139</sup>

narrative.html: Norma Sarabia was a correspondent for Tabasco Hoy and the secretary of the Ramón Herrera elementary school in Villa Chontalpa, Huimanguillo, Tabasco, where she hoped to become a teacher. She was 46 years old and was about to graduate from the University of Chontalpa with a degree in psychology before her death.140 Sarabia covered local crime and politics, particularly fuel theft near the federal Cárdenas-Coatzacoalcos highway. In the week preceding her death, Tabasco Hoy published a report without a cited byline accusing Mayor José del Carmen Torruco of corruption and nepotism in the Municipal Police Department, headed by Marino Reyes Delgado.141 CPJ reported that in 2014 Sarabia had reported to state authorities receiving threats from local police officers after she covered the alleged involvement of police in kidnappings.142 Media reports further indicated that she had received multiple death threats and feared for her life.143

CPJ reported that in 2014 Sarabia had reported to state authorities receiving threats from local police officers after she covered the alleged involvement of police in kidnappings. Media reports further indicated that she had received multiple death threats and feared for her life.

narrative.html: On the evening of 11 June 2019, at approximately 9:30 p.m., Sarabia was shot by two armed men as she entered her home on Nicolás Bravo Avenue, in the Club Liberal neighbourhood. Her body was found at the bottom of the stairs. The Tabasco State Attorney General opened an investigation and ordered protection measures for Sarabia’s family members.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:144">144</sup> In December 2020, a man identified as Uriel “N” — a police commander and head of a homicide unit in the Frontera municipality who worked in Huimanguillo — was detained as a suspect. Sarabia had confronted Uriel “N” shortly before her death, accusing him of illegally arresting two teenagers and attempting to extort their families. Notably, the state prosecutor’s office arrested him for alleged extortion and did not publicly mention Sarabia’s killing in connection with his apprehension.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:145">145</sup>

narrative.html: Marcos Miranda Cogco, known as “Marmiko,” was the founder of Noticias A Tiempo, a Facebook-based media outlet in Boca del Río, Veracruz. He specialised in reporting on crime and violence. In a video widely quoted but since deleted that he released after his abduction, Miranda Cogco stated that it was the third time in six to eight years that someone had attacked or attempted to kidnap him, but vowed that he would not be intimidated, declaring that he would continue his criticism of the government.146 In the same video, he noted that he suspected the government may have been behind his abduction, citing his critique of the Morena party of Cuitláhuac.147

He specialised in reporting on crime and violence. In a video widely quoted but since deleted that he released after his abduction, Miranda Cogco stated that it was the third time in six to eight years that someone had attacked or attempted to kidnap him, but vowed that he would not be intimidated, declaring that he would continue his criticism of the government.  In the same video, he noted that he suspected the government may have been behind his abduction, citing his critique of the Morena party of Cuitláhuac.

narrative.html: On 12 June 2019, at approximately 8:00 a.m., Miranda Cogco was kidnapped while taking his child to school. Two trucks blocked his vehicle near his home, and armed men abducted him. In a video he posted on his media outlet<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:148">148</sup> after being rescued that has since been taken down, he described being taken to a room, stripped naked, photographed, and repeatedly struck in the neck and head. The video was partially preserved by journalist Circo Gomez Leyva in a post on Leyva’s own Facebook page.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:149">149</sup> Police rescued Miranda Cogco later that day by intercepting a suspicious vehicle travelling down a dirt road; a shootout ensued with three apparent captors, who escaped on foot, and Miranda Cogco was discovered tied up in the back of the car. Three firearms were seized at the scene, including an Uzi-type weapon and two revolvers.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:150">150</sup>

narrative.html: Lydia Cacho is a renowned Mexican journalist best-known for her investigative reporting into the sexual exploitation of young girls by Mexican politicians and businessmen, and her international reporting. She is an advocate for girls and women, and is the founder and director of the Centro Integral de Atención a las Mujeres in Cancún, a crisis center and shelter for victims of sex crimes, gender-based violence and trafficking.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:151">151</sup>
narrative.text: Lydia Cacho is a renowned Mexican journalist best-known for her investigative reporting into the sexual exploitation of young girls by Mexican politicians and businessmen, and her international reporting. She is an advocate for girls and women, and is the founder and director of the Centro Integral de Atención a las Mujeres in Cancún, a crisis center and shelter for victims of sex crimes, gender-based violence and trafficking.

narrative.html: At approximately 6:30 p.m. on 21 July 2019, attackers broke into Cacho’s home in Puerto Morelos, Quintana Roo after cutting the security camera cables and disabling the alarm.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:152">152</sup> Attackers killed her two dogs and stole work equipment, including an audio recorder, three cameras, several memory cards, a laptop computer, and ten hard drives with information of high public interest related to cases of pedophilia. Cacho had security protection the night of the attack, but it is unclear if they were assigned through the federal Protection Mechanism.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:153">153</sup>
narrative.text: At approximately 6:30 p.m. on 21 July 2019, attackers broke into Cacho’s home in Puerto Morelos, Quintana Roo after cutting the security camera cables and disabling the alarm. Attackers killed her two dogs and stole work equipment, including an audio recorder, three cameras, several memory cards, a laptop computer, and ten hard drives with information of high public interest related to cases of pedophilia. Cacho had security protection the night of the attack, but it is unclear if they were assigned through the federal Protection Mechanism.

narrative.html: Following the attack, Cacho immediately left Mexico and went to the United States. In the week after, Cacho says it was determined by Interpol the attackers were sicarios from the Sinaloa cartel.154 Ricardo Sánchez Pérez del Pozo, head of the office of the Federal Special Prosecutor for Attention to Crimes Committed Against Freedom of Expression, told CPJ that his office had opened an investigation into the burglary.155 Cacho moved permanently to Spain, where she was naturalized in 2021.156

In the week after, Cacho says it was determined by Interpol the attackers were sicarios from the Sinaloa cartel. Ricardo Sánchez Pérez del Pozo, head of the office of the Federal Special Prosecutor for Attention to Crimes Committed Against Freedom of Expression, told CPJ that his office had opened an investigation into the burglary. Cacho moved permanently to Spain, where she was naturalized in 2021.

narrative.html: Cacho has been attacked for her reporting for decades. In 1999, Cacho was raped and beaten in the bathroom of a bus station. She suspects the attack was related to her work.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:157">157</sup> She was kidnapped and tortured for 20 hours by state police in 2005 after publishing "The Demons of Eden," her 2005 book that exposed a pedophile ring operating in Puebla and Quintana Roo states.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:158">158</sup> A recording of a conversation between Lebanese businessman Kamel Nacif Borge and then-governor of Puebla Mario Marín Torres that revealed Nacif thanking Torres for arresting Cacho was discovered by the media in 2006. Cacho took these recordings to the Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation, where the judges determined in 2007 that the violations of her rights had not been serious.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:159">159</sup>

She was kidnapped and tortured for 20 hours by state police in 2005 after publishing "The Demons of Eden," her 2005 book that exposed a pedophile ring operating in Puebla and Quintana Roo states. A recording of a conversation between Lebanese businessman Kamel Nacif Borge and then-governor of Puebla Mario Marín Torres that revealed Nacif thanking Torres for arresting Cacho was discovered by the media in 2006. Cacho took these recordings to the Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation, where the judges determined in 2007 that the violations of her rights had not been serious.

narrative.html: In 2007, Cacho alleged that her car was tampered with in an attempt to cause an accident. Her bodyguards discovered that the nuts had been loosened on one of the wheels, nearly causing the car to crash.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:160">160</sup> The attack came on 7 May 2007, five days after Cacho appeared at the trial of accused pedophile Jean Succar Kuri, one of the men she wrote about in her 2005 book. In 2009, Cachao was granted protection from the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:161">161</sup>

narrative.html: In 2018, the UN Human Rights Committee ruled that Cacho's rights had been violated and ordered the Mexican state to re-open the investigation into the attack, and to give her adequate compensation. This judgment has led to several arrests of state agents in Puebla, including a former governor and chief of the judicial police and several police officers. In 2019, just months before the July break-in, the Mexican government publicly apologized to Cacho in an unprecedented ceremony arbited by Alejandro Encinas, Undersecretary of Human Rights.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:162">162</sup>

narrative.html: Nidya Hernández was the director of the digital media outlet Domingo 7 in Tehuacán, Puebla. She had been known for speaking out about problems with the government of Ernestina Fernández for three years, and had served briefly as Director of Social Communications for the Fernández administration before resigning over what she perceived as corruption.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:167">167</sup> She had recently criticised former police commanders who were dismissed for corruption involving the municipal government.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:168">168</sup>
narrative.text: Nidya Hernández was the director of the digital media outlet Domingo 7 in Tehuacán, Puebla. She had been known for speaking out about problems with the government of Ernestina Fernández for three years, and had served briefly as Director of Social Communications for the Fernández administration before resigning over what she perceived as corruption. She had recently criticised former police commanders who were dismissed for corruption involving the municipal government.

narrative.html: On 23 July 2019, at approximately 10:40 p.m., unknown men fired upon her home, which also served as the office for her news outlet.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:169">169</sup> The bullets penetrated a window and the main door, though no one was physically injured. Although Hernández stated she had not received prior direct threats, she believed the attack was connected to her journalistic work, particularly her recent reporting on corruption in the Municipal Public Security Department.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:170">170</sup> She publicly called on the state governor, the governor-elect, and President López Obrador to intervene and investigate the attack.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:171">171</sup>

narrative.html: Rogelio Barragán Pérez, aged 47, was the director of the news outlet Guerrero al Instante. Before founding his own media outlet, he worked for local media including Ecos de Guerrero and Agencia Informativa Guerrero.172 RSF contacted his colleagues, who revealed that Barragán Pérez had decided to stop signing his articles for security reasons, as had other colleagues at the same outlet.173
narrative.text: Rogelio Barragán Pérez, aged 47, was the director of the news outlet Guerrero al Instante. Before founding his own media outlet, he worked for local media including Ecos de Guerrero and Agencia Informativa Guerrero. RSF contacted his colleagues, who revealed that Barragán Pérez had decided to stop signing his articles for security reasons, as had other colleagues at the same outlet.

narrative.html: According to those close to Barragán, he left Chilpancingo, Guerrero around 7:00 p.m. on July 29 to travel to Zacatepec, Morelos to visit his family.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:174">174</sup> Barragán’s family reported losing touch with him after his departure. His body was found on 30 July 2019 inside the trunk of his car at the corner of 21 de Marzo and Circunvalación streets, in the Benito Juárez neighbourhood of Zacatepec, Morelos. According to forensic authorities, the body showed bruises on the face and a lesion in the brain area, indicating he was tortured before death.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:175">175</sup> The Morelos Prosecutor’s Office opened an investigation file. The CNDH condemned the killing and demanded a thorough investigation without discarding the victim’s journalistic work as a line of inquiry.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:176">176</sup> The state government activated the protection mechanism for the journalist’s family after his death.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:177">177</sup> Based on the available evidence, no one has been arrested, charged, tried, or convicted for the killing of Barragán Pérez. As of 2 August 2019, the head of FEADLE told CPJ that his office had not opened an investigation into Barragán's murder.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:178">178</sup>
narrative.text: According to those close to Barragán, he left Chilpancingo, Guerrero around 7:00 p.m. on July 29 to travel to Zacatepec, Morelos to visit his family. Barragán’s family reported losing touch with him after his departure. His body was found on 30 July 2019 inside the trunk of his car at the corner of 21 de Marzo and Circunvalación streets, in the Benito Juárez neighbourhood of Zacatepec, Morelos. According to forensic authorities, the body showed bruises on the face and a lesion in the brain area, indicating he was tortured before death. The Morelos Prosecutor’s Office opened an investigation file. The CNDH condemned the killing and demanded a thorough investigation without discarding the victim’s journalistic work as a line of inquiry. The state government activated the protection mechanism for the journalist’s family after his death. Based on the available evidence, no one has been arrested, charged, tried, or convicted for the killing of Barragán Pérez. As of 2 August 2019, the head of FEADLE told CPJ that his office had not opened an investigation into Barragán's murder.

narrative.html: Jorge Celestino Ruíz Vázquez was a journalist in the Actopán region of Veracruz who had reported death threats after being threatened by the Actopán mayor for his reporting on corruption. In 2018, he was the victim of two recorded attacks: on 24 October, his car was beaten with bats; and on 17 November, bullets were fired into his home and car windshield.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:179">179</sup> On 24 October 2018, Ruíz Vázquez was incorporated into the Veracruz State Public Security Secretariat’s security protocol under the Specialized Prosecutor's Office for Electoral Crimes and Crimes against Freedom of Expression.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:180">180</sup> He received home protection measures, but no bodyguards.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:181">181</sup> 15 days before his murder, using Ruíz Vázquez’s boss as an  emissary, the mayor attempted to pay off the journalist for damages to his car and home with 10,000 pesos in exchange for dropping charges he had filed against the mayor, an offer he rejected. Days before his murder, he published an article pointing to an alleged embezzlement of 10 to 12 million pesos by José Paulino Domínguez Sánchez, municipal president of Actopán.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:182">182</sup>
narrative.text: Jorge Celestino Ruíz Vázquez was a journalist in the Actopán region of Veracruz who had reported death threats after being threatened by the Actopán mayor for his reporting on corruption. In 2018, he was the victim of two recorded attacks: on 24 October, his car was beaten with bats; and on 17 November, bullets were fired into his home and car windshield. On 24 October 2018, Ruíz Vázquez was incorporated into the Veracruz State Public Security Secretariat’s security protocol under the Specialized Prosecutor's Office for Electoral Crimes and Crimes against Freedom of Expression. He received home protection measures, but no bodyguards. 15 days before his murder, using Ruíz Vázquez’s boss as an  emissary, the mayor attempted to pay off the journalist for damages to his car and home with 10,000 pesos in exchange for dropping charges he had filed against the mayor, an offer he rejected. Days before his murder, he published an article pointing to an alleged embezzlement of 10 to 12 million pesos by José Paulino Domínguez Sánchez, municipal president of Actopán.

narrative.html: On 2 August 2019, Ruíz Vázquez was attacked with a firearm at approximately 9:15 p.m. in a small convenience store he owned in the town of La Bocanita.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:183">183</sup> The Veracruz Attorney General’s Office opened an investigation and announced that it would investigate why the protection measures issued in the victim’s favour were not being complied with.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:184">184</sup> On 8 November 2019, state authorities arrested Facundo “N”—the father of Florencio Barradas, the personal bodyguard of Mayor Domínguez—who allegedly carried out the killing at the mayor’s order. On 5 May 2022, Facundo “N” was sentenced to 32 years in prison. However, both Domínguez and Barradas fled while under investigation and their whereabouts remained unknown as of August 2023.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:185">185</sup>
narrative.text: On 2 August 2019, Ruíz Vázquez was attacked with a firearm at approximately 9:15 p.m. in a small convenience store he owned in the town of La Bocanita. The Veracruz Attorney General’s Office opened an investigation and announced that it would investigate why the protection measures issued in the victim’s favour were not being complied with. On 8 November 2019, state authorities arrested Facundo “N”—the father of Florencio Barradas, the personal bodyguard of Mayor Domínguez—who allegedly carried out the killing at the mayor’s order. On 5 May 2022, Facundo “N” was sentenced to 32 years in prison. However, both Domínguez and Barradas fled while under investigation and their whereabouts remained unknown as of August 2023.

narrative.html: Mitzi Yanet Torres Quintero was a television reporter for CB Televisión, a local news channel in Morelia, Michoacán, covering infrastructure issues, public services, and community affairs.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:195">195</sup> In the early morning hours of 20 August 2019, Torres Quintero was the victim of an attempted sexual assault and called 911 for help.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:196">196</sup> Three municipal police officers arrived at the scene but, according to ARTICLE 19, were persuaded by the aggressor that no assault had occurred. They detained Torres Quintero without explanation.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:197">197</sup> Once inside the patrol car, upon learning she was a journalist, the officers’ physical and verbal violence intensified: they struck her in the face and body, questioned her clothing, and told her that her professional connections would not help her.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:198">198</sup> She was detained for approximately eight hours at the municipal detention centre, where officers mocked her profession, calling her “poor little reporter.”<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:199">199</sup> The medical examiner refused to certify her visible injuries or perform a medical examination; several hours later a judge refused to acknowledge her injuries due to the lack of a medical record.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:200">200</sup> Torres Quintero was released and fined by a civic judge for disturbing the peace; having been released before the 24-hour arrest period she was also assigned community service.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:201">201</sup>
narrative.text: Mitzi Yanet Torres Quintero was a television reporter for CB Televisión, a local news channel in Morelia, Michoacán, covering infrastructure issues, public services, and community affairs. In the early morning hours of 20 August 2019, Torres Quintero was the victim of an attempted sexual assault and called 911 for help. Three municipal police officers arrived at the scene but, according to ARTICLE 19, were persuaded by the aggressor that no assault had occurred. They detained Torres Quintero without explanation. Once inside the patrol car, upon learning she was a journalist, the officers’ physical and verbal violence intensified: they struck her in the face and body, questioned her clothing, and told her that her professional connections would not help her. She was detained for approximately eight hours at the municipal detention centre, where officers mocked her profession, calling her “poor little reporter.” The medical examiner refused to certify her visible injuries or perform a medical examination; several hours later a judge refused to acknowledge her injuries due to the lack of a medical record. Torres Quintero was released and fined by a civic judge for disturbing the peace; having been released before the 24-hour arrest period she was also assigned community service.

narrative.html: The CNDH condemned the police aggressions and the conduct of the medical examiner, and requested precautionary measures to protect Torres Quintero and her family.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:202">202</sup> Three officers were suspended pending investigation, and the Michoacán state prosecutor opened an investigation.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:203">203</sup> However, a judge subsequently declined to bring charges against the three officers, concluding there were not enough elements to link the officers to the allegations of abuse and injury against Torres Quintero.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:204">204</sup> Torres Quintero further reported that following her public denunciation, municipal police officers used fake social media profiles to discredit her account, and the municipal government engaged in a campaign to delegitimize her testimony.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:205">205</sup>

narrative.html: Nevith Condés Jaramillo, aged 42, was the founder and director of El Observatorio del Sur, an online news site based in Tejupilco, Estado de México, which he founded in 2015. He had previously worked as a radio show host and reporter for the local station Radio Roca.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:206">206</sup> His journalism focused on citizen complaints, including coverage of infrastructure failures, hospital medication shortages, flood damage, police extortion, and the failure of elected officials to fulfil campaign promises.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:207">207</sup> Jaramillo also ran a citizen complaint program in Tejupilco called “De Frente al Sur.”<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:208">208</sup> He reported on stories in the Tierra Caliente region—an area encompassing communities in Estado de México, Guerrero, and Michoacán—marked by significant violence.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:209">209</sup>
narrative.text: Nevith Condés Jaramillo, aged 42, was the founder and director of El Observatorio del Sur, an online news site based in Tejupilco, Estado de México, which he founded in 2015. He had previously worked as a radio show host and reporter for the local station Radio Roca. His journalism focused on citizen complaints, including coverage of infrastructure failures, hospital medication shortages, flood damage, police extortion, and the failure of elected officials to fulfil campaign promises. Jaramillo also ran a citizen complaint program in Tejupilco called “De Frente al Sur.” He reported on stories in the Tierra Caliente region—an area encompassing communities in Estado de México, Guerrero, and Michoacán—marked by significant violence.

narrative.html: Condés Jaramillo had reported receiving threats on several occasions, including from municipal government officials in Tejupilco. In May 2018, he publicly denounced on video that he had received threats from the then-municipal president, Anthony Domínguez Vargas, stating that since 2017 individuals associated with Domínguez had warned him to cease his reporting or face consequences.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:210">210</sup> In June 2019, he received further threats after breaking the news that a helicopter crash near Sultepec had been caused by gunmen shooting the pilot,<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:211">211</sup> which state authorities initially denied and later confirmed.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:212">212</sup> The federal Mechanism attempted to enroll him in a protection scheme in January 2018 and again in June 2019 after receiving requests from ARTICLE 19,<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:213">213</sup> but he ultimately declined protection, allegedly due to the onerous bureaucratic procedures and travel involved.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:214">214</sup> Jaramillo did make several reports to the Mechanism after receiving threats from municipal government officials in Tejupilco.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:215">215</sup> Two days before his death, he communicated via WhatsApp that he continued to receive threats from the family of the municipal president.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:216">216</sup>
narrative.text: Condés Jaramillo had reported receiving threats on several occasions, including from municipal government officials in Tejupilco. In May 2018, he publicly denounced on video that he had received threats from the then-municipal president, Anthony Domínguez Vargas, stating that since 2017 individuals associated with Domínguez had warned him to cease his reporting or face consequences. In June 2019, he received further threats after breaking the news that a helicopter crash near Sultepec had been caused by gunmen shooting the pilot, which state authorities initially denied and later confirmed. The federal Mechanism attempted to enroll him in a protection scheme in January 2018 and again in June 2019 after receiving requests from ARTICLE 19, but he ultimately declined protection, allegedly due to the onerous bureaucratic procedures and travel involved. Jaramillo did make several reports to the Mechanism after receiving threats from municipal government officials in Tejupilco. Two days before his death, he communicated via WhatsApp that he continued to receive threats from the family of the municipal president.

narrative.html: On 24 August 2019, his body was found in Cerro de Cacalotepec, Tejupilco, bearing multiple stab wounds—with one report indicating as many as 100 stab wounds.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:217">217</sup> His last broadcast for El Observatorio del Sur had been the previous evening.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:218">218</sup> The FGJEM opened an investigation with three lines of inquiry: two related to his journalistic activity and one of a personal nature. ONU-DH condemned the killing and called for a diligent and impartial investigation. UNESCO’s Director-General also condemned the murder. CNDH called for Jaramillo’s family to be assigned protection, and recommended an investigation of his murder in relation to his work as a journalist.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:219">219</sup> In August 2021, journalists in Estado de México protested outside the FGJEM demanding justice.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:220">220</sup> As of August 2025—more than six years after the killing—the FGJEM and FEADLE had not identified any suspects, nor progressed in the investigation.
narrative.text: On 24 August 2019, his body was found in Cerro de Cacalotepec, Tejupilco, bearing multiple stab wounds—with one report indicating as many as 100 stab wounds. His last broadcast for El Observatorio del Sur had been the previous evening. The FGJEM opened an investigation with three lines of inquiry: two related to his journalistic activity and one of a personal nature. ONU-DH condemned the killing and called for a diligent and impartial investigation. UNESCO’s Director-General also condemned the murder. CNDH called for Jaramillo’s family to be assigned protection, and recommended an investigation of his murder in relation to his work as a journalist. In August 2021, journalists in Estado de México protested outside the FGJEM demanding justice. As of August 2025—more than six years after the killing—the FGJEM and FEADLE had not identified any suspects, nor progressed in the investigation.

narrative.html: Paúl Velázquez Benítez was an independent activist and citizen journalist based in Los Mochis, Ahome Municipality, Sinaloa. He operated a YouTube channel and Facebook page titled Ni un corrupto más (“Not one more corrupt official”), through which he published videos criticising local officials and denouncing alleged corruption, particularly in the Ahome municipal government.221 On 2 April 2019, he attended President López Obrador’s morning press conference and publicly accused the mayor of Ahome, Manuel Guillermo Chapman Moreno, of corruption, including an alleged network of false-invoice companies linked to the tax authority.222
narrative.text: Paúl Velázquez Benítez was an independent activist and citizen journalist based in Los Mochis, Ahome Municipality, Sinaloa. He operated a YouTube channel and Facebook page titled Ni un corrupto más (“Not one more corrupt official”), through which he published videos criticising local officials and denouncing alleged corruption, particularly in the Ahome municipal government. On 2 April 2019, he attended President López Obrador’s morning press conference and publicly accused the mayor of Ahome, Manuel Guillermo Chapman Moreno, of corruption, including an alleged network of false-invoice companies linked to the tax authority.

narrative.html: On 18 December 2019, a day before the attack, during a municipal event at which Mayor Chapman offered a court-ordered public apology for committing gender-based political violence against the city attorney,<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:223">223</sup> event attendees called for Velázquez Benítez’s lynching, and a municipal official reportedly told another journalist that “the next one is Paul.”<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:224">224</sup> Velázquez Benítez stated that Mayor Chapman was present and permitted these comments. Additionally, the síndica de la Central, Irma Delgado, reportedly called on her supporters to attack him at the end of the session.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:225">225</sup>
narrative.text: On 18 December 2019, a day before the attack, during a municipal event at which Mayor Chapman offered a court-ordered public apology for committing gender-based political violence against the city attorney, event attendees called for Velázquez Benítez’s lynching, and a municipal official reportedly told another journalist that “the next one is Paul.” Velázquez Benítez stated that Mayor Chapman was present and permitted these comments. Additionally, the síndica de la Central, Irma Delgado, reportedly called on her supporters to attack him at the end of the session.

narrative.html: On the evening of 19 December 2019, Velázquez Benítez was shot while in a pharmacy parking lot in central Los Mochis. Security camera footage<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:226">226</sup> showed an individual exiting a vehicle, approaching him, and firing at close range toward his head; the bullet struck his neck and mandible area. He survived and re-entered the pharmacy to request help.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:227">227</sup> The bullet exited through one side of his face, and he required multiple surgeries, including maxillofacial reconstruction.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:228">228</sup>
narrative.text: On the evening of 19 December 2019, Velázquez Benítez was shot while in a pharmacy parking lot in central Los Mochis. Security camera footage showed an individual exiting a vehicle, approaching him, and firing at close range toward his head; the bullet struck his neck and mandible area. He survived and re-entered the pharmacy to request help. The bullet exited through one side of his face, and he required multiple surgeries, including maxillofacial reconstruction.

narrative.html: Cristian Pérez Ojeda, also known as Cris Percovich, was the head of the Facebook social media pages Sin Censura Noticias, Inspector Choyero, and La Vox de Los Cabos. He was known for his reporting on corruption and financial mismanagement of the Los Cabos city council, in Baja California Sur.235 In September 2019, Pérez was fired from his job at the social communication directorate of the council without reason. He filed a labor lawsuit for unfair dismissal.236
narrative.text: Cristian Pérez Ojeda, also known as Cris Percovich, was the head of the Facebook social media pages Sin Censura Noticias, Inspector Choyero, and La Vox de Los Cabos. He was known for his reporting on corruption and financial mismanagement of the Los Cabos city council, in Baja California Sur. In September 2019, Pérez was fired from his job at the social communication directorate of the council without reason. He filed a labor lawsuit for unfair dismissal.

narrative.html: On 7 January 2020, Pérez received a text message from Héctor Miranda Burgueño, director of social communication for the Los Cabos city council, reading: “Come on! Tone it down a bit in your posts – the boss is already fed up, and I recommend you don't get on her bad side. I’m warning you."<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:237">237</sup>
narrative.text: On 7 January 2020, Pérez received a text message from Héctor Miranda Burgueño, director of social communication for the Los Cabos city council, reading: “Come on! Tone it down a bit in your posts – the boss is already fed up, and I recommend you don't get on her bad side. I’m warning you."

narrative.html: At around 8:15 p.m. on 29 February 2020, Pérez accompanied his wife to close a family business in San José del Cabo. He noticed a light-colored Ford Escape SUV parked close by, and asked his wife to close the business while he walked away from the store to avoid putting her at risk.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:238">238</sup> Two hooded men carrying long guns forced him into the vehicle and drove toward the nearby town of Santa Anita. Once the car was stopped on the outskirts of the town, Pérez was brutally beaten, reporting that his attackers told him "to stop messing around and stop publishing articles," and that they repeatedly told him they were going to kill him for not toning down his articles.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:239">239</sup> Pérez Ojeda ran away from his attackers when they returned to the car to retrieve what he believed to be a knife.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:240">240</sup> He was able to make it to a housing development and get a ride back to San José del Cabo, after which time he went to a hospital. Pérez Ojeda later alleged that he was tricked into signing an initial report of events by local police at the hospital that minimized his attack.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:241">241</sup>
narrative.text: At around 8:15 p.m. on 29 February 2020, Pérez accompanied his wife to close a family business in San José del Cabo. He noticed a light-colored Ford Escape SUV parked close by, and asked his wife to close the business while he walked away from the store to avoid putting her at risk. Two hooded men carrying long guns forced him into the vehicle and drove toward the nearby town of Santa Anita. Once the car was stopped on the outskirts of the town, Pérez was brutally beaten, reporting that his attackers told him "to stop messing around and stop publishing articles," and that they repeatedly told him they were going to kill him for not toning down his articles. Pérez Ojeda ran away from his attackers when they returned to the car to retrieve what he believed to be a knife. He was able to make it to a housing development and get a ride back to San José del Cabo, after which time he went to a hospital. Pérez Ojeda later alleged that he was tricked into signing an initial report of events by local police at the hospital that minimized his attack.

narrative.html: Pérez Ojeda blamed the attack on the mayor of Los Cabos, Armida Castro, a member of the Morena party, and other officials in her administration, including the director of Social Communication, Héctor Manuel Miranda Burgueño, and the director of public safety, Captain Juan José Zamorano. The council denies any orchestration of the attack on Pérez Ojeda.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:242">242</sup>

The council denies any orchestration of the attack on Pérez Ojeda.

incidents.heading: María Elena Ferral Hernández – Killed, 30 March 2020, Veracruz
incidents.place: central Papantla
incidents.identity: María Elena Ferral Hernández was a veteran journalist with 30 years of professional experience, based in Veracruz.

persons.name: María Elena Ferral Hernández

narrative.html: María Elena Ferral Hernández was a veteran journalist with 30 years of professional experience, based in Veracruz.244 She served as a correspondent for the regional newspapers Diario de Xalapa and El Heraldo de Poza Rica, and was the founder and director of the digital outlet Quinto Poder de Veracruz.245 Her reporting focused on enforced disappearances, corruption, and abuses of authority in the region, including cases in which local police were implicated.246
narrative.text: María Elena Ferral Hernández was a veteran journalist with 30 years of professional experience, based in Veracruz. She served as a correspondent for the regional newspapers Diario de Xalapa and El Heraldo de Poza Rica, and was the founder and director of the digital outlet Quinto Poder de Veracruz. Her reporting focused on enforced disappearances, corruption, and abuses of authority in the region, including cases in which local police were implicated.

narrative.html: Ferral’s investigative work placed her in direct conflict with powerful local actors, and she experienced a prolonged pattern of threats and intimidation directly linked to her journalism.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:247">247</sup> In her journalism, she documented the operations of a political network she termed the “Totonacapan Group,” which she identified as being led by the politician Basilio Camerino Picazo.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:248">248</sup>
narrative.text: Ferral’s investigative work placed her in direct conflict with powerful local actors, and she experienced a prolonged pattern of threats and intimidation directly linked to her journalism. In her journalism, she documented the operations of a political network she termed the “Totonacapan Group,” which she identified as being led by the politician Basilio Camerino Picazo.

narrative.html: On 29 March 2016, she reported to authorities a threat by Picazo, who she stated told her he had already “let her live for too long.”249 Following that threat, the Comisión Estatal para la Atención y Protección a Periodistas (State Commission for the Care and Protection of Journalists, “CEAPP”) assigned her protective measures, including a bodyguard and a GPS device.250 However, the Veracruz secretary for public security unilaterally withdrew the protection in 2017, without consulting the CEAPP, on the stated ground that Ferral was not making good use of it.251
narrative.text: On 29 March 2016, she reported to authorities a threat by Picazo, who she stated told her he had already “let her live for too long.” Following that threat, the Comisión Estatal para la Atención y Protección a Periodistas (State Commission for the Care and Protection of Journalists, “CEAPP”) assigned her protective measures, including a bodyguard and a GPS device. However, the Veracruz secretary for public security unilaterally withdrew the protection in 2017, without consulting the CEAPP, on the stated ground that Ferral was not making good use of it.

narrative.html: On 30 March 2020, at approximately 2:00 PM, Ferral was leaving a notary office in central Papantla after a meeting with her lawyer when two unidentified men on a motorcycle opened fire on her.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:252">252</sup> According to an anonymous witness account reported by ARTICLE 19, the assailants had been waiting near her car. Ferral suffered eight gunshot wounds, several of which perforated her liver and lung.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:253">253</sup> She was transferred to a hospital and died hours later.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:254">254</sup>
narrative.text: On 30 March 2020, at approximately 2:00 PM, Ferral was leaving a notary office in central Papantla after a meeting with her lawyer when two unidentified men on a motorcycle opened fire on her. According to an anonymous witness account reported by ARTICLE 19, the assailants had been waiting near her car. Ferral suffered eight gunshot wounds, several of which perforated her liver and lung. She was transferred to a hospital and died hours later.

narrative.html: Veracruz judicial authorities detained several individuals and acknowledged that the murder was directly linked to Ferral’s journalistic work.255 The Veracruz State Attorney General’s Office obtained 30-year prison sentences against three individuals—Carlos “N,” Alfredo “N,” and Othoniel “N”—for the homicide.256 A fourth individual, Nicasio “N,” was sentenced to 30 years a few weeks later.257 A fifth individual, José “N,”—identified by the president in a press conference as a crime reporter himself—received a 15-year sentence, and a sixth, Luis Alfonso “N,” was sentenced to 20 years.258 Critically, despite the Veracruz government’s public allegation that former local deputy Picazo was the intellectual author of the killing, he had not been detained as of this writing.259 The attack on Ferral was followed by a further assassination attempt: on 24 May 2020, unknown individuals fired upon Ferral’s daughter, María Fernanda De Luna Ferral—who had assumed directorship of Quinto Poder—while she was travelling with state-provided escorts in Gutiérrez Zamora, Veracruz.260 Fernanda was given protection under the Veracruz Public Security Secretariat (SSP) following the attack, and was enrolled in the federal Mechanism in 2020.261 Her protection under SSP was revoked on 20 February 2026, without a stated reason.262 On 28 February 2024, a civil judge ordered the release of one of the alleged perpetrators of Ferral’s murder not yet sentenced.263 A year later on 28 August 2025, a second alleged perpetrator was released under an injunction arguing the lack of evidence against him.264
narrative.text: Veracruz judicial authorities detained several individuals and acknowledged that the murder was directly linked to Ferral’s journalistic work. The Veracruz State Attorney General’s Office obtained 30-year prison sentences against three individuals—Carlos “N,” Alfredo “N,” and Othoniel “N”—for the homicide. A fourth individual, Nicasio “N,” was sentenced to 30 years a few weeks later. A fifth individual, José “N,”—identified by the president in a press conference as a crime reporter himself—received a 15-year sentence, and a sixth, Luis Alfonso “N,” was sentenced to 20 years. Critically, despite the Veracruz government’s public allegation that former local deputy Picazo was the intellectual author of the killing, he had not been detained as of this writing. The attack on Ferral was followed by a further assassination attempt: on 24 May 2020, unknown individuals fired upon Ferral’s daughter, María Fernanda De Luna Ferral—who had assumed directorship of Quinto Poder—while she was travelling with state-provided escorts in Gutiérrez Zamora, Veracruz. Fernanda was given protection under the Veracruz Public Security Secretariat (SSP) following the attack, and was enrolled in the federal Mechanism in 2020. Her protection under SSP was revoked on 20 February 2026, without a stated reason. On 28 February 2024, a civil judge ordered the release of one of the alleged perpetrators of Ferral’s murder not yet sentenced. A year later on 28 August 2025, a second alleged perpetrator was released under an injunction arguing the lack of evidence against him.

narrative.html: Armenta had been enrolled in the federal Protection Mechanism since 2016, following the onset of threats against him.269 His protection measures were reinforced following a 2019 risk assessment.270 A crime reporter at El Tiempo told CPJ that Armenta and members of his editorial staff had received numerous threats in recent years from criminal organizations angered by the outlet’s reporting on killings in Ciudad Obregón.271
narrative.text: Armenta had been enrolled in the federal Protection Mechanism since 2016, following the onset of threats against him. His protection measures were reinforced following a 2019 risk assessment. A crime reporter at El Tiempo told CPJ that Armenta and members of his editorial staff had received numerous threats in recent years from criminal organizations angered by the outlet’s reporting on killings in Ciudad Obregón.

narrative.html: On the afternoon of 16 May 2020, at approximately 3:30 PM, unidentified armed men opened fire on Armenta and two Cajeme municipal police officers serving as his bodyguards under the mechanism as they left a restaurant on Calle Chihuahua in Colonia Centro, Ciudad Obregón.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:272">272</sup> Armenta and one bodyguard, Orlando Antonio Ruvalcaba Flores, died during transport to the Hospital General de Cajeme. A second officer, Cruz Rafael “N,” was injured.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:273">273</sup> The Sonora Attorney General stated that no line of investigation would be ruled out, and investigators recovered spent casings indicating the use of multiple weapons of different calibres.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:274">274</sup>
narrative.text: On the afternoon of 16 May 2020, at approximately 3:30 PM, unidentified armed men opened fire on Armenta and two Cajeme municipal police officers serving as his bodyguards under the mechanism as they left a restaurant on Calle Chihuahua in Colonia Centro, Ciudad Obregón. Armenta and one bodyguard, Orlando Antonio Ruvalcaba Flores, died during transport to the Hospital General de Cajeme. A second officer, Cruz Rafael “N,” was injured. The Sonora Attorney General stated that no line of investigation would be ruled out, and investigators recovered spent casings indicating the use of multiple weapons of different calibres.

narrative.html: The killing was condemned by the CNDH, ONU-DH, and a joint statement of the EU delegation in Mexico together with Norway and Switzerland, which noted that Armenta was under the protection of the federal mechanism at the time of the attack and urged an expeditious and transparent investigation.275 As of September 2025—more than five years after the killing—Medios Obson published a column noting that 1,953 days had passed and describing the case as remaining in total impunity. No arrests, charges, or convictions have been publicly reported.276
