narrative.html: Marco Antonio Duarte Vargas is the founder and editor of the online news outlet Ciudad Obregón Sin Censura, which publishes on Facebook and focuses on corruption and abuses by local authorities in Cajeme, Sonora.277 Duarte Vargas had experienced a sustained campaign of intimidation prior to the attack. In August 2019, he received death threats from Ascensión López Durán, a Cajeme municipal official, in connection with his reporting.278 In October 2019, unknown individuals stole cameras and computers from his home and poisoned one of his dogs.279 In December 2019, two individuals threatened him with shooting, after which another of his dogs was found dead.280 He took down a separate news website following these threats.281 Duarte Vargas had been in contact with the federal Protection Mechanism to seek enrollment, but protection had not materialised as of May 2020.282
narrative.text: Marco Antonio Duarte Vargas is the founder and editor of the online news outlet Ciudad Obregón Sin Censura, which publishes on Facebook and focuses on corruption and abuses by local authorities in Cajeme, Sonora. Duarte Vargas had experienced a sustained campaign of intimidation prior to the attack. In August 2019, he received death threats from Ascensión López Durán, a Cajeme municipal official, in connection with his reporting. In October 2019, unknown individuals stole cameras and computers from his home and poisoned one of his dogs. In December 2019, two individuals threatened him with shooting, after which another of his dogs was found dead. He took down a separate news website following these threats. Duarte Vargas had been in contact with the federal Protection Mechanism to seek enrollment, but protection had not materialised as of May 2020.

narrative.html: On 27 May 2020, at approximately 11:30 PM, unknown assailants used a Molotov cocktail to set fire to Duarte Vargas’s car while it was parked in the garage of his residence; he and his family were inside the home at the time.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:283">283</sup> The Sonora state prosecutor’s office opened an investigation. Duarte Vargas noted that the Sonora State Public Security Secretariat assigned patrols to his home as a security measure in consequence to the attack, but that they ceased by June 2.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:284">284</sup> In a further act of apparent retaliation, Duarte Vargas and a colleague, Miguel Valdez Miranda, were detained on 30 June 2020 on fabricated extortion charges.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:285">285</sup> They were imprisoned for eleven months and twelve days before a judge ruled on 12 July 2021 that there was no evidence for the alleged extortion and absolved them.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:286">286</sup> On 28 April 2023, a federal judge ordered two Sonora state prosecutors, Roberto Quintanar Rivas and Carlos Andrés Jaime López, to issue a public apology to Duarte Vargas and Valdez Miranda for impeding their communication with family and counsel during detention.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:287">287</sup>
narrative.text: On 27 May 2020, at approximately 11:30 PM, unknown assailants used a Molotov cocktail to set fire to Duarte Vargas’s car while it was parked in the garage of his residence; he and his family were inside the home at the time. The Sonora state prosecutor’s office opened an investigation. Duarte Vargas noted that the Sonora State Public Security Secretariat assigned patrols to his home as a security measure in consequence to the attack, but that they ceased by June 2. In a further act of apparent retaliation, Duarte Vargas and a colleague, Miguel Valdez Miranda, were detained on 30 June 2020 on fabricated extortion charges. They were imprisoned for eleven months and twelve days before a judge ruled on 12 July 2021 that there was no evidence for the alleged extortion and absolved them. On 28 April 2023, a federal judge ordered two Sonora state prosecutors, Roberto Quintanar Rivas and Carlos Andrés Jaime López, to issue a public apology to Duarte Vargas and Valdez Miranda for impeding their communication with family and counsel during detention.

narrative.html: Pablo Morrugares Parraguirre, aged 48, was the founder and editor of PM Noticias, a digital news outlet covering politics, security, and crime in Iguala, Guerrero.288 Before founding PM Noticias, Morrugares had worked as a spokesperson for the Iguala municipal government during the mayoral administration of José Luis Abarca, who was arrested on 4 November 2014 for his alleged involvement in the mass abduction and suspected assassination of 43 students from the Escuela Normal Rural de Ayotzinapa on 26 September 2014.289 In August 2022, the Comisión para la Verdad y Acceso a la Justicia del Caso Ayotzinapa (CoVAJ) identified Morrugares as one of 26 key individuals killed in the preceding eight years who had possessed information about the 2014 mass disappearance.290
narrative.text: Pablo Morrugares Parraguirre, aged 48, was the founder and editor of PM Noticias, a digital news outlet covering politics, security, and crime in Iguala, Guerrero. Before founding PM Noticias, Morrugares had worked as a spokesperson for the Iguala municipal government during the mayoral administration of José Luis Abarca, who was arrested on 4 November 2014 for his alleged involvement in the mass abduction and suspected assassination of 43 students from the Escuela Normal Rural de Ayotzinapa on 26 September 2014. In August 2022, the Comisión para la Verdad y Acceso a la Justicia del Caso Ayotzinapa (CoVAJ) identified Morrugares as one of 26 key individuals killed in the preceding eight years who had possessed information about the 2014 mass disappearance.

narrative.html: Morrugares had been enrolled in the federal Protection Mechanism since 2015. On 7 April 2016, he and his wife survived an armed attack by unidentified gunmen in Iguala.291 Following that attack, the Mechanism relocated him to a safe house at an undisclosed location in 2018, where he remained under federal protection until the end of 2019.292 He returned to Iguala at his own request in January 2020 and was assigned two state police officers as bodyguards.293 In the months before the killing, Morrugares was threatened in a Facebook video allegedly posted by a criminal gang active in the Iguala area, and on a narcomanta—a banner used by criminal groups to convey messages—that also named other local reporters.294
narrative.text: Morrugares had been enrolled in the federal Protection Mechanism since 2015. On 7 April 2016, he and his wife survived an armed attack by unidentified gunmen in Iguala. Following that attack, the Mechanism relocated him to a safe house at an undisclosed location in 2018, where he remained under federal protection until the end of 2019. He returned to Iguala at his own request in January 2020 and was assigned two state police officers as bodyguards. In the months before the killing, Morrugares was threatened in a Facebook video allegedly posted by a criminal gang active in the Iguala area, and on a narcomanta—a banner used by criminal groups to convey messages—that also named other local reporters.

narrative.html: Just before 1:00 AM on 2 August 2020, Morrugares opened the PM Noticias Facebook page and began a live broadcast from “Búfalos,” the restaurant he owned in central Iguala, discussing violence attributed to the criminal group Los Tlacos in nearby Huitzuco.295 Recently, Morrugares had published a piece on the detention of two suspects in a homicide case, and another on an ambush on police forces by organized crime.296 Minutes after the broadcast ended, occupants of a vehicle arrived at the establishment and opened fire. Investigators recovered 55 shell casings of .223 calibre from AR-15 assault rifles.297 Two heavily armed men entered the restaurant and killed Morrugares instantly. State police officer Roberto Hernández, assigned as Morrugares’s bodyguard through the Mechanism, was also killed.298
narrative.text: Just before 1:00 AM on 2 August 2020, Morrugares opened the PM Noticias Facebook page and began a live broadcast from “Búfalos,” the restaurant he owned in central Iguala, discussing violence attributed to the criminal group Los Tlacos in nearby Huitzuco. Recently, Morrugares had published a piece on the detention of two suspects in a homicide case, and another on an ambush on police forces by organized crime. Minutes after the broadcast ended, occupants of a vehicle arrived at the establishment and opened fire. Investigators recovered 55 shell casings of .223 calibre from AR-15 assault rifles. Two heavily armed men entered the restaurant and killed Morrugares instantly. State police officer Roberto Hernández, assigned as Morrugares’s bodyguard through the Mechanism, was also killed.

narrative.html: The ONU-DH condemned the killing and called for investigation in accordance with international due diligence standards.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:299">299</sup> On approximately 7 August 2020, the Guerrero state Fiscalía arrested eight suspects in a safe house near Iguala; a burned vehicle suspected to have been used in the attack was also recovered.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:300">300</sup> One detainee was linked to the homicide through ballistic comparison.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:301">301</sup> Following Morrugares’s killing, local journalists in Iguala were added to a WhatsApp group by individuals believed to be gang members, who issued a barrage of threats.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:302">302</sup> At least four reporters subsequently fled the city, and the newspaper La Tarde ceased its print edition.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:303">303</sup> The community of reporters covering organised crime in Iguala—estimated at approximately 15—dwindled significantly.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:304">304</sup> No conviction has been publicly reported as of the research date.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:305">305</sup>
narrative.text: The ONU-DH condemned the killing and called for investigation in accordance with international due diligence standards. On approximately 7 August 2020, the Guerrero state Fiscalía arrested eight suspects in a safe house near Iguala; a burned vehicle suspected to have been used in the attack was also recovered. One detainee was linked to the homicide through ballistic comparison. Following Morrugares’s killing, local journalists in Iguala were added to a WhatsApp group by individuals believed to be gang members, who issued a barrage of threats. At least four reporters subsequently fled the city, and the newspaper La Tarde ceased its print edition. The community of reporters covering organised crime in Iguala—estimated at approximately 15—dwindled significantly. No conviction has been publicly reported as of the research date.

location.quote: Two heavily armed men entered the restaurant and killed Morrugares instantly.

quotes: In the months before the killing, Morrugares was threatened in a Facebook video allegedly posted by a criminal gang active in the Iguala area, and on a narcomanta—a banner used by criminal groups to convey messages—that also named other local reporters.
Morrugares had been enrolled in the federal Protection Mechanism since 2015
Following that attack, the Mechanism relocated him to a safe house at an undisclosed location in 2018, where he remained under federal protection until the end of 2019.
He returned to Iguala at his own request in January 2020 and was assigned two state police officers as bodyguards.
State police officer Roberto Hernández, assigned as Morrugares’s bodyguard through the Mechanism, was also killed.

status.quote: On approximately 7 August 2020, the Guerrero state Fiscalía arrested eight suspects in a safe house near Iguala; a burned vehicle suspected to have been used in the attack was also recovered.

narrative.html: Juan Nelcio Espinoza Menera was an independent journalist and the creator of the digital outlet El Valedor TV, based in the border city of Piedras Negras, Coahuila. He operated his outlet primarily through a Facebook page, publishing news and live broadcasts covering local events, violence, and public security.306 ONU-DH noted that the journalist’s family had alleged prior aggressions or threats by police agents linked to his journalistic activity.307
narrative.text: Juan Nelcio Espinoza Menera was an independent journalist and the creator of the digital outlet El Valedor TV, based in the border city of Piedras Negras, Coahuila. He operated his outlet primarily through a Facebook page, publishing news and live broadcasts covering local events, violence, and public security. ONU-DH noted that the journalist’s family had alleged prior aggressions or threats by police agents linked to his journalistic activity.

narrative.html: On the evening of 20 August 2020, following an attack on state police in Piedras Negras that triggered a major security mobilisation, Espinoza Menera and fellow journalist Néstor Guerra were conducting a live broadcast covering the violent incidents.308 In the early hours of 21 August, the two journalists were detained by state police at a checkpoint on Bulevar Mar de Cortés.309 Authorities claimed the journalists had verbally and physically confronted officers and were allegedly intoxicated.310 The Coahuila state prosecutor, Gerardo Márquez, initially stated that Espinoza Menera’s death was caused by broncoaspiración (obstruction of airways) and characterised it as a natural cause.311 However, medical personnel at Hospital General Doctor Salvador Chavarría reported that Espinoza Menera’s body bore signs of torture and a knife wound to the throat, and that he had been brought to the facility in two unmarked vehicles by Fiscalía General del Estado agents.312 Néstor Guerra, detained simultaneously, was subsequently released.313
narrative.text: On the evening of 20 August 2020, following an attack on state police in Piedras Negras that triggered a major security mobilisation, Espinoza Menera and fellow journalist Néstor Guerra were conducting a live broadcast covering the violent incidents. In the early hours of 21 August, the two journalists were detained by state police at a checkpoint on Bulevar Mar de Cortés. Authorities claimed the journalists had verbally and physically confronted officers and were allegedly intoxicated. The Coahuila state prosecutor, Gerardo Márquez, initially stated that Espinoza Menera’s death was caused by broncoaspiración (obstruction of airways) and characterised it as a natural cause. However, medical personnel at Hospital General Doctor Salvador Chavarría reported that Espinoza Menera’s body bore signs of torture and a knife wound to the throat, and that he had been brought to the facility in two unmarked vehicles by Fiscalía General del Estado agents. Néstor Guerra, detained simultaneously, was subsequently released.

narrative.html: ONU-DH called on authorities to investigate in accordance with the Minnesota Protocol on the Investigation of Potentially Unlawful Death.314 The CNDH issued an acuerdo de atracción (attraction agreement) to investigate possible human rights violations.315 Espinoza Menera’s mother filed a complaint with the FGR on 26 August 2020; on 31 August 2020, FGR forensic personnel exhumed the body and conducted an autopsy under the Minnesota Protocol.316 On 2 November 2021, ARTICLE 19 announced it had obtained evidence confirming that Espinoza Menera was tortured, presumably by state authorities, and formally added him to its list of journalists killed in connection with their work.317 In April 2022, the FGR determined that Espinoza Menera was the victim of torture and homicidio calificado (aggravated homicide) perpetrated by police officers of Piedras Negras, and that the killing was carried out with the purpose of punishing the exercise of journalism and freedom of expression.318 Arrest warrants were obtained against the material perpetrators. The FGR also obtained the vinculación a Proceso (formal charging) of the former coordinator of Servicios Periciales of the Coahuila state Fiscalía for cover-up of torture, issuance of false forensic reports, document alteration, and concealment of evidence—having manipulated autopsy records to simulate that Espinoza Menera died of respiratory problems upon arrival at the hospital.319
narrative.text: ONU-DH called on authorities to investigate in accordance with the Minnesota Protocol on the Investigation of Potentially Unlawful Death. The CNDH issued an acuerdo de atracción (attraction agreement) to investigate possible human rights violations. Espinoza Menera’s mother filed a complaint with the FGR on 26 August 2020; on 31 August 2020, FGR forensic personnel exhumed the body and conducted an autopsy under the Minnesota Protocol. On 2 November 2021, ARTICLE 19 announced it had obtained evidence confirming that Espinoza Menera was tortured, presumably by state authorities, and formally added him to its list of journalists killed in connection with their work. In April 2022, the FGR determined that Espinoza Menera was the victim of torture and homicidio calificado (aggravated homicide) perpetrated by police officers of Piedras Negras, and that the killing was carried out with the purpose of punishing the exercise of journalism and freedom of expression. Arrest warrants were obtained against the material perpetrators. The FGR also obtained the vinculación a Proceso (formal charging) of the former coordinator of Servicios Periciales of the Coahuila state Fiscalía for cover-up of torture, issuance of false forensic reports, document alteration, and concealment of evidence—having manipulated autopsy records to simulate that Espinoza Menera died of respiratory problems upon arrival at the hospital.

incidents.title: Julio Valdivia Rodríguez
incidents.heading: Julio Valdivia Rodríguez – Killed, 9 September 2020, Veracruz
incidents.place: the train tracks in the locality of Motzorongo, roughly eight kilometres from Tezonapa
incidents.identity: Julio Valdivia Rodríguez, aged 41, was a correspondent for the daily newspaper El Mundo de Córdoba, based in the municipality of Tezonapa, Veracruz.

persons.name: Julio Valdivia Rodríguez
persons.roleStated: Julio Valdivia Rodríguez, aged 41, was a correspondent for the daily newspaper El Mundo de Córdoba, based in the municipality of Tezonapa, Veracruz.
persons.outcomeQuote: His body was discovered at approximately 2:30 PM, decapitated, on the train tracks in the locality of Motzorongo, roughly eight kilometres from Tezonapa.

narrative.html: Julio Valdivia Rodríguez, aged 41, was a correspondent for the daily newspaper El Mundo de Córdoba, based in the municipality of Tezonapa, Veracruz.320 He had worked for El Mundo since 2014, covering a broad range of issues, though his most recent reporting focused heavily on crime and security.321 Colleagues described him as dedicated, covering stories at any hour; when his income from journalism was insufficient, he supplemented it by working as a bricklayer or selling tamales.322
narrative.text: Julio Valdivia Rodríguez, aged 41, was a correspondent for the daily newspaper El Mundo de Córdoba, based in the municipality of Tezonapa, Veracruz. He had worked for El Mundo since 2014, covering a broad range of issues, though his most recent reporting focused heavily on crime and security. Colleagues described him as dedicated, covering stories at any hour; when his income from journalism was insufficient, he supplemented it by working as a bricklayer or selling tamales.

narrative.html: In 2015, Valdivia received protective measures from the State Commission for the Attention and Protection of Journalists (CEAPP) following the killing of his colleague Armando Saldaña Morales, also from Tezonapa.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:323">323</sup> However, the measures were subsequently withdrawn.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:324">324</sup> Although the CEAPP stated Valdivia had not reported any threats, colleagues told Animal Político that he had informed them on various occasions about threats he had received due to his journalistic work.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:325">325</sup> A colleague told the press that Valdivia had recounted being kidnapped and intimidated on multiple occasions because of his crime reporting, but continued because of his passion for journalism.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:326">326</sup>
narrative.text: In 2015, Valdivia received protective measures from the State Commission for the Attention and Protection of Journalists (CEAPP) following the killing of his colleague Armando Saldaña Morales, also from Tezonapa. However, the measures were subsequently withdrawn. Although the CEAPP stated Valdivia had not reported any threats, colleagues told Animal Político that he had informed them on various occasions about threats he had received due to his journalistic work. A colleague told the press that Valdivia had recounted being kidnapped and intimidated on multiple occasions because of his crime reporting, but continued because of his passion for journalism.

narrative.html: On 9 September 2020, Valdivia told a colleague he was leaving his residence on the newspaper-provided motorcycle to report on a story. His last published report, dated 7–8 September 2020, covered a shootout involving police and a criminal group in Oaxaca.327 His body was discovered at approximately 2:30 PM, decapitated, on the train tracks in the locality of Motzorongo, roughly eight kilometres from Tezonapa.328 His motorcycle, bearing the El Mundo logo, was found nearby.329 The body showed signs of torture.330 Forensic analysis indicated that Valdivia had been killed elsewhere and his body subsequently transported to the train tracks, where his motorcycle was also placed.331 Indeed, the Veracruz state attorney’s office initially stated that the death would be ruled an accident, but reversed course after forensic experts ruled out that possibility, stating that it would investigate the killing as a homicide, with the victim’s journalism as a line of inquiry.332
narrative.text: On 9 September 2020, Valdivia told a colleague he was leaving his residence on the newspaper-provided motorcycle to report on a story. His last published report, dated 7–8 September 2020, covered a shootout involving police and a criminal group in Oaxaca. His body was discovered at approximately 2:30 PM, decapitated, on the train tracks in the locality of Motzorongo, roughly eight kilometres from Tezonapa. His motorcycle, bearing the El Mundo logo, was found nearby. The body showed signs of torture. Forensic analysis indicated that Valdivia had been killed elsewhere and his body subsequently transported to the train tracks, where his motorcycle was also placed. Indeed, the Veracruz state attorney’s office initially stated that the death would be ruled an accident, but reversed course after forensic experts ruled out that possibility, stating that it would investigate the killing as a homicide, with the victim’s journalism as a line of inquiry.

narrative.html: ONU-DH, the UN Secretary-General, UNESCO, and RSF all condemned the killing. According to Mexico News Daily, Valdivia was the 25th journalist killed in Veracruz since 2010 and the third during the administration of Governor Cuitláhuac García Jiménez.333 On 31 March 2022—eighteen months after the killing—a multi-agency operation arrested Gustavo Abigaíl Díaz (“El Pino”), identified as a leader of the CJNG in the Veracruz–Oaxaca border region.334 On approximately 7 April 2022, the Veracruz Fiscalía obtained a vinculación a Proceso against El Pino for homicidio doloso calificado.335 Federal security secretary Rosa Icela Rodríguez publicly identified El Pino as the son of former PRI state deputy Gustavo Díaz Sánchez (“El Gato”), who was himself arrested in November 2021.336 No final sentence or conviction has been publicly reported to date.337
narrative.text: ONU-DH, the UN Secretary-General, UNESCO, and RSF all condemned the killing. According to Mexico News Daily,  Valdivia was the 25th journalist killed in Veracruz since 2010 and the third during the administration of Governor Cuitláhuac García Jiménez. On 31 March 2022—eighteen months after the killing—a multi-agency operation arrested Gustavo Abigaíl Díaz (“El Pino”), identified as a leader of the CJNG in the Veracruz–Oaxaca border region. On approximately 7 April 2022, the Veracruz Fiscalía obtained a vinculación a Proceso against El Pino for homicidio doloso calificado. Federal security secretary Rosa Icela Rodríguez publicly identified El Pino as the son of former PRI state deputy Gustavo Díaz Sánchez (“El Gato”), who was himself arrested in November 2021. No final sentence or conviction has been publicly reported to date.

incidents.heading: Víctor Manuel Jiménez Campos — Killed, 1 November 2020, Guanajuato
incidents.place: the community of Elguera, on the border between the municipalities of Celaya and Villagrán
incidents.identity: Víctor Manuel Jiménez Campos, aged 38 and known by the nicknames “El Gordo” and “Vic,” was an independent journalist based in Celaya, Guanajuato, specialising in crime reporting

narrative.html: Víctor Manuel Jiménez Campos, aged 38 and known by the nicknames “El Gordo” and “Vic,” was an independent journalist based in Celaya, Guanajuato, specialising in crime reporting.338 He worked for the Facebook-based news pages Nota Roja de Celaya Guanajuato, Digital Noticias, and Rotativa Digital de Guanajuato, as well as the portal Informativo Ágora, covering crime and security for approximately four years in a region marked by extreme violence between the CJNG and the Santa Rosa de Lima Cartel.339
narrative.text: Víctor Manuel Jiménez Campos, aged 38 and known by the nicknames “El Gordo” and “Vic,” was an independent journalist based in Celaya, Guanajuato, specialising in crime reporting. He worked for the Facebook-based news pages Nota Roja de Celaya Guanajuato, Digital Noticias, and Rotativa Digital de Guanajuato, as well as the portal Informativo Ágora, covering crime and security for approximately four years in a region marked by extreme violence between the CJNG and the Santa Rosa de Lima Cartel.

narrative.html: On the afternoon of 1 November 2020, Jiménez Campos left his home to cover a baseball game in the community of Elguera, on the border between the municipalities of Celaya and Villagrán.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:340">340</sup> He stopped responding to messages during or after his time at the event.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:341">341</sup> His disappearance was reported on 4 November 2020.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:342">342</sup> In the days following, friends and colleagues organised search parties in surrounding agricultural fields and found a shirt and a tennis shoe belonging to Jiménez Campos, both stained with blood.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:343">343</sup>
narrative.text: On the afternoon of 1 November 2020, Jiménez Campos left his home to cover a baseball game in the community of Elguera, on the border between the municipalities of Celaya and Villagrán. He stopped responding to messages during or after his time at the event. His disappearance was reported on 4 November 2020. In the days following, friends and colleagues organised search parties in surrounding agricultural fields and found a shirt and a tennis shoe belonging to Jiménez Campos, both stained with blood.

narrative.html: Three years and seven months after his disappearance, on 10 June 2024, the state attorney general of Guanajuato informed Jiménez Campos’s family that skeletal remains had been discovered and identified as his through DNA analysis.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:344">344</sup> His remains were found inside an abandoned water well in the community of San Salvador de Torrecillas, municipality of Villagrán; the site functioned as a clandestine grave, as additional unidentified human remains were also found there.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:345">345</sup> The prosecutor’s office did not publicly disclose the cause of death. On 5 March 2025, the Guanajuato FGE determined there was no evidence connecting Jiménez Campos’s murder  to his journalistic work.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:346">346</sup> No arrests or convictions have been reported.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:347">347</sup>
narrative.text: Three years and seven months after his disappearance, on 10 June 2024, the state attorney general of Guanajuato informed Jiménez Campos’s family that skeletal remains had been discovered and identified as his through DNA analysis. His remains were found inside an abandoned water well in the community of San Salvador de Torrecillas, municipality of Villagrán; the site functioned as a clandestine grave, as additional unidentified human remains were also found there. The prosecutor’s office did not publicly disclose the cause of death. On 5 March 2025, the Guanajuato FGE determined there was no evidence connecting Jiménez Campos’s murder  to his journalistic work. No arrests or convictions have been reported.

narrative.html: In the early morning of 9 November 2020, Vázquez received a tip about the discovery of human remains left in plastic bags on a street in the Colonia Villa Salamanca 400.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:349">349</sup> Vázquez drove to the scene in predawn darkness, arriving before any police officers, and approached on foot. As he prepared to broadcast a Facebook Live stream for El Salmantino, armed assailants arrived and shot him at least five times, including when he was already on the ground.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:350">350</sup> National Guard units responded to the shooting, and called in support from the Red Cross to transfer Vázquez to receive medical attention.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:351">351</sup> He was transported to Hospital Regional PEMEX, where he died during or after surgery around midday.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:352">352</sup> The subsequent FGR investigation determined that the remains had been deliberately placed as a lure to draw the journalist to the location.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:353">353</sup> Neither Vázquez nor El Salmantino had reported receiving threats, and the Federal Mechanism confirmed it had not been aware of any threats against either.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:354">354</sup>
narrative.text: In the early morning of 9 November 2020, Vázquez received a tip about the discovery of human remains left in plastic bags on a street in the Colonia Villa Salamanca 400. Vázquez drove to the scene in predawn darkness, arriving before any police officers, and approached on foot. As he prepared to broadcast a Facebook Live stream for El Salmantino, armed assailants arrived and shot him at least five times, including when he was already on the ground. National Guard units responded to the shooting, and called in support from the Red Cross to transfer Vázquez to receive medical attention. He was transported to Hospital Regional PEMEX, where he died during or after surgery around midday. The subsequent FGR investigation determined that the remains had been deliberately placed as a lure to draw the journalist to the location. Neither Vázquez nor El Salmantino had reported receiving threats, and the Federal Mechanism confirmed it had not been aware of any threats against either.

narrative.html: ONU-DH condemned the killing, noting Vázquez was the second journalist killed in Mexico within days of the International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:355">355</sup> Local journalists protested outside the Ayuntamiento in Salamanca demanding justice.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:356">356</sup> In a widely denounced response, Salamanca mayor María Beatriz Hernández Cruz stated that journalists sometimes “take too many risks” and questioned why Vázquez went to a dangerous neighbourhood without police present.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:357">357</sup>
narrative.text: ONU-DH condemned the killing, noting Vázquez was the second journalist killed in Mexico within days of the International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists. Local journalists protested outside the Ayuntamiento in Salamanca demanding justice. In a widely denounced response, Salamanca mayor María Beatriz Hernández Cruz stated that journalists sometimes “take too many risks” and questioned why Vázquez went to a dangerous neighbourhood without police present.

narrative.html: Six days after the attack, the Guanajuato state Fiscalía detained two suspects: Martín Eduardo López Orozco (“El Tacones”) and José Luis Martínez Aguilera (“El Pizzero”).<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:358">358</sup> The FGR’s FEADLE subsequently attracted the investigation to the federal level. On 14 December 2021, López Orozco was sentenced to 20 years in prison after entering a guilty plea; the judge stated the homicide was committed with the objective of limiting Vázquez’s freedom of expression.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:359">359</sup> On 7 September 2023, Martínez Aguilera was found guilty of Vázquez’s murder. FEADLE presented evidence demonstrating that the accused, along with López Orozco, lured the journalist to a predetermined location to assault him as retaliation for a news article in which he published the face of a criminal leader in the area.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:360">360</sup> On 14 September 2023, Martínez Aguilera was sentenced to 27 years and 6 months in prison and ordered to pay reparación integral del daño to Vázquez’s daughters.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:361">361</sup> However, the judge ruled that Vázquez’s status as a journalist was not a determinative factor in the sentencing, indicating there was not enough evidence pointing to Vázquez’s work as a motive.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:362">362</sup> FEADLE, which had requested the maximum 35-year sentence, announced an appeal. CPJ welcomed the conviction but expressed concern that the journalistic motive was not recognised.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:363">363</sup>
narrative.text: Six days after the attack, the Guanajuato state Fiscalía detained two suspects: Martín Eduardo López Orozco (“El Tacones”) and José Luis Martínez Aguilera (“El Pizzero”). The FGR’s FEADLE subsequently attracted the investigation to the federal level. On 14 December 2021, López Orozco was sentenced to 20 years in prison after entering a guilty plea; the judge stated the homicide was committed with the objective of limiting Vázquez’s freedom of expression. On 7 September 2023, Martínez Aguilera was found guilty of Vázquez’s murder. FEADLE presented evidence demonstrating that the accused, along with López Orozco, lured the journalist to a predetermined location to assault him as retaliation for a news article in which he published the face of a criminal leader in the area. On 14 September 2023, Martínez Aguilera was sentenced to 27 years and 6 months in prison and ordered to pay reparación integral del daño to Vázquez’s daughters. However, the judge ruled that Vázquez’s status as a journalist was not a determinative factor in the sentencing, indicating there was not enough evidence pointing to Vázquez’s work as a motive. FEADLE, which had requested the maximum 35-year sentence, announced an appeal. CPJ welcomed the conviction but expressed concern that the journalistic motive was not recognised.

narrative.html: Jaime Daniel Castaño Zacarías was a photojournalist and the director of the digital news portal Prensa Libre MX, based in Jerez, Zacatecas. He had approximately 20 years of professional experience, having previously worked for the regional newspaper El Sol de Zacatecas, and also served in the public communications office of the Jerez municipal government.364
narrative.text: Jaime Daniel Castaño Zacarías was a photojournalist and the director of the digital news portal Prensa Libre MX, based in Jerez, Zacatecas. He had approximately 20 years of professional experience, having previously worked for the regional newspaper El Sol de Zacatecas, and also served in the public communications office of the Jerez municipal government.

narrative.html: On the morning of 9 December 2020, Castaño Zacarías attended a municipal government event and, while returning, encountered the bodies of two men on Federal Highway 23.365 The victims displayed bound hands, gunshot wounds, visible signs of torture, and a narcomensaje.366 Police had not yet arrived at the scene. Two journalistic sources told ARTICLE 19 that armed individuals at the scene confronted the journalist about the photographs he had taken and demanded he delete them.367 Castaño Zacarías refused to surrender or delete his photographs, mounted his motorcycle, and departed. A few kilometres further on, occupants of another vehicle caught up with him and opened fire, killing him.368 The gunmen then removed the memory card from his camera.369 According to the mayor's office, Castaño Zacarías was attended to by Civil Protection personnel, who confirmed his death.370
narrative.text: On the morning of 9 December 2020, Castaño Zacarías attended a municipal government event and, while returning, encountered the bodies of two men on Federal Highway 23. The victims displayed bound hands, gunshot wounds, visible signs of torture, and a narcomensaje. Police had not yet arrived at the scene. Two journalistic sources told ARTICLE 19 that armed individuals at the scene confronted the journalist about the photographs he had taken and demanded he delete them. Castaño Zacarías refused to surrender or delete his photographs, mounted his motorcycle, and departed. A few kilometres further on, occupants of another vehicle caught up with him and opened fire, killing him. The gunmen then removed the memory card from his camera. According to the mayor's office, Castaño Zacarías was attended to by Civil Protection personnel, who confirmed his death.

narrative.html: ARTICLE 19 stated it had no evidence of prior threats or intimidation against him before his killing.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:371">371</sup> ONU-DH condemned the killing, with its representative in Mexico stating that the attack was an assault on Mexican society as a whole.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:372">372</sup> UNESCO Director-General Audrey Azoulay called on Mexico to investigate and bring the perpetrators to trial.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:373">373</sup> ARTICLE 19 called on FEADLE to attract the case and apply the Protocolo Homologado de Investigación de Delitos contra la Libertad de Expresión.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:374">374</sup> Local journalists and civil society groups organised a protest on 11 December 2020 demanding justice. Despite the case being considered the first killing of a journalist in Zacatecas since 2014, no subsequent public follow-up occurred, and it remained unclear whether federal authorities were involved in the investigation.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:375">375</sup> No arrests or convictions have been reported.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:376">376</sup>

narrative.html: Jorge Molontzín Centlal was a journalist who worked as a reporter for the Semanario Confidencial, a weekly news magazine and website based in the town of Caborca, in the northern Mexican state of Sonora.377 Originally from the state of Chiapas, Molontzín had spent over twelve years covering the municipalities of the Sonoran Desert.378 His reporting focused on public works, local politics, and social affairs. He also distributed copies of the magazine throughout the region and supplemented his journalistic income by selling products—such as car windshields and sacks of potatoes—during his travels, using those trips to gather information from local authorities for his reporting.379
narrative.text: Jorge Molontzín Centlal was a journalist who worked as a reporter for the Semanario Confidencial, a weekly news magazine and website based in the town of Caborca, in the northern Mexican state of Sonora. Originally from the state of Chiapas, Molontzín had spent over twelve years covering the municipalities of the Sonoran Desert. His reporting focused on public works, local politics, and social affairs. He also distributed copies of the magazine throughout the region and supplemented his journalistic income by selling products—such as car windshields and sacks of potatoes—during his travels, using those trips to gather information from local authorities for his reporting.

narrative.html: Confidencial’s editor, José Alfredo Gastón Gastélum, told CPJ that the magazine had “mostly stopped publishing stories about crime” after receiving threats over its coverage several years prior, though no recent threats had been reported and Gastón Gastélum was unaware of threats specifically targeting Molontzín.380 An official of the federal Protection Mechanism confirmed to CPJ that the Mechanism had not been in contact with Molontzín and was unaware of any threats against him.381
narrative.text: Confidencial’s editor, José Alfredo Gastón Gastélum, told CPJ that the magazine had “mostly stopped publishing stories about crime” after receiving threats over its coverage several years prior, though no recent threats had been reported and Gastón Gastélum was unaware of threats specifically targeting Molontzín. An official of the federal Protection Mechanism confirmed to CPJ that the Mechanism had not been in contact with Molontzín and was unaware of any threats against him.

narrative.html: On the morning of 10 March 2021, Molontzín was driving a red pickup truck from the town of Benjamín Hill toward Santa Ana, accompanied by his friend Eudocio Cruz Méndez, a horticulturist from Puebla who frequently accompanied him on his travels.382 Confidencial’s editor spoke with him that morning; his nephew, attorney Lázaro Molontzín, stated the journalist last communicated with his family at approximately 2:00 PM.383 After their last known contact, calls to the mobile phones of both Molontzín and Cruz Méndez went directly to voicemail. Neither man has been seen or heard from since. Colleagues at Confidencial presumed the two men had been forcibly taken.384
narrative.text: On the morning of 10 March 2021, Molontzín was driving a red pickup truck from the town of Benjamín Hill toward Santa Ana, accompanied by his friend Eudocio Cruz Méndez, a horticulturist from Puebla who frequently accompanied him on his travels. Confidencial’s editor spoke with him that morning; his nephew, attorney Lázaro Molontzín, stated the journalist last communicated with his family at approximately 2:00 PM. After their last known contact, calls to the mobile phones of both Molontzín and Cruz Méndez went directly to voicemail. Neither man has been seen or heard from since. Colleagues at Confidencial presumed the two men had been forcibly taken.

narrative.html: Confidencial published a statement on 17 March 2021 publicly denouncing the disappearance and requesting government action.385 A spokesperson for the Sonora state prosecutor’s office confirmed to CPJ that an investigation had been opened.386 As of September 2024, LatAm Journalism Review reported that Molontzín Centlal remained among five journalists still missing from the López Obrador administration period.387 No arrests, charges, or convictions in connection with the disappearance have been publicly reported.388
narrative.text: Confidencial published a statement on 17 March 2021 publicly denouncing the disappearance and requesting government action. A spokesperson for the Sonora state prosecutor’s office confirmed to CPJ that an investigation had been opened. As of September 2024, LatAm Journalism Review reported that Molontzín Centlal remained among five journalists still missing from the López Obrador administration period. No arrests, charges, or convictions in connection with the disappearance have been publicly reported.

narrative.html: Pablo Felipe Romero Chávez was a journalist based in Guaymas, Sonora, who worked as a crime reporter (“nota roja”) for the radio station FM 105.3 and the newspaper El Vigía, both of which belonged to the Grupo Padilla Hermanos media conglomerate.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:389">389</sup> Romero Chávez was 33 years old at the time of his disappearance, had earned a degree in criminology, and had begun working as a reporter at a local radio station approximately six years prior.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:390">390</sup> After an initial period in journalism, he took a three-year hiatus to manage a funeral home before returning to crime reporting in February 2021—only one month before his disappearance.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:391">391</sup>
narrative.text: Pablo Felipe Romero Chávez was a journalist based in Guaymas, Sonora, who worked as a crime reporter (“nota roja”) for the radio station FM 105.3 and the newspaper El Vigía, both of which belonged to the Grupo Padilla Hermanos media conglomerate. Romero Chávez was 33 years old at the time of his disappearance, had earned a degree in criminology, and had begun working as a reporter at a local radio station approximately six years prior. After an initial period in journalism, he took a three-year hiatus to manage a funeral home before returning to crime reporting in February 2021—only one month before his disappearance.

narrative.html: No specific prior threats, surveillance measures, or enrollment in a protection programme pertaining to Romero Chávez individually have been documented in available reporting. His disappearance occurred in the context of a broader pattern of violence against journalists in Sonora: he was the second journalist to disappear in the state in March 2021, following the disappearance of Jorge Molontzín Centlal fifteen days earlier.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:392">392</sup>

narrative.html: Family members and colleagues lost all communication with Romero Chávez on the morning of 25 March 2021.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:393">393</sup> His grandmother went to his home in the Colonia Las Palmas neighbourhood of Guaymas at approximately 8:00 a.m. and found the doors of the house wide open and his vehicle parked in front, unlocked; his mobile phone was switched off and he could not be reached.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:394">394</sup> The Fiscalía General de Justicia del Estado de Sonora confirmed on 26 March 2021 that it had received the disappearance report and opened an investigation.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:395">395</sup> The Colectivo Guerreras Buscadoras de Sonora, a civilian search collective, published an informational flyer to assist in locating him.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:396">396</sup> On 30 March 2021, a virtual meeting was held between Sonora state government officials and representatives of the Federal Protection Mechanism, out of concern for the disappearance of Romero Chávez and Jorge Molontzín Centlal, who disappeared fifteen days prior.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:397">397</sup> In May 2021, Romero Chávez’s mother publicly appealed for information, describing the period since his disappearance as a “nightmare.”<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:398">398</sup>
narrative.text: Family members and colleagues lost all communication with Romero Chávez on the morning of 25 March 2021. His grandmother went to his home in the Colonia Las Palmas neighbourhood of Guaymas at approximately 8:00 a.m. and found the doors of the house wide open and his vehicle parked in front, unlocked; his mobile phone was switched off and he could not be reached. The Fiscalía General de Justicia del Estado de Sonora confirmed on 26 March 2021 that it had received the disappearance report and opened an investigation. The Colectivo Guerreras Buscadoras de Sonora, a civilian search collective, published an informational flyer to assist in locating him. On 30 March 2021, a virtual meeting was held between Sonora state government officials and representatives of the Federal Protection Mechanism, out of concern for the disappearance of Romero Chávez and Jorge Molontzín Centlal, who disappeared fifteen days prior. In May 2021, Romero Chávez’s mother publicly appealed for information, describing the period since his disappearance as a “nightmare.”

narrative.html: As of September 2024, Romero Chávez remained among five journalists still missing from the López Obrador administration period.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:399">399</sup> No arrests, charges, or convictions in connection with his disappearance have been publicly reported.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:400">400</sup>

narrative.html: Gabriela Lizeth Talamante Cázarez, known publicly as “Katana Cázarez,” was a 37-year-old radio broadcaster and social media content creator based in Magdalena de Kino, Sonora. She worked at the radio station Casa de Toño and operated a social media news page called La Vox, through which she published local news content.401
narrative.text: Gabriela Lizeth Talamante Cázarez, known publicly as “Katana Cázarez,” was a 37-year-old radio broadcaster and social media content creator based in Magdalena de Kino, Sonora. She worked at the radio station Casa de Toño and operated a social media news page called La Vox, through which she published local news content.

narrative.html: On 10 April 2021, while en route to her workplace, a man intercepted Talamante Cázarez as she was boarding her vehicle, forced her at gunpoint to drive to a location on the outskirts of the city, threatened her specifically over her creation of the news page La Vox, demanded she shut down her social media accounts, and then subjected her to a severe physical assault.402 A video subsequently published on social media and since deleted,403 showed her with multiple contusions on her face, arms, legs, and mouth.404 Following the attack, her personal social media accounts and the La Vox page were taken down—a direct and successful act of censorship through violence.405
narrative.text: On 10 April 2021, while en route to her workplace, a man intercepted Talamante Cázarez as she was boarding her vehicle, forced her at gunpoint to drive to a location on the outskirts of the city, threatened her specifically over her creation of the news page La Vox, demanded she shut down her social media accounts, and then subjected her to a severe physical assault. A video subsequently published on social media and since deleted, showed her with multiple contusions on her face, arms, legs, and mouth. Following the attack, her personal social media accounts and the La Vox page were taken down—a direct and successful act of censorship through violence.

narrative.html: The Sonora state prosecutor’s office opened an investigation into the physical assault, classifying the offences as injuries, threats, and robbery; however, the attacker responsible for the 10 April 2021 assault has not been publicly identified or apprehended. The office undertook the investigation as gender violence, assault, intimidation, extortion, and an attack on freedom of expression, with the perpetrator potentially facing a minimum sentence of 10 years in prison.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:406">406</sup>

The Associated Press described his coverage as including community events, police activity, and crime.

narrative.html: On the evening of 2 May 2021, Morales’ family lost contact with him at approximately 19:00 in Sonoyta after he had covered a campaign event for Julio Casanova, a candidate for mayor.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:409">409</sup> Municipal police subsequently located his abandoned white pickup truck with the keys in the ignition near Ejido Morelia. The National Guard found his body at kilometre 165+200 on the Caborca–Sonoyta highway; he had sustained multiple gunshot wounds.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:410">410</sup> Police reported that a piece of cardboard bearing a message had been left with his body.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:411">411</sup> The day before his abduction, Morales had publicly denounced receiving anonymous threats through social media in a since-deleted video posted to his Facebook page.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:412">412</sup> However, a Protection Mechanism official told CPJ that they had not been made aware of threats against him and had not communicated with him prior to his death. No protection measures were in place.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:413">413</sup>
narrative.text: On the evening of 2 May 2021, Morales’ family lost contact with him at approximately 19:00 in Sonoyta after he had covered a campaign event for Julio Casanova, a candidate for mayor. Municipal police subsequently located his abandoned white pickup truck with the keys in the ignition near Ejido Morelia. The National Guard found his body at kilometre 165+200 on the Caborca–Sonoyta highway; he had sustained multiple gunshot wounds. Police reported that a piece of cardboard bearing a message had been left with his body. The day before his abduction, Morales had publicly denounced receiving anonymous threats through social media in a since-deleted video posted to his Facebook page. However, a Protection Mechanism official told CPJ that they had not been made aware of threats against him and had not communicated with him prior to his death. No protection measures were in place.

narrative.html: The Sonora State Attorney General’s Office stated it was investigating multiple lines of inquiry, including personal, family, and work-related hypotheses.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:414">414</sup> CPJ reported that it sent several requests for comment to the Sonora prosecutors and received no replies.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:415">415</sup> ONU-DH and UNESCO condemned the killing.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:416">416</sup> No arrests or convictions in connection with Morales’s murder have been publicly reported.

CPJ reported that it sent several requests for comment to the Sonora prosecutors and received no replies. ONU-DH and UNESCO condemned the killing. No arrests or convictions in connection with Morales’s murder have been publicly reported.

narrative.html: Gustavo Sánchez Cabrera was the director of the news website Noticias Minuto a Minuto and the television channel Panorama Pacífico TV, both based in the Isthmus of Tehuantepec region of Oaxaca. He reported primarily on local politics and crime.417
narrative.text: Gustavo Sánchez Cabrera was the director of the news website Noticias Minuto a Minuto and the television channel Panorama Pacífico TV, both based in the Isthmus of Tehuantepec region of Oaxaca. He reported primarily on local politics and crime.

narrative.html: The case of Sánchez Cabrera constitutes one of the most extensively documented failures of Mexico’s federal Protection Mechanism. He was first incorporated into the Mechanism in 2014 after receiving death threats but was subsequently removed for unspecified reasons; the Mechanism removed the camera it had installed at Sánchez Cabrera’s home while he was enrolled after it determined he was no longer at risk.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:418">418</sup> On 13 July 2020, he survived an assassination attempt; the Oaxaca Attorney General’s Office issued an arrest warrant against a suspect named Esteban de la Cruz Lagunas, but the warrant was voided on 30 November 2023 and a new one was not requested until 13 March 2021.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:419">419</sup> Following this attack, Sánchez requested  re-enrollment into the Mechanism, but his case was not evaluated until January 2021. According to RSF, a protection plan for Sánchez Cabrera was validated in May 2021; and protection measures—including cameras outside his home, a personal escort, and a bulletproof vest—were approved on 1 June 2021.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:420">420</sup> None of these measures were implemented before his killing, sixteen days later.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:421">421</sup> RSF reported that it had pressed the Mechanism to provide the promised protection up to the day before Sánchez Cabrera was murdered.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:422">422</sup> Sánchez Cabrera himself also emailed the Mechanism the day before his murder requesting his protective measures be enforced; he was told that “the notifications corresponding to the protection plan set out by the government board have been made. We’re on time for said measures to be implemented.”<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:423">423</sup>
narrative.text: The case of Sánchez Cabrera constitutes one of the most extensively documented failures of Mexico’s federal Protection Mechanism. He was first incorporated into the Mechanism in 2014 after receiving death threats but was subsequently removed for unspecified reasons; the Mechanism removed the camera it had installed at Sánchez Cabrera’s home while he was enrolled after it determined he was no longer at risk. On 13 July 2020, he survived an assassination attempt; the Oaxaca Attorney General’s Office issued an arrest warrant against a suspect named Esteban de la Cruz Lagunas, but the warrant was voided on 30 November 2023 and a new one was not requested until 13 March 2021. Following this attack, Sánchez requested  re-enrollment into the Mechanism, but his case was not evaluated until January 2021. According to RSF, a protection plan for Sánchez Cabrera was validated in May 2021; and protection measures—including cameras outside his home, a personal escort, and a bulletproof vest—were approved on 1 June 2021. None of these measures were implemented before his killing, sixteen days later. RSF reported that it had pressed the Mechanism to provide the promised protection up to the day before Sánchez Cabrera was murdered. Sánchez Cabrera himself also emailed the Mechanism the day before his murder requesting his protective measures be enforced; he was told that “the notifications corresponding to the protection plan set out by the government board have been made. We’re on time for said measures to be implemented.”

narrative.html: At approximately 8:00 on 17 June 2021, while Sánchez Cabrera was riding a motorcycle near the town of Morro Mazatán with his 15-year-old son, two unidentified individuals in a car deliberately crashed into the motorcycle. After Sánchez and his son fell, the assailants exited the vehicle and shot Sánchez Cabrera, killing him with a bullet to the head. At least fifteen 9mm cartridge casings were recovered at the scene. Sánchez’s son sustained mild injuries from the fall but was not shot.
narrative.text: At approximately 8:00 on 17 June 2021, while Sánchez Cabrera was riding a motorcycle near the town of Morro Mazatán with his 15-year-old son, two unidentified individuals in a car deliberately crashed into the motorcycle. After Sánchez and his son fell, the assailants exited the vehicle and shot Sánchez Cabrera, killing him with a bullet to the head. At least fifteen 9mm cartridge casings were recovered at the scene. Sánchez’s son sustained mild injuries from the fall but was not shot.

narrative.html: The Oaxaca state prosecutor’s office opened an investigation.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:424">424</sup> ONU-DH condemned the killing and called on authorities to investigate promptly.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:425">425</sup> On 17 June 2024—three years after the murder—the Government of Oaxaca issued a public apology to Sánchez’s family, formally acknowledging that his death could have been prevented had the State provided adequate protection.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:426">426</sup> CNDH concluded that the Mechanism had been negligent.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:427">427</sup> On 20 August 2024, the General Inspector of the Oaxaca State General Attorney’s Office ruled that two prosecutors had been negligent in their professional duties to Sánchez Cabrera following his July 2020 assassination attempt. It was determined that the lack of follow-up in issuing a second arrest warrant left Sánchez Cabrera unprotected, and that there was no meaningful attempt to implement protective measures.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:428">428</sup>
narrative.text: The Oaxaca state prosecutor’s office opened an investigation. ONU-DH condemned the killing and called on authorities to investigate promptly. On 17 June 2024—three years after the murder—the Government of Oaxaca issued a public apology to Sánchez’s family, formally acknowledging that his death could have been prevented had the State provided adequate protection. CNDH concluded that the Mechanism had been negligent. On 20 August 2024, the General Inspector of the Oaxaca State General Attorney’s Office ruled that two prosecutors had been negligent in their professional duties to Sánchez Cabrera following his July 2020 assassination attempt. It was determined that the lack of follow-up in issuing a second arrest warrant left Sánchez Cabrera unprotected, and that there was no meaningful attempt to implement protective measures.

narrative.html: In total, Sánchez Cabrera had received fourteen threats and acts of intimidation, requested government protection on seventeen occasions, and survived four prior attacks before his killing.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:429">429</sup> On 30 April 2025, a suspect identified as Esteban “C” was finally linked to proceedings for the July 2020 attempted homicide against Sánchez Cabrera.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:430">430</sup>
narrative.text: In total, Sánchez Cabrera had received fourteen threats and acts of intimidation, requested government protection on seventeen occasions, and survived four prior attacks before his killing. On 30 April 2025, a suspect identified as Esteban “C” was finally linked to proceedings for the July 2020 attempted homicide against Sánchez Cabrera.

narrative.html: Felipe Enrique García García, also known as “Kike,” was a journalist and communicator from the Estado de México who had worked for El Sol de Toluca and held institutional communications roles with the state government and security secretariat.431 He was also reported to have handled media relations for an incoming mayor. At the time of his killing, García García was supplementing his income by working as a driver for the ride-hailing platform DiDi.432
narrative.text: Felipe Enrique García García, also known as “Kike,” was a journalist and communicator from the Estado de México who had worked for El Sol de Toluca and held institutional communications roles with the state government and security secretariat. He was also reported to have handled media relations for an incoming mayor. At the time of his killing, García García was supplementing his income by working as a driver for the ride-hailing platform DiDi.

narrative.html: On the evening of 16 June 2021, García García left in his vehicle and was reported missing by family members when he failed to return.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:433">433</sup> His body was found in  his vehicle with gunshot wounds in Metepec. According to the state prosecutor’s investigative account, three people requested a ride via the platform; during the trip, one of the passengers allegedly ordered the others to shoot the driver.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:434">434</sup>
narrative.text: On the evening of 16 June 2021, García García left in his vehicle and was reported missing by family members when he failed to return. His body was found in  his vehicle with gunshot wounds in Metepec. According to the state prosecutor’s investigative account, three people requested a ride via the platform; during the trip, one of the passengers allegedly ordered the others to shoot the driver.

narrative.html: The Attorney General’s Office opened an investigation the day after García García’s murder.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:435">435</sup> ONU-DH stated there was no information about prior threats against García García but called on authorities to advance investigations without discarding the hypothesis that the attack was linked to his journalistic activity.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:436">436</sup> In October 2021, two suspects—Joseph Argenis “N” and Kimberly Isabel “N”—were arrested and linked to proceedings.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:437">437</sup> In May 2023, they were initially sentenced to 47 years of imprisonment. On appeal, Joseph’s sentence was reduced to 43 years and nine months, while Kimberly’s trial was annulled on grounds that the Venezuelan embassy was not notified of her arrest, violating her consular rights.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:438">438</sup> In 2024, the retrial was extended to both defendants on grounds that their trial was not held within a reasonable time. As of February 2025, the journalist’s wife, Carolina Rodríguez, publicly denounced that two key witnesses had failed to appear at the retrial, a forensic doctor and an eyewitness, raising concerns that the accused might be released.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:439">439</sup>
narrative.text: The Attorney General’s Office opened an investigation the day after García García’s murder. ONU-DH stated there was no information about prior threats against García García but called on authorities to advance investigations without discarding the hypothesis that the attack was linked to his journalistic activity. In October 2021, two suspects—Joseph Argenis “N” and Kimberly Isabel “N”—were arrested and linked to proceedings. In May 2023, they were initially sentenced to 47 years of imprisonment. On appeal, Joseph’s sentence was reduced to 43 years and nine months, while Kimberly’s trial was annulled on grounds that the Venezuelan embassy was not notified of her arrest, violating her consular rights. In 2024, the retrial was extended to both defendants on grounds that their trial was not held within a reasonable time. As of February 2025, the journalist’s wife, Carolina Rodríguez, publicly denounced that two key witnesses had failed to appear at the retrial, a forensic doctor and an eyewitness, raising concerns that the accused might be released.

His coverage generally encompassed sports, crime, and security matters. He combined his journalistic work with employment at a local maquiladora assembly plant.440

His coverage generally encompassed sports, crime, and security matters. He combined his journalistic work with employment at a local maquiladora assembly plant.

narrative.html: Editors of both outlets told CPJ they were not aware of direct threats to Tijerina’s life, though they indicated he had had “problems” with two coworkers at the factory whom they believed may have had ties to a drug trafficking gang.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:441">441</sup> The LA Times reported that Saúl Tijerina Rentería repeatedly sought help from the Protection Mechanism days before he was murdered, having received death threats due to his reporting; his request went unanswered.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:442">442</sup> ARTICLE 19 highlighted that the precarious economic conditions in which many Mexican journalists work—forcing them to hold second or third jobs—not only increases their exposure to risk but also creates opportunities for authorities to “stigmatize or revictimize” them by arguing they were not truly journalists.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:443">443</sup>

narrative.html: Tijerina disappeared after leaving his factory shift in the early morning hours of 22 June 2021. His body was found later that morning near his vehicle in Ciudad Acuña with multiple stab wounds to the neck.444 Other reporting claims Tijernia was found tied up in the trunk of his car.445 A narcomensaje was found with his body, reading: “This is what will happen to all the snitches in the state or those who collaborate with the state. CDN”—a reference to the Cartel del Noreste, a splinter group of the Zetas.446

incidents.identity: Abraham Mendoza Mendoza was a radio journalist in Morelia, Michoacán, who had worked for Voces Radio since 2013 as news director, producer, and programme host.

narrative.html: Abraham Mendoza Mendoza was a radio journalist in Morelia, Michoacán, who had worked for Voces Radio since 2013 as news director, producer, and programme host. At the time of his killing, he contributed to the radio programme “Observatorio” on Uve Radio 98.1 FM at the Vasco de Quiroga University and served as a presenter of Panorama Informativo Michoacán of Grupo ACIR.449 He had previously worked with Radio ACIR, EXA, Central TV, and CB Televisión.450 RSF reported that on social media Mendoza was often outspoken in his criticism of political corruption at the local and federal levels.451
narrative.text: Abraham Mendoza Mendoza was a radio journalist in Morelia, Michoacán, who had worked for Voces Radio since 2013 as news director, producer, and programme host. At the time of his killing, he contributed to the radio programme “Observatorio” on Uve Radio 98.1 FM at the Vasco de Quiroga University and served as a presenter of Panorama Informativo Michoacán of Grupo ACIR. He had previously worked with Radio ACIR, EXA, Central TV, and CB Televisión. RSF reported that on social media Mendoza was often outspoken in his criticism of political corruption at the local and federal levels.

narrative.html: On 19 July 2021, at approximately 15:30, Mendoza was shot at close range as he was leaving a gym on Avenida Madero Poniente in the Nueva Valladolid neighbourhood of Morelia. He was getting into his vehicle when a gunman approached and opened fire; a second individual was reported to have been conducting surveillance from a nearby car.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:452">452</sup> An ice-pop vendor at the scene was also wounded by gunfire.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:453">453</sup>
narrative.text: On 19 July 2021, at approximately 15:30, Mendoza was shot at close range as he was leaving a gym on Avenida Madero Poniente in the Nueva Valladolid neighbourhood of Morelia. He was getting into his vehicle when a gunman approached and opened fire; a second individual was reported to have been conducting surveillance from a nearby car. An ice-pop vendor at the scene was also wounded by gunfire.

narrative.html: RSF reported that Mendoza had not reported receiving threats recently.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:454">454</sup> ONU-DH’s Puntal “In Memoriam” entry indicated that he did not have protection measures in place.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:455">455</sup> The Michoacán State Attorney General’s Office detained three men on the day of the killing following a search operation. ONU-DH confirmed the detentions on 27 July 2021.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:456">456</sup> In October 2023, a court sentenced two of the accused—José Wilbert G. and Kevin P.—to 35 years and 6 months in prison and ordered payment of reparations.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:457">457</sup> However, although the material perpetrators were convicted, there has been no reported investigation into who may have ordered the killing or whether it was connected to Mendoza’s outspoken criticism of political corruption.
narrative.text: RSF reported that Mendoza had not reported receiving threats recently. ONU-DH’s Puntal “In Memoriam” entry indicated that he did not have protection measures in place. The Michoacán State Attorney General’s Office detained three men on the day of the killing following a search operation. ONU-DH confirmed the detentions on 27 July 2021. In October 2023, a court sentenced two of the accused—José Wilbert G. and Kevin P.—to 35 years and 6 months in prison and ordered payment of reparations. However, although the material perpetrators were convicted, there has been no reported investigation into who may have ordered the killing or whether it was connected to Mendoza’s outspoken criticism of political corruption.

narrative.html: Ricardo Domínguez López was the founder and director of InfoGuaymas, a digital news outlet with more than 300,000 Facebook followers that covered municipal, state, national, and crime news in Guaymas, Sonora. He also served as president of the Asociación Metropolitana de Periodistas Independientes de Guaymas-Empalme and secretary general of the Sindicato Nacional de Redactores de la Prensa (SNRP), Delegación 11.458
narrative.text: Ricardo Domínguez López was the founder and director of InfoGuaymas, a digital news outlet with more than 300,000 Facebook followers that covered municipal, state, national, and crime news in Guaymas, Sonora. He also served as president of the Asociación Metropolitana de Periodistas Independientes de Guaymas-Empalme and secretary general of the Sindicato Nacional de Redactores de la Prensa (SNRP), Delegación 11.

narrative.html: Domínguez López had been the victim of multiple digital attacks, threats, smear campaigns, and forced internal displacement prior to his killing. He was the president of the Metropolitan Association of Independent Journalists of Guaymas-Empalme.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:459">459</sup> In November 2020, he publicly denounced in a video that the Guaymas municipal police, under the direction of Comisario de Seguridad Pública Andrés Humberto Cano Ahuir, had created fake social media accounts to defame and discredit him and other journalists; he held Cano Ahuir personally responsible for any harm that might come to him.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:460">460</sup> In March 2021, he stated at a press conference that he had received death threats from criminal groups over his reporting and that local police had used a Facebook page to falsely accuse him of having ties to organized crime.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:461">461</sup> The video has since been deleted.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:462">462</sup> He relocated from Guaymas to his native Cajeme due to the threats and filed a formal complaint with the FGR, registered under case number FGR-0000804/2021.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:463">463</sup>
narrative.text: Domínguez López had been the victim of multiple digital attacks, threats, smear campaigns, and forced internal displacement prior to his killing. He was the president of the Metropolitan Association of Independent Journalists of Guaymas-Empalme. In November 2020, he publicly denounced in a video that the Guaymas municipal police, under the direction of Comisario de Seguridad Pública Andrés Humberto Cano Ahuir, had created fake social media accounts to defame and discredit him and other journalists; he held Cano Ahuir personally responsible for any harm that might come to him. In March 2021, he stated at a press conference that he had received death threats from criminal groups over his reporting and that local police had used a Facebook page to falsely accuse him of having ties to organized crime. The video has since been deleted. He relocated from Guaymas to his native Cajeme due to the threats and filed a formal complaint with the FGR, registered under case number FGR-0000804/2021.

narrative.html: Jacinto Romero Flores was a veteran reporter and radio announcer for Ori Stéreo FM in Veracruz, whose coverage focused on politics and crime in the Zongolica/Altas Montañas region. Since 2015, he had also hosted a Facebook programme titled “Un Café con El Enano con Jacinto Romero Flores.”473
narrative.text: Jacinto Romero Flores was a veteran reporter and radio announcer for Ori Stéreo FM in Veracruz, whose coverage focused on politics and crime in the Zongolica/Altas Montañas region. Since 2015, he had also hosted a Facebook programme titled “Un Café con El Enano con Jacinto Romero Flores.”

narrative.html: At about 10:45 AM on 19 August 2021, unidentified attackers in a vehicle shot Romero Flores multiple times while he was driving in a vehicle marked “Prensa,” or “Press,” on Reforma Boulevard in Potrerillo.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:474">474</sup> He died at the scene; his body was found inside his vehicle near the Reforma bridge. Romero Flores had received threatening messages prior to his killing, including messages reported as early as February 2021 warning him to stop writing.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:475">475</sup> La Jornada reported that on the day of the murder, Romero Flores had left his home to collect aid for people in need who had called his radio program to ask for help, raising the possibility that a trap may have been set in advance for him to walk into the attack, since Romero Flores frequently supported his audience this way.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:476">476</sup> CPJ reported that he had been granted protection from state authorities after being threatened that did not include a bodyguard or vehicle escort protections;<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:477">477</sup> an official document from March 2021 instructed the authorities to provide protection due to documented threats.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:478">478</sup> ARTICLE 19 confirmed that he had received death threats linked to his journalistic work.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:479">479</sup>
narrative.text: At about 10:45 AM on 19 August 2021, unidentified attackers in a vehicle shot Romero Flores multiple times while he was driving in a vehicle marked “Prensa,” or “Press,” on Reforma Boulevard in Potrerillo. He died at the scene; his body was found inside his vehicle near the Reforma bridge. Romero Flores had received threatening messages prior to his killing, including messages reported as early as February 2021 warning him to stop writing. La Jornada reported that on the day of the murder, Romero Flores had left his home to collect aid for people in need who had called his radio program to ask for help, raising the possibility that a trap may have been set in advance for him to walk into the attack, since Romero Flores frequently supported his audience this way. CPJ reported that he had been granted protection from state authorities after being threatened that did not include a bodyguard or vehicle escort protections; an official document from March 2021 instructed the authorities to provide protection due to documented threats. ARTICLE 19 confirmed that he had received death threats linked to his journalistic work.

narrative.html: CNDH and UNESCO condemned the murder of Romero Flores.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:480">480</sup> On 12 November 2021, the Veracruz State Attorney General’s Office reported the detention of three suspects, including a municipal councillor-elect and an elected councilman for Ixtaczoquitlán.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:481">481</sup> A judge subsequently ordered pretrial detention and linked them to criminal proceedings. However, in October 2022, all three were released after a court granted amparo relief against the order linking them to proceedings.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:482">482</sup> CPJ’s 2022 global impunity report noted that the suspects were freed due to lack of evidence. The case thus reverted to impunity.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:483">483</sup>
narrative.text: CNDH and UNESCO condemned the murder of Romero Flores. On 12 November 2021, the Veracruz State Attorney General’s Office reported the detention of three suspects, including a municipal councillor-elect and an elected councilman for Ixtaczoquitlán. A judge subsequently ordered pretrial detention and linked them to criminal proceedings. However, in October 2022, all three were released after a court granted amparo relief against the order linking them to proceedings. CPJ’s 2022 global impunity report noted that the suspects were freed due to lack of evidence. The case thus reverted to impunity.
