narrative.html: Jesús Manuel González Reyes, aged 55, was the founder, director, and administrator of Portal Morelos Noticias (also known as “Agencia PM Noticias”), a Facebook-based news outlet with approximately 260,000 followers that covered political news, cultural events, crime, and other local affairs in the state of Morelos.484
narrative.text: Jesús Manuel González Reyes, aged 55, was the founder, director, and administrator of Portal Morelos Noticias (also known as “Agencia PM Noticias”), a Facebook-based news outlet with approximately 260,000 followers that covered political news, cultural events, crime, and other local affairs in the state of Morelos.

narrative.html: In the June 2021 municipal elections, González Reyes had been a mayoral candidate in Emiliano Zapata municipality for the Partido para el Bienestar; after losing the election, he continued his journalistic work.485 In the weeks before his death, Portal Morelos Noticias had covered several homicides in and around Cuernavaca.486 Unnamed colleagues told the media he had been conducting “special investigations” at the time of his killing.487
narrative.text: In the June 2021 municipal elections, González Reyes had been a mayoral candidate in Emiliano Zapata municipality for the Partido para el Bienestar; after losing the election, he continued his journalistic work. In the weeks before his death, Portal Morelos Noticias had covered several homicides in and around Cuernavaca. Unnamed colleagues told the media he had been conducting “special investigations” at the time of his killing.

narrative.html: On 28 September 2021, at approximately 4:30 PM, González Reyes was shot and killed on Calle Leandro Valle in the Colonia Miraval neighbourhood of Cuernavaca. According to eyewitness accounts, two men approached him on a motorcycle after he had finished eating at a food stall and shot him with pistols.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:488">488</sup> He died at the scene; casings from 9mm rounds were recovered. The Morelos Prosecutor’s Office reported that González García was carrying his press credentials at the time of the murder, and stated the victim sustained gunshot wounds to the head at close range.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:489">489</sup> RSF described the attack as an “apparent contract killing.”<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:490">490</sup>

According to eyewitness accounts, two men approached him on a motorcycle after he had finished eating at a food stall and shot him with pistols. He died at the scene; casings from 9mm rounds were recovered. narrative.html: A federal Mechanism official told CPJ that the agency was not aware of threats to González Reyes and that he had not been enrolled in a protection programme. narrative.html: Fredy Fernando López Arévalo was a veteran journalist with a career spanning nearly four decades, originally from the municipality of Yajalon, Chiapas. He had served as a correspondent in Central America for the newspapers El Universal and El Financiero, worked as regional coordinator for Mexico’s state news agency Notimex, and covered landmark events.495 At the time of his death, he directed the magazine Revista Jovel and broadcast on XERA-Radio Uno in San Cristóbal de las Casas. His recent publications included reporting on a criminal group known as “MOTONETOS,” and his last post, on 28 October 2021, covered the dismissal of 200 municipal employees by the mayor.496
narrative.text: Fredy Fernando López Arévalo was a veteran journalist with a career spanning nearly four decades, originally from the municipality of Yajalon, Chiapas. He had served as a correspondent in Central America for the newspapers El Universal and El Financiero, worked as regional coordinator for Mexico’s state news agency Notimex, and covered landmark events. At the time of his death, he directed the magazine Revista Jovel and broadcast on XERA-Radio Uno in San Cristóbal de las Casas. His recent publications included reporting on a criminal group known as “MOTONETOS,” and his last post, on 28 October 2021, covered the dismissal of 200 municipal employees by the mayor.

narrative.html: On the evening of 28 October 2021, at approximately 19:45–20:00, López Arévalo was shot and killed outside his home in Colonia Las Rosas as he was unloading items from his vehicle. He was returning with his wife and children from Tuxtla Gutiérrez, where they had celebrated his mother’s birthday.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:497">497</sup> A lone gunman approached, shot him in the head, and fled on a motorcycle. His wife and daughters were present during the attack.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:498">498</sup>
narrative.text: On the evening of 28 October 2021, at approximately 19:45–20:00, López Arévalo was shot and killed outside his home in Colonia Las Rosas as he was unloading items from his vehicle. He was returning with his wife and children from Tuxtla Gutiérrez, where they had celebrated his mother’s birthday. A lone gunman approached, shot him in the head, and fled on a motorcycle. His wife and daughters were present during the attack.

narrative.html: A federal Mechanism official told CPJ the agency was unaware of threats against López Arévalo and that he had not been enrolled in a protection programme. However, a journalist colleague in Chiapas who knew him personally told CPJ that López Arévalo had written about organized crime and drug trafficking in the region and believed the killing was connected to his work.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:499">499</sup> Neighbours reported that, in the days before the attack, a young man had been seen surveilling the area around his home.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:500">500</sup>

However, a journalist colleague in Chiapas who knew him personally told CPJ that López Arévalo had written about organized crime and drug trafficking in the region and believed the killing was connected to his work. Neighbours reported that, in the days before the attack, a young man had been seen surveilling the area around his home.

narrative.html: Alfredo Cardoso Echeverría was a photojournalist based in Acapulco de Juárez, Guerrero, and the founder and editor of the online news outlet Las Dos Costas. He had previously worked as a photographer for several media outlets in Acapulco.504 On 28 October 2021, masked armed men abducted Cardoso from his home in Acapulco. He was found the following day near his residence with at least five gunshot wounds and was transported to the IMSS Regional Hospital for treatment.505 After undergoing surgery, Cardoso died in hospital on 31 October 2021.506
narrative.text: Alfredo Cardoso Echeverría was a photojournalist based in Acapulco de Juárez, Guerrero, and the founder and editor of the online news outlet Las Dos Costas. He had previously worked as a photographer for several media outlets in Acapulco. On 28 October 2021, masked armed men abducted Cardoso from his home in Acapulco. He was found the following day near his residence with at least five gunshot wounds and was transported to the IMSS Regional Hospital for treatment. After undergoing surgery, Cardoso died in hospital on 31 October 2021.

narrative.html: The Guerrero State Prosecutor’s Office opened an investigation on 29 October 2021. Governor Evelyn Salgado condemned the killing and stated she had instructed her government to provide protection to Cardoso’s family.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:507">507</sup> On 23 November 2021, a suspect identified as Roberto “N” was arrested.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:508">508</sup> FEADLE took over the case on 17 March 2022. On 9 August 2022, a federal judge sentenced Roberto “N” to 13 years and four months in prison as the material perpetrator of the murder, though it was noted that he was one of several armed men who abducted Cardoso.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:509">509</sup> The FGR determined that “sufficient and effective evidence was found to determine that the murder of the journalist materialized as a reprisal for his journalistic work.”<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:510">510</sup> Notably, in January 2025, a judge ordered an ex-municipal police officer in Acapulco de Juárez identified as Jorge “G” to be held in pretrial detention due to his role as the “instigator” of Cardoso’s killing; it was found that Cardoso published several articles criticizing the actions of Jorge “G.”.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:511">511</sup>
narrative.text: The Guerrero State Prosecutor’s Office opened an investigation on 29 October 2021. Governor Evelyn Salgado condemned the killing and stated she had instructed her government to provide protection to Cardoso’s family. On 23 November 2021, a suspect identified as Roberto “N” was arrested. FEADLE took over the case on 17 March 2022. On 9 August 2022, a federal judge sentenced Roberto “N” to 13 years and four months in prison as the material perpetrator of the murder, though it was noted that he was one of several armed men who abducted Cardoso. The FGR determined that “sufficient and effective evidence was found to determine that the murder of the journalist materialized as a reprisal for his journalistic work.” Notably, in January 2025, a judge ordered an ex-municipal police officer in Acapulco de Juárez identified as Jorge “G” to be held in pretrial detention due to his role as the “instigator” of Cardoso’s killing; it was found that Cardoso published several articles criticizing the actions of Jorge “G.”.

narrative.html: José Luis Gamboa Arenas was the founder and general director of the digital news outlets Inforegio and La Noticia, based in the Port of Veracruz. He followed in the footsteps of his journalist father,512 transitioning into digital media, where he became known for live broadcasts on social media platforms in which he consistently criticized the wave of violence afflicting the state and the extortion of local businesses.513 Previously, he had been deeply involved in local politics in the port, having been the Municipal Leader of the Revolutionary Youth Front of the Institutional Revolutionary Party.514 In the months before his murder, Gamboa had intensified his criticism of local authorities, publishing reports accusing municipal officials of colluding with criminal organizations to allow the extortion of protection money in neighbourhoods throughout the port city, naming both the officials and the criminal groups responsible.515 ARTICLE 19 reported that among his most recent publications were investigative works titled ‘La Guerra por la Narco Política’ and ‘Prospectiva parte 1,’ which documented regional violence and criticized the government’s failure to combat it.516
narrative.text: José Luis Gamboa Arenas was the founder and general director of the digital news outlets Inforegio and La Noticia, based in the Port of Veracruz. He followed in the footsteps of his journalist father, transitioning into digital media, where he became known for live broadcasts on social media platforms in which he consistently criticized the wave of violence afflicting the state and the extortion of local businesses. Previously, he had been deeply involved in local politics in the port, having been the Municipal Leader of the Revolutionary Youth Front of the Institutional Revolutionary Party. In the months before his murder, Gamboa had intensified his criticism of local authorities, publishing reports accusing municipal officials of colluding with criminal organizations to allow the extortion of protection money in neighbourhoods throughout the port city, naming both the officials and the criminal groups responsible. ARTICLE 19 reported that among his most recent publications were investigative works titled ‘La Guerra por la Narco Política’ and ‘Prospectiva parte 1,’ which documented regional violence and criticized the government’s failure to combat it.

narrative.html: On 10 January 2022, Gamboa was found with multiple stab wounds in the Floresta neighbourhood of the Port of Veracruz.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:517">517</sup> Conflicting press reports indicate that he was either dead upon discovery or died in hospital three days later.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:518">518</sup> Critically, it took four days for his body to be identified. Because his identity and profession were initially unknown, the State Prosecutor’s Office of Veracruz opened an investigation into aggravated homicide with a presumed robbery motive, a classification that may have delayed or prevented the resources needed for an investigation into whether Gamboa’s murder was related to his profession..<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:519">519</sup>
narrative.text: On 10 January 2022, Gamboa was found with multiple stab wounds in the Floresta neighbourhood of the Port of Veracruz. Conflicting press reports indicate that he was either dead upon discovery or died in hospital three days later. Critically, it took four days for his body to be identified. Because his identity and profession were initially unknown, the State Prosecutor’s Office of Veracruz opened an investigation into aggravated homicide with a presumed robbery motive, a classification that may have delayed or prevented the resources needed for an investigation into whether Gamboa’s murder was related to his profession..

narrative.html: On 16 January 2022, the State Commission for the Attention and Protection of Journalists called on the Veracruz state prosecutor’s office to apply the Protocol for the Investigation of Crimes Against Freedom of Expression to Gamboa’s murder.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:520">520</sup> Authorities stated that they had no record of prior threats against Gamboa related to his journalistic work, and CPJ noted that initial press reports suggested the homicide may have occurred during an attempted robbery.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:521">521</sup> Gamboa was not enrolled in any protection programme, and no protection measures were in place at the time of the attack.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:522">522</sup>
narrative.text: On 16 January 2022, the State Commission for the Attention and Protection of Journalists called on the Veracruz state prosecutor’s office to apply the Protocol for the Investigation of Crimes Against Freedom of Expression to Gamboa’s murder. Authorities stated that they had no record of prior threats against Gamboa related to his journalistic work, and CPJ noted that initial press reports suggested the homicide may have occurred during an attempted robbery. Gamboa was not enrolled in any protection programme, and no protection measures were in place at the time of the attack.

narrative.html: In April 2022, Eduardo “N,” a nephew of José Luis Gamboa, was arrested for his murder.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:523">523</sup> Two months after this arrest, López Obrador publicly asserted that the murder was “a family matter” and unrelated to Gamboa’s journalistic work in Veracruz—a characterization that press freedom organizations challenged as premature and dismissive.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:524">524</sup> A second suspect, Sebastián Alejandro “N,” was arrested in connection with the murder in May 2024.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:525">525</sup> The case remains under investigation, and no conviction has been publicly reported as of the date of this report.
narrative.text: In April 2022, Eduardo “N,” a nephew of José Luis Gamboa, was arrested for his murder. Two months after this arrest, López Obrador publicly asserted that the murder was “a family matter” and unrelated to Gamboa’s journalistic work in Veracruz—a characterization that press freedom organizations challenged as premature and dismissive. A second suspect, Sebastián Alejandro “N,” was arrested in connection with the murder in May 2024. The case remains under investigation, and no conviction has been publicly reported as of the date of this report.

narrative.html: Alfonso Margarito Martínez Esquivel was a freelance photojournalist based in Tijuana, Baja California, who specialized in crime scene photography—a beat that placed him in direct and sustained contact with the activities of organized criminal groups operating along the U.S.–Mexico border.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:526">526</sup> According to CPJ, the head of a local Tijuana Cartel cell considered Martínez responsible for publishing photographs on social media that detailed the structure of the criminal gang led by Christian Adán Velázquez José, known as “El Cabo 16.”<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:527">527</sup>
narrative.text: Alfonso Margarito Martínez Esquivel was a freelance photojournalist based in Tijuana, Baja California, who specialized in crime scene photography—a beat that placed him in direct and sustained contact with the activities of organized criminal groups operating along the U.S.–Mexico border. According to CPJ, the head of a local Tijuana Cartel cell considered Martínez responsible for publishing photographs on social media that detailed the structure of the criminal gang led by Christian Adán Velázquez José, known as “El Cabo 16.”

narrative.html: On 17 January 2022, Martínez was shot and killed outside his home. He had briefly returned from a reporting assignment and was preparing to depart again when he was ambushed.  According to friends and colleagues, Martínez had reported threats on several occasions in the years preceding his death.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:528">528</sup> An official with the federal Protection Mechanism confirmed to CPJ that the agency had contacted Martínez several times, but that he stopped responding. Alianza de Medios reported that the heavy bureaucracy involved in the enrollment process discouraged Martínez from finalizing materials for incorporation in the protection program.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:529">529</sup> Martínez had sought to enroll in December 2021 after being publicly accused by a social media user of managing Facebook pages that exposed the identities and activities of drug traffickers, placing him at grave risk.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:530">530</sup>
narrative.text: On 17 January 2022, Martínez was shot and killed outside his home. He had briefly returned from a reporting assignment and was preparing to depart again when he was ambushed.  According to friends and colleagues, Martínez had reported threats on several occasions in the years preceding his death. An official with the federal Protection Mechanism confirmed to CPJ that the agency had contacted Martínez several times, but that he stopped responding. Alianza de Medios reported that the heavy bureaucracy involved in the enrollment process discouraged Martínez from finalizing materials for incorporation in the protection program. Martínez had sought to enroll in December 2021 after being publicly accused by a social media user of managing Facebook pages that exposed the identities and activities of drug traffickers, placing him at grave risk.

narrative.html: The prosecution’s investigation subsequently determined that on 15 January 2022, “El Cabo 16” had contacted José Ochoa Díaz, alias “El Huesos,” who in turn engaged Adrián Nicolás Ramos, alias “El Uber,” to carry out the killing and video-record the execution.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:531">531</sup> The contracted price for the murder was approximately 40,000 Mexican pesos.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:532">532</sup>

The contracted price for the murder was approximately 40,000 Mexican pesos.

narrative.html: Adrián Nicolás Ramos and José Heriberto Ochoa Díaz were sentenced in December 2022 for the murder, each receiving 25 years.533 Christian Adán Velázquez José, identified as the individual who ordered the killing, declined a plea agreement and in 2023 announced he would proceed to trial.534 Press reports indicate that he may also have been involved in the killing of Lourdes Maldonado López, discussed below. The LA Times subsequently reported that the murders of Martínez and Maldonado were more likely driven by political considerations than by purely criminal motives.535

narrative.html: Lourdes Maldonado López was a freelance reporter and correspondent for several outlets and the host of the programme Brebaje on Radio Sintoniza Sin Fronteras in Tijuana, Baja California. She had previously worked for Primer Sistema de Noticias, a news outlet owned by Jaime Bonilla Valdez, a wealthy businessman who served as Governor of Baja California from 2019 to late 2021.536 In her most recent broadcasts, Maldonado covered a range of topics including criticism of municipal government expenditures and the murder of her colleague Margarito Martínez. She had been pursuing an investigation into possible corruption by the previous state government and had, just days before her murder, won a nine-year labour lawsuit against Bonilla’s media company, which would have paid up to 500,000 pesos ($25,000 USD) in unpaid wages.537
narrative.text: Lourdes Maldonado López was a freelance reporter and correspondent for several outlets and the host of the programme Brebaje on Radio Sintoniza Sin Fronteras in Tijuana, Baja California. She had previously worked for Primer Sistema de Noticias, a news outlet owned by Jaime Bonilla Valdez, a wealthy businessman who served as Governor of Baja California from 2019 to late 2021. In her most recent broadcasts, Maldonado covered a range of topics including criticism of municipal government expenditures and the murder of her colleague Margarito Martínez. She had been pursuing an investigation into possible corruption by the previous state government and had, just days before her murder, won a nine-year labour lawsuit against Bonilla’s media company, which would have paid up to 500,000 pesos ($25,000 USD)  in unpaid wages.

narrative.html: In a moment that would become one of the most widely cited episodes in the crisis of press freedom in Mexico, Maldonado addressed AMLO directly at his morning press conference on 26 March 2019, asking him for protection and stating publicly that she feared for her life due to her labour dispute with Jaime Bonilla.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:538">538</sup> She was subsequently enrolled in the Baja California State Journalists Protection Program and received certain precautionary measures, including a panic button, police patrols at her residence at night, and a state patrol escort upon her arrival home—measures specifically tailored to the moment she identified as her most vulnerable: the transition from her car to her home.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:539">539</sup>
narrative.text: In a moment that would become one of the most widely cited episodes in the crisis of press freedom in Mexico, Maldonado addressed AMLO directly at his morning press conference on 26 March 2019, asking him for protection and stating publicly that she feared for her life due to her labour dispute with Jaime Bonilla. She was subsequently enrolled in the Baja California State Journalists Protection Program and received certain precautionary measures, including a panic button, police patrols at her residence at night, and a state patrol escort upon her arrival home—measures specifically tailored to the moment she identified as her most vulnerable: the transition from her car to her home.

narrative.html: On 23 January 2022—barely six days after the murder of Margarito Martínez—Maldonado was shot and killed inside her car as she arrived at her home. The attackers waited for her protection detail to leave before executing the attack, demonstrating both advanced surveillance and awareness of her security arrangements.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:540">540</sup> The killing drew immediate condemnation from the IACHR.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:541">541</sup> In the wake of her murder, then-Governor of Baja California Jaime Bonilla denied ever having threatened Lourdes Maldonado in a radio interview with El Weso de W Radio, saying: “There was only a labor lawsuit, which was for no more than 400 or 500 thousand pesos, which wasn’t enough to kill anyone.”<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:542">542</sup>
narrative.text: On 23 January 2022—barely six days after the murder of Margarito Martínez—Maldonado was shot and killed inside her car as she arrived at her home. The attackers waited for her protection detail to leave before executing the attack, demonstrating both advanced surveillance and awareness of her security arrangements. The killing drew immediate condemnation from the IACHR. In the wake of her murder, then-Governor of Baja California Jaime Bonilla denied ever having threatened Lourdes Maldonado in a radio interview with El Weso de W Radio, saying: “There was only a labor lawsuit, which was for no more than 400 or 500 thousand pesos, which wasn’t enough to kill anyone.”

narrative.html: Regarding federal protection, conflicting accounts persist: the advisor to the State System for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders and Journalists stated that Maldonado was also enrolled in the federal mechanism, while at his 25 January 2022 morning press conference two days after her murder, AMLO stated that Maldonado was not registered in the federal mechanism, a claim echoed by SEGOB.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:543">543</sup>

narrative.html: In February 2022, Erick Eduardo Contreras Ramos, Kevin Alberto Villarino Hernández, and Guillermo Julián Garzón  were arrested for Maldonado’s murder.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:544">544</sup> In October 2022, Contreras Ramos and Villarino Hernández were sentenced to 20 years in prison, while Julián Garzón was sentenced to 24 years as the shooter.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:545">545</sup> According to the Secretariat of Public and Citizen Security, the perpetrators were hired by the Arellano Félix Cartel to kill Maldonado after she reported on the group’s activities.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:546">546</sup> The involvement of the same cartel cell implicated in the Martínez killing raises serious questions about whether these murders were coordinated and whether the protection mechanisms—both state and federal—failed by design or through negligence.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:547">547</sup> In March 2026, a judge charged Jaime Bonilla with embezzlement and abuse of power, after detecting possible irregularities in the handling of public resources during his time as Governor of Baja California.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:548">548</sup> The charges did not relate to the murder of Maldonado, and Bonilla has reportedly not been summoned in the course of the murder investigation. Despite the arrests of Maldonado’s alleged killers, no progress on the investigation has been reported.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:549">549</sup>
narrative.text: In February 2022, Erick Eduardo Contreras Ramos, Kevin Alberto Villarino Hernández, and Guillermo Julián Garzón  were arrested for Maldonado’s murder. In October 2022, Contreras Ramos and Villarino Hernández were sentenced to 20 years in prison, while Julián Garzón was sentenced to 24 years as the shooter. According to the Secretariat of Public and Citizen Security, the perpetrators were hired by the Arellano Félix Cartel to kill Maldonado after she reported on the group’s activities. The involvement of the same cartel cell implicated in the Martínez killing raises serious questions about whether these murders were coordinated and whether the protection mechanisms—both state and federal—failed by design or through negligence. In March 2026, a judge charged Jaime Bonilla with embezzlement and abuse of power, after detecting possible irregularities in the handling of public resources during his time as Governor of Baja California. The charges did not relate to the murder of Maldonado, and Bonilla has reportedly not been summoned in the course of the murder investigation. Despite the arrests of Maldonado’s alleged killers, no progress on the investigation has been reported.

narrative.html: Roberto Toledo was a camera operator, photographer, and video editor for Monitor Michoacán, a digital news outlet based in Zitácuaro, Michoacán, that was the only news source in the city that systematically investigated municipal government corruption.550 The outlet operated from a law office that also financed it. Toledo had published a November 2020 article titled “Cheap Works or Crony Deals?” exposing alleged corruption in public works funded by the municipal government, and his most recent assignment concerned the alleged illicit enrichment of authorities at the Zitácuaro Senior Citizens’ Home. Four days before Toledo’s murder, Monitor Michoacán published a commentary criticizing state authorities for allegedly altering records of individuals arrested on drug possession charges.551
narrative.text: Roberto Toledo was a camera operator, photographer, and video editor for Monitor Michoacán, a digital news outlet based in Zitácuaro, Michoacán, that was the only news source in the city that systematically investigated municipal government corruption. The outlet operated from a law office that also financed it. Toledo had published a November 2020 article titled “Cheap Works or Crony Deals?” exposing alleged corruption in public works funded by the municipal government, and his most recent assignment concerned the alleged illicit enrichment of authorities at the Zitácuaro Senior Citizens’ Home. Four days before Toledo’s murder, Monitor Michoacán published a commentary criticizing state authorities for allegedly altering records of individuals arrested on drug possession charges.

narrative.html: On 31 January 2022, Toledo was shot in the courtyard of the law office that housed Monitor Michoacán. He had been returning from a corner store when he was approached by two men who asked him “where the lawyer was,” in reference to Joel Vera Terrazas, whose law office financed the paper.552 Toledo walked into the courtyard; the men followed and shot him in the torso and forearms, fleeing by motorcycle.553 Minutes later, one of the killers returned to the crime scene and left two cardboard narcomensaje . One, signed by the CJNG, read: “This is what will happen to all the lawyers who handle cases for La Familia Michoacana.” Vera has rejected the claim that he represented any members of organized crime groups; evidence suggests the target was the entire newsroom.554
narrative.text: On 31 January 2022, Toledo was shot in the courtyard of the law office that housed Monitor Michoacán. He had been returning from a corner store when he was approached by two men who asked him “where the lawyer was,” in reference to Joel Vera Terrazas, whose law office financed the paper. Toledo walked into the courtyard; the men followed and shot him in the torso and forearms, fleeing by motorcycle. Minutes later, one of the killers returned to the crime scene and left two cardboard narcomensaje . One, signed by the CJNG, read: “This is what will happen to all the lawyers who handle cases for La Familia Michoacana.” Vera has rejected the claim that he represented any members of organized crime groups; evidence suggests the target was the entire newsroom.

narrative.html: Armando Linares, the news director of Monitor Michoacán, stated publicly that the outlet had been receiving escalating threats as a result of its sustained reporting on corruption in local government.555 “We are not armed, we don’t carry weapons; our only defense is a pen, a pencil, and a notebook,” he said while announcing Toledo’s murder.556 These threats were reported to local authorities, and the team contacted the Attorney General’s Office to alert them to the risk they faced, but their concerns were not taken seriously.557
narrative.text: Armando Linares, the news director of Monitor Michoacán, stated publicly that the outlet had been receiving escalating threats as a result of its sustained reporting on corruption in local government. “We are not armed, we don’t carry weapons; our only defense is a pen, a pencil, and a notebook,” he said while announcing Toledo’s murder. These threats were reported to local authorities, and the team contacted the Attorney General’s Office to alert them to the risk they faced, but their concerns were not taken seriously.

narrative.html: In the immediate aftermath of the murder, a concerted effort emerged at the municipal and federal levels to deny that Toledo was a journalist.558 The mayor of Zitácuaro—whom Monitor Michoacán had investigated—claimed Toledo was not registered in the local journalism registrar. Jesús Ramírez Cuevas, AMLO’s spokesman, initially condemned “the murder of journalist Roberto Toledo” on Twitter.559 However, that same evening, he Tweeted a revised statement: “According to judicial investigations, Roberto Toledo, the citizen murdered today, worked as an assistant at a law firm, not as a journalist.”560 Ricardo Sánchez Pérez del Pozo, the special prosecutor for the city, told the New York Times that the case fell outside his jurisdiction and that analysis had determined that nothing Toledo had published linked him to the circumstances of the murder.561 Following Toledo’s murder, Joel Vera — the lawyer financing Monitor Michoacán — and another member of the team went into hiding under federal protection. Armando Linares, the news director, refused to leave Zitácuaro. He was killed forty-three days later.562

narrative.html: Heber López Vázquez was the founder and editor of NoticiasWeb and RCP Noticias, based in Salina Cruz, Oaxaca. He was a general assignment journalist who, at the time of his death, was covering political issues and the federal megaproject known as the Interoceanic Corridor of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec.563 The day before he was killed, López had published a report accusing local politician Arminda Espinosa Cartas of corruption and mismanagement in the construction of a breakwater in Salinas del Marqués, specifically alleging that she coerced construction workers to vote for her in upcoming elections under threat of dismissal.564
narrative.text: Heber López Vázquez was the founder and editor of NoticiasWeb and RCP Noticias, based in Salina Cruz, Oaxaca. He was a general assignment journalist who, at the time of his death, was covering political issues and the federal megaproject known as the Interoceanic Corridor of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec. The day before he was killed, López had published a report accusing local politician Arminda Espinosa Cartas of corruption and mismanagement in the construction of a breakwater in Salinas del Marqués, specifically alleging that she coerced construction workers to vote for her in upcoming elections under threat of dismissal.

narrative.html: On 10 February 2022, two men in a pickup truck arrived at the radio studio that López operated from his home. One of them entered the studio and shot López dead. López’s twelve-year-old son, who was present in the home, managed to hide until the gunmen departed.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:565">565</sup> López had reportedly received threats related to his journalism as early as 2019.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:566">566</sup> His family was offered protection measures following his murder, though it is unclear whether these were taken up. Mexico’s OHCHR office condemned the murder.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:567">567</sup>
narrative.text: On 10 February 2022, two men in a pickup truck arrived at the radio studio that López operated from his home. One of them entered the studio and shot López dead. López’s twelve-year-old son, who was present in the home, managed to hide until the gunmen departed. López had reportedly received threats related to his journalism as early as 2019. His family was offered protection measures following his murder, though it is unclear whether these were taken up. Mexico’s OHCHR office condemned the murder.

narrative.html: Notably, one of the men arrested shortly after the murder was Ricardo Espinosa Cartas,<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:568">568</sup> the brother of Arminda Espinosa Cartas—the politician about whom López had published multiple articles alleging corruption, including the report published the day before his death.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:569">569</sup> Ricardo Espinosa Cartas and a co-defendant, Ricardo G. R., were convicted as the perpetrators of the homicide and sentenced to thirty-five and forty years’ imprisonment, respectively.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:570">570</sup> This case represents one of the rare instances in which a direct causal link between the victim’s reporting and the murder was established through prosecution, and in which perpetrators received substantial sentences.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:571">571</sup>

Ricardo Espinosa Cartas and a co-defendant, Ricardo G. R., were convicted as the perpetrators of the homicide and sentenced to thirty-five and forty years’ imprisonment, respectively. narrative.html: Jorge Luis Camero Zazueta, known as “El Choche,” was the director and reporter for El Informativo, a news outlet in Empalme, Sonora. In September 2021, he assumed the position of private secretary to Mayor Luis Fuentes Aguilar.572 Two weeks before his murder, Camero requested a leave of absence from that municipal position to return to journalism, following the circulation of a video on social media in which Daniel Palafox Suárez—a former congressman who was kidnapped and killed between 28 January and 4 February 2022—was interrogated by cartel operatives and alleged that Camero was involved in uploading information to media pages that reported on cartel activities.573

In September 2021, he assumed the position of private secretary to Mayor Luis Fuentes Aguilar. Two weeks before his murder, Camero requested a leave of absence from that municipal position to return to journalism, following the circulation of a video on social media in which Daniel Palafox Suárez—a former congressman who was kidnapped and killed between 28 January and 4 February 2022—was interrogated by cartel operatives and alleged that Camero was involved in uploading information to media pages that reported on cartel activities.

narrative.html: On 24 February 2022, Camero was shot eight times while working out at a local gym in Empalme.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:574">574</sup> Following his death, the Sonora Attorney General’s Office and the State Security Secretariat publicly declared that, based on their investigation, “freedom of expression does not appear to be a motive. Definitely not. This is related, rather, to drug dealing.”<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:575">575</sup>  On February 25, Mayor Fuentes Aguilar, whose office had Camero worked in, condemned the murder, stating it had been portrayed as an attempt to “curtail freedom of expression, when I feel that this is not the case.”<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:576">576</sup> ARTICLE 19 challenged this characterization, noting the pattern of authorities rapidly dismissing journalistic motives in the killing of reporters.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:577">577</sup> No arrests have been publicly reported in connection with Camero’s murder.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:578">578</sup>

narrative.html: Juan Carlos Muñiz was a journalist who reported on organized crime for Testigo Minero, writing under the pseudonyms “Rigoberto” and “El TX” to protect his identity.579 Like many journalists in Mexico, Muñiz also worked as a taxi driver to supplement his income from journalism. ARTICLE 19 observed that his case highlighted the economic precarity of journalism in Mexico, where reporters commonly hold multiple jobs—a reality that facilitates official efforts to rule out journalistic motives for murder when the victim held other employment.580
narrative.text: Juan Carlos Muñiz was a journalist who reported on organized crime for Testigo Minero, writing under the pseudonyms “Rigoberto” and “El TX” to protect his identity. Like many journalists in Mexico, Muñiz also worked as a taxi driver to supplement his income from journalism. ARTICLE 19 observed that his case highlighted the economic precarity of journalism in Mexico, where reporters commonly hold multiple jobs—a reality that facilitates official efforts to rule out journalistic motives for murder when the victim held other employment.

narrative.html: On 4 March 2022, Muñiz was found shot dead in his car — which he used both for reporting assignments and as a taxi — in the Los Olivos neighbourhood of Fresnillo, Zacatecas.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:581">581</sup> The same day, the Zacatecas Attorney General's Office declared that it had opened an investigation into the homicide in accordance with cases of attacks against freedom of expression.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:582">582</sup> On 15 March 2022, the Zacatecas Attorney General’s Office announced the arrest of Emanuel de Jesús “N” as the alleged murderer.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:583">583</sup> However, the journalistic community expressed serious concern that the suspect — who was arrested for two separate crimes — was being scapegoated to provide the appearance of resolution and close the case.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:584">584</sup> No clear evidentiary connection between the detainee and Muñiz’s murder has been publicly established.
narrative.text: On 4 March 2022, Muñiz was found shot dead in his car — which he used both for reporting assignments and as a taxi — in the Los Olivos neighbourhood of Fresnillo, Zacatecas. However, the journalistic community expressed serious concern that the suspect — who was arrested for two separate crimes — was being scapegoated to provide the appearance of resolution and close the case. No clear evidentiary connection between the detainee and Muñiz’s murder has been publicly established.

persons.name: Armando Linares López
persons.roleStated: Armando Linares was the founder and news director of Monitor Michoacán
persons.outcomeQuote: The day after Linares’s death, the lawyer financing Monitor Michoacán shut the outlet down and went into hiding, where he remains.

narrative.html: Armando Linares was the founder and news director of Monitor Michoacán, the same outlet for which Roberto Toledo, killed on 31 January 2022, had worked. Linares founded the publication on the premise that if Mexico were to escape the cycle of violence consuming it, the press would have to investigate the politicians who enabled and facilitated organized crime.585 The outlet reported on contract fraud, bribery, and police extortion, and was the only news source in Zitácuaro that systematically scrutinized city hall.586 Among his principal subjects was the mayor, Juan Antonio Ixtláhuac Orihuela, who twelve years earlier had been arrested by federal agents after his name appeared on the CJNG’s payroll, but whose case collapsed and who subsequently regained his office.587
narrative.text: Armando Linares was the founder and news director of Monitor Michoacán, the same outlet for which Roberto Toledo, killed on 31 January 2022, had worked. Linares founded the publication on the premise that if Mexico were to escape the cycle of violence consuming it, the press would have to investigate the politicians who enabled and facilitated organized crime. The outlet reported on contract fraud, bribery, and police extortion, and was the only news source in Zitácuaro that systematically scrutinized city hall. Among his principal subjects was the mayor, Juan Antonio Ixtláhuac Orihuela, who twelve years earlier had been arrested by federal agents after his name appeared on the CJNG’s payroll, but whose case collapsed and who subsequently regained his office.

narrative.html: Linares and his team had received direct threats from the CJNG “to stop burning the local government and the prosecutor’s office.” The outlet’s lawyer reported these threats to a federal official, providing a list of nine politicians — including the mayor and the local prosecutor — whom the newsroom believed were behind the threats.588 According to the New York Times, the federal official “didn’t seem to take the story very seriously, stating that these kinds of threats happened often and that the matter would most likely calm down on its own.” In desperation, the outlet paid approximately $24,000 USD to the CJNG in an attempt to secure the safety of the newsroom. Linares made a public request for protection in the federal Mechanism after this incident, but it is unclear whether it received a response.589 After Toledo’s murder, Linares told CPJ that he was receiving direct death threats.590 He was offered protection and assistance in leaving Zitácuaro, which he refused.591 There are conflicting accounts of whether Linares ever accepted protective measures; the Associated Press reported that his wife stated he had National Guard protection for one month after Toledo’s murder, and CPJ was told by an official of the federal Mechanism that Linares was in-progress of enrolment at the time of his murder.592 However, most other outlets report that he denied protective measures altogether. Authorities subsequently cited this refusal to characterize him as not in danger due to his work. SEGOB Undersecretary for Human Rights Alejandro Encinas later stated that Linares’ decision not to enroll in the federal Mechanism was the reason for his death.593 Federal investigators also sought a court order to wiretap the phones of Linares and the outlet’s lawyer; a judge denied the request, ruling that victims of a crime should not be subjected to such surveillance.594

According to the New York Times, the federal official “didn’t seem to take the story very seriously, stating that these kinds of threats happened often and that the matter would most likely calm down on its own.” In desperation, the outlet paid approximately $24,000 USD to the CJNG in an attempt to secure the safety of the newsroom. Linares made a public request for  protection in the federal Mechanism after this incident, but it is unclear whether it received a response. After Toledo’s murder, Linares told CPJ that he was receiving direct death threats. He was offered protection and assistance in leaving Zitácuaro, which he refused. There are conflicting accounts of whether Linares ever accepted protective measures; the Associated Press reported that his wife stated he had National Guard protection for one month after Toledo’s murder, and CPJ was told by an official of the federal Mechanism that Linares was in-progress of enrolment at the time of his murder. However, most other outlets report that he denied protective measures altogether. Authorities subsequently cited this refusal to characterize him as not in danger due to his work. SEGOB Undersecretary for Human Rights Alejandro Encinas later stated that Linares’ decision not to enroll in the federal Mechanism was the reason for his death. Federal investigators also sought a court order to wiretap the phones of Linares and the outlet’s lawyer; a judge denied the request, ruling that victims of a crime should not be subjected to such surveillance.

narrative.html: On 15 March 2022, forty-three days after Toledo’s murder, a man was observed on security footage approaching Linares as he walked to his apartment.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:595">595</sup> The two were seen speaking before entering together. Minutes later, the man fled the scene. Linares was found inside, shot eight times. Surveillance footage also showed two lookouts casing the area hours before the killing.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:596">596</sup>

The two were seen speaking before entering together. Minutes later, the man fled the scene. Linares was found inside, shot eight times. Surveillance footage also showed two lookouts casing the area hours before the killing.

narrative.html: The day after Linares’s death, the lawyer financing Monitor Michoacán shut the outlet down and went into hiding, where he remains.597 The murders had a devastating chilling effect on independent reporting in the region. At a press conference following Linares’ death, then-mayor and frequent target of Monitor Michoacán reporting Antonio Ixtláhuac warned media outlets and commentators to be very careful with their accusations, saying, “I think there needs to be a lot of care in the expressions of commentators and media outlets, although they are respected, of course, but the municipal government of Zitácuaro cannot allow such flippant expressions either… And I think that sometimes there are intentions to destabilize.”598 Citing data they collected in 2021, ARTICLE 19 wrote that Linares’ muder and the response of authorities sits in a context where 44.25% of journalists attacked cover corruption and politics.599

narrative.html: At Linares’s wake, four unknown men arrived; one approached journalists covering the funeral, waved a pistol, and told them: “If you don’t leave in two minutes, you’ll be sorry.”<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:600">600</sup> Carlos Gerardo Sánchez Mendoza, identified as a CJNG member, was arrested in August 2023 for the murder.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:601">601</sup> However, he was released in March 2025 due to “lack of conclusive evidence.”<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:602">602</sup> In August 2025, a different individual, Magdiel “N,” was arrested for the murder.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:603">603</sup> In a highly-unusual move, the judge revoked Magdiel’s mandatory pretrial detention order, allowing him to face his trial while free.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:604">604</sup> The special prosecutor who had previously dismissed the Toledo case as outside his jurisdiction made the same determination for Linares’s death.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:605">605</sup> In June 2026, two judges involved in the acquittal of Sánchez Mendoza were suspended for alleged irregularities during the investigation first filed in a complaint in December 2025.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:606">606</sup> The administrative investigation into their activities is ongoing.
narrative.text: At Linares’s wake, four unknown men arrived; one approached journalists covering the funeral, waved a pistol, and told them: “If you don’t leave in two minutes, you’ll be sorry.” Carlos Gerardo Sánchez Mendoza, identified as a CJNG member, was arrested in August 2023 for the murder. However, he was released in March 2025 due to “lack of conclusive evidence.” In August 2025, a different individual, Magdiel “N,” was arrested for the murder. In a highly-unusual move, the judge revoked Magdiel’s mandatory pretrial detention order, allowing him to face his trial while free. The special prosecutor who had previously dismissed the Toledo case as outside his jurisdiction made the same determination for Linares’s death. In June 2026, two judges involved in the acquittal of Sánchez Mendoza were suspended for alleged irregularities during the investigation first filed in a complaint in December 2025. The administrative investigation into their activities is ongoing.

narrative.html: Luis Enrique Ramírez Ramos was a veteran journalist with a forty-year career who had contributed to some of Mexico’s leading national newspapers and who covered local political issues in Culiacán, Sinaloa.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:607">607</sup> In a 2015 interview, Ramírez disclosed that he and three friends—all of whom were subsequently murdered—had been privy to sensitive information about former Sinaloa Governor Mario López Valdez and ex-government secretary Gerardo Vargas Landeros.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:608">608</sup> Ramírez stated that the threats he had received originated from the state government. He had gone into hiding in 2011 following these threats, taking temporary refuge in Mexico City.

narrative.html: Yesenia Mollinedo Falconi was the founder and director of El Veraz, a local news outlet in Cosoleacaque, Veracruz, which she established in 2015.615 Sheila Johana García was a camera operator for the outlet who had been trained by Mollinedo and issued a press credential only five days before her death, on 4 May 2022.616 Cosoleacaque is located in the southern border area of Veracruz, near Minatitlán, where thirteen people were killed in a mass shooting in 2019.617 The threats against Mollinedo began after she published articles critical of the Veracruz State Public Security Secretariat.618
narrative.text: Yesenia Mollinedo Falconi was the founder and director of El Veraz, a local news outlet in Cosoleacaque, Veracruz, which she established in 2015. Sheila Johana García was a camera operator for the outlet who had been trained by Mollinedo and issued a press credential only five days before her death, on 4 May 2022. Cosoleacaque is located in the southern border area of Veracruz, near Minatitlán, where thirteen people were killed in a mass shooting in 2019. The threats against Mollinedo began after she published articles critical of the Veracruz State Public Security Secretariat.

narrative.html: On 9 May 2022, armed men shot both journalists at least seven times outside a convenience store at the intersection of Benito Juárez and Francisco I. Madero streets in Cosoleacaque at approximately 4:00 p.m.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:619">619</sup> The victims were about to enter a vehicle when gunmen who appeared to have been lying in wait opened fire.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:620">620</sup> Both women were transported to hospital, where they died of their injuries. García’s death was almost certainly collateral: Mollinedo, the target, was the journalist whose reporting had provoked threats.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:621">621</sup> Prior to her death, Mollinedo had told her mother that she was afraid and had been receiving threats by telephone. She was also aware of suspicious individuals following her habitual routes. On 30 April 2022, approximately nine days before the attack, she was threatened by men who were following her. These threats reportedly began when Yesenia started publishing articles critical of the Veracruz State Public Security Secretariat.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:622">622</sup>
narrative.text: On 9 May 2022, armed men shot both journalists at least seven times outside a convenience store at the intersection of Benito Juárez and Francisco I. Madero streets in Cosoleacaque at approximately 4:00 p.m. The victims were about to enter a vehicle when gunmen who appeared to have been lying in wait opened fire. Both women were transported to hospital, where they died of their injuries. García’s death was almost certainly collateral: Mollinedo, the target, was the journalist whose reporting had provoked threats. Prior to her death, Mollinedo had told her mother that she was afraid and had been receiving threats by telephone. She was also aware of suspicious individuals following her habitual routes. On 30 April 2022, approximately nine days before the attack, she was threatened by men who were following her. These threats reportedly began when Yesenia started publishing articles critical of the Veracruz State Public Security Secretariat.

narrative.html: In the chaotic aftermath, the Veracruz prosecutor’s office mistakenly detained a university student and food delivery worker from Xalapa who happened to share the same name as a suspect, Antonio de Jesús “N” (“El Mara”). The wrongfully detained individual was released the same evening, hours after his detention on 17 May 2022, following public protests demanding his release.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:623">623</sup> Subsequently, Armando “N” (“El Trascabo”) was arrested on 6 June 2022, and Víctor Manuel “N” (“El Calaco”) on 8 June 2022. Both were formally charged with the murders.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:624">624</sup> The correct Antonio de Jesús “N” (“El Mara”) was arrested on 28 October 2022 and charged on 4 November 2022 for both murders.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:625">625</sup> It is unclear what stage the investigation is currently in.

narrative.html: Antonio de la Cruz was a reporter for El Expreso in Ciudad Victoria, Tamaulipas, where he had worked for more than two decades.626 While his beat for the newspaper focused on environmental issues—particularly drought and water shortages—De la Cruz also used his personal social media accounts to call out government officials for corruption, exposing alleged malfeasance by local politicians.627
narrative.text: Antonio de la Cruz was a reporter for El Expreso in Ciudad Victoria, Tamaulipas, where he had worked for more than two decades. While his beat for the newspaper focused on environmental issues—particularly drought and water shortages—De la Cruz also used his personal social media accounts to call out government officials for corruption, exposing alleged malfeasance by local politicians.

narrative.html: On 29 June 2022, at approximately 9:15 AM., De la Cruz was shot dead outside his home as he sat in his car with his twenty-three-year-old daughter, whom he was taking to work. Two armed men on motorcycles opened fire, killing him with four bullets fired from a .40 caliber weapon for the exclusive use of the Army.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:628">628</sup> His daughter was struck in the head. She was taken to a hospital, where emergency surgery was unsuccessful and she died.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:629">629</sup>
narrative.text: On 29 June 2022, at approximately 9:15 AM., De la Cruz was shot dead outside his home as he sat in his car with his twenty-three-year-old daughter, whom he was taking to work. Two armed men on motorcycles opened fire, killing him with four bullets fired from a .40 caliber weapon for the exclusive use of the Army. His daughter was struck in the head. She was taken to a hospital, where emergency surgery was unsuccessful and she died.

narrative.html: No direct threats against De la Cruz were documented prior to the attack, and he was not enrolled in the journalism protection mechanism.630 However, on 20 December 2018—nineteen days into the AMLO presidency—a severed human head and hands were left outside the offices of El Expreso, constituting a general threat against the publication.631
narrative.text: No direct threats against De la Cruz were documented prior to the attack, and he was not enrolled in the journalism protection mechanism. However, on 20 December 2018—nineteen days into the AMLO presidency—a severed human head and hands were left outside the offices of El Expreso, constituting a general threat against the publication.

narrative.html: The federal Attorney General assumed jurisdiction after allegations emerged that municipal authorities may have been involved in the murder.632 ONU-DU and CNDH condemned the murder.633 In 2025, FEADLE determined that De la Cruz’s murder was indeed attributable to his journalistic reporting: specifically, that hitmen from organized crime had travelled from Nuevo Laredo to Ciudad Victoria to kill him in retaliation for information he published about a criminal gang in El Expreso.634 Rafael Santiago Arano Rodríguez, “El Piña,” was first identified as a suspect in November 2022 and has been imprisoned in a state facility in Nuevo Laredo since 2023 for alleged responsibility in the crime, though the trial has been delayed by defence appeals.635

In 2025, FEADLE determined that De la Cruz’s murder was indeed attributable to his journalistic reporting: specifically, that hitmen from organized crime had travelled from Nuevo Laredo to Ciudad Victoria to kill him in retaliation for information he published about a criminal gang in El Expreso. Rafael Santiago Arano Rodríguez, “El Piña,” was first identified as a suspect in November 2022 and has been imprisoned  in a state facility in Nuevo Laredo since 2023 for alleged responsibility in the crime, though the trial has been delayed by defence appeals.

narrative.html: Rubén Haro Madero was the founder of Noticias de la Red, a digital news outlet in Sonora, and also served as a public relations official for the municipal government of Nogales.636 On 17 July 2022, at approximately 2:00 a.m., assailants in a white Honda pickup truck pulled alongside Haro’s car on a road in the Fundó Legal neighbourhood of Ciudad Obregón and fired five shots at him. Haro survived the attack.637 Approximately one hour before the shooting, Haro’s news outlet had published two videos of shootings in Ciudad Obregón.638 Haro told CPJ that he had never previously received threats or been targeted. Sonora’s Attorney General’s Office opened an investigation and referred the case to the FEADLE Sonora office.639 Following the attack, Haro contacted the federal Protection Mechanism with a view to joining a protection programme, but no further details are publicly available regarding the outcome.640

narrative.html: Ernesto Méndez was the editorial director of local news website Tu Voz, and also contributed to Periódico Correo and Zona Franca. While he primarily covered general news, ARTICLE 19 disclosed that he had a history of threats dating back seven years, linked to the administration of the late mayor of San Luis de la Paz, Guanajuato, Timoteo Villa.641 On 2 August 2022, Méndez was shot and killed along with two other people at a bar that he owned, at approximately 23:00. Two others were injured in the attack.642 On 11 August 2022, the SSPC reported that the murder was related to the extortion of the family business and announced the arrest of one suspect, Roberto “N,” identified as one of two alleged perpetrators. No further update has been provided.643

narrative.html: On 11 August 2022, Allan González, a radio announcer at Switch 105.9 FM, along with three non-editorial colleagues—including Armando Guerrero, the operations manager, as well as Lino Flores and Alejandro Arriaga—were recording a promotional segment with a mobile unit outside a Little Caesar’s pizzeria on Ejército Nacional Avenue in Ciudad Juárez when they were killed by an armed group.644 The attack occurred during a broader wave of coordinated violence by alleged members of organized crime across the neighbourhood, in which civilians were targeted and businesses were set ablaze.645 In an interview with ARTICLE 19, anonymous sources confirmed that none of the outlet’s contributors had reported prior threats; González’s programming focused primarily on music. Although the attacks were attributed to the Los Mexicles gang, affiliated with the Sinaloa Cartel, the killing of the radio station employees may have been incidental to the broader campaign of terror.646 Filming publicly in Ciudad Juárez on a day where 11 people were killed may have made the journalists a target.647 Six members of Los Mexicles were arrested for their participation in the violent acts. Following the attack, other employees of the radio station received threats related to their coverage of the events.648

narrative.html: In a finding of significant relevance to this report, investigative reporting by Lighthouse Reports and Haaretz revealed that, on 21 August 2022—the day before Román’s murder—his phone was targeted using telecommunications surveillance infrastructure.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:651">651</sup> Confidential network data showed that a global title leased by a Swiss surveillance broker was used to attempt to extract location data and other information from Román’s device, a technique consistent with SS7 network exploitation.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:652">652</sup> While the precise individual who issued the surveillance command remains unknown, the use of sophisticated telecommunications interception capabilities against a journalist—on the eve of his assassination—raises grave concerns about the involvement of state or state-adjacent actors.

narrative.html: On 22 August 2022, at approximately 4:30 p.m., two men on a motorcycle approached Román as he got into his car outside his home and shot him dead. His death came just one month after his son, Bladimir Román, was shot and killed in Ocotito.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:653">653</sup> During the funeral procession, Román’s relatives revealed that they had received death threats from alleged members of organized crime.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:654">654</sup> On the same day as Román’s funeral, more than fifty journalists protested against impunity for the killing of Román and other Mexican journalists outside the Attorney General’s Office in Mexico City.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:655">655</sup>

His death came just one month after his son, Bladimir Román, was shot and killed in Ocotito. During the funeral procession, Román’s relatives revealed that they had received death threats from alleged members of organized crime. On the same day as Román’s funeral, more than fifty journalists protested against impunity for the killing of Román and other Mexican journalists outside the Attorney General’s Office in Mexico City.

narrative.html: The Guerrero Attorney General’s Office opened an investigation examining whether Román’s journalistic work motivated the murder and whether it was connected to his son’s killing.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:656">656</sup> Investigative lines have included a turf war between rival criminal factions over the poultry distribution industry in Chilpancingo, specifically between the Citizen Police of El Ocotito (the armed wing of Los Ardillos, led by José David Barrientos Salazar “El Deivid”) and Los Jaleacos.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:657">657</sup> Barrientos has publicly accused the Román family of having ties to the CJNG and has claimed that allegations linking him to the journalist’s murder are part of a strategy by a rival cartel.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:658">658</sup> In February 2023, José “N,” alias “El Deibi,” was arrested for Román’s murder.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:659">659</sup> “El Deibi” is reportedly the head of a community policing organization affiliated with the armed wing of the criminal group “Los Ardillos.” He was formally charged with Román’s murder in April 2023; no public updates on the case have been shared since.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:660">660</sup>

narrative.text: Roberto Carlos Flores Mendoza, aged 41, was the founder and director of Chiapas Denuncia YA, a Facebook-based news outlet he created in October 2018 covering local and state politics, public security, and citizen complaints of alleged official corruption and abuse in the Comitán de Domínguez region of Chiapas. By 2022 the page had roughly 66,000 followers and published citizens' reports about crime, security, and alleged government corruption. Before turning to journalism, Flores Mendoza had worked for the Comitán de Domínguez municipal government.

narrative.html: On the morning of 20 September 2022, at approximately 11:30 a.m., Flores Mendoza was last seen in the city of Comitán de Domínguez, in the La Pileta neighborhood, according to the missing-person report his wife filed with the FGE of Chiapas.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:663">663</sup> The FGE opened an investigation, and state authorities notified the federal Comisión Nacional de Búsqueda on 21 September. Relatives told local media that he had been intercepted by men traveling in a pickup truck while driving his own vehicle; the official FGE bulletin records only that he was last seen by his wife and does not characterize the disappearance as an abduction. A spokesperson for the FGE told CPJ that authorities had not yet determined whether Flores was abducted, and as of the following week authorities had not established whether the case was connected to his journalistic work.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:664">664</sup>

The FGE opened an investigation, and state authorities notified the federal Comisión Nacional de Búsqueda on 21 September. Relatives told local media that he had been intercepted by men traveling in a pickup truck while driving his own vehicle; the official FGE bulletin records only that he was last seen by his wife and does not characterize the disappearance as an abduction. A spokesperson for the FGE told CPJ that authorities had not yet determined whether Flores was abducted, and as of the following week authorities had not established whether the case was connected to his journalistic work.

narrative.html: Around the time of his disappearance, Chiapas Denuncia YA had posted a report about criminal gangs in the area, which was removed shortly afterward; multiple outlets reported that the deleted post concerned an alleged internal dispute within the Sinaloa Cartel in Chiapas. ARTICLE 19 documented the case and reported, based on testimony it gathered, that Flores had indicated he was the target of intimidating messages and that his final post, addressing organized crime, was removed on 19 September. ARTICLE 19 urged the Chiapas government and the federal Secretaría de Gobernación to coordinate with the Comisión Nacional de Búsqueda under the Protocolo Homologado para la Búsqueda de Personas, and CPJ called on Mexican authorities to undertake a credible and exhaustive investigation, noting that 2022 was the deadliest year on record for the country's press.

narrative.html: Ciro Gómez Leyva was one of Mexico’s most prominent broadcast journalists, serving as the presenter of Imagen Televisión’s nightly national news programme and host of the radio show Por la Mañana. His high-profile position made him a frequent subject of public commentary, including by AMLO himself.665
narrative.text: Ciro Gómez Leyva was one of Mexico’s most prominent broadcast journalists, serving as the presenter of Imagen Televisión’s nightly national news programme and host of the radio show Por la Mañana. His high-profile position made him a frequent subject of public commentary, including by AMLO himself.

narrative.html: In 2021, AMLO introduced a weekly segment to his morning press conference, “Who’s Who in Lies,” which was used to publicly single out and discredit journalists and media figures.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:666">666</sup> In the segment broadcast on 14 December 2022, two days before Gómez Leyva’s assassination attempt, the President targeted him and two other journalists, stating that “if you listen to them too much, you might even develop a brain tumour.”<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:667">667</sup> AMLO had previously criticized Gómez Leyva publicly on numerous occasions, suggesting that the journalist was overpaid.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:668">668</sup>
narrative.text: In 2021, AMLO introduced a weekly segment to his morning press conference, “Who’s Who in Lies,” which was used to publicly single out and discredit journalists and media figures. In the segment broadcast on 14 December 2022, two days before Gómez Leyva’s assassination attempt, the President targeted him and two other journalists, stating that “if you listen to them too much, you might even develop a brain tumour.” AMLO had previously criticized Gómez Leyva publicly on numerous occasions, suggesting that the journalist was overpaid.

narrative.html: On the evening of 15 December 2022, Gómez Leyva was driving through Coyoacán Avenue in southern Mexico City when a motorcycle carrying two individuals approached his vehicle. One of the riders turned, drew a firearm, pointed it at the journalist’s head, and opened fire.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:669">669</sup> Gómez Leyva survived solely because the vehicle’s armoured plating and bulletproof windows stopped the rounds.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:670">670</sup> The armoured car had been provided to him by his network for the short nightly journey between the studio and his house, following earlier threats related to his reporting on Mexico’s northern prisons.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:671">671</sup>
narrative.text: On the evening of 15 December 2022, Gómez Leyva was driving through Coyoacán Avenue in southern Mexico City when a motorcycle carrying two individuals approached his vehicle. One of the riders turned, drew a firearm, pointed it at the journalist’s head, and opened fire. Gómez Leyva survived solely because the vehicle’s armoured plating and bulletproof windows stopped the rounds. The armoured car had been provided to him by his network for the short nightly journey between the studio and his house, following earlier threats related to his reporting on Mexico’s northern prisons.

narrative.html: Alan García Aguilar was the founder of Escenario Calentano, a Facebook-based news page covering the Tierra Caliente region of Guerrero. In the months leading up to his disappearance, the page had published extensive coverage of the activities of La Familia Michoacana, a criminal organization operating in the region.678
narrative.text: Alan García Aguilar was the founder of Escenario Calentano, a Facebook-based news page covering the Tierra Caliente region of Guerrero. In the months leading up to his disappearance, the page had published extensive coverage of the activities of La Familia Michoacana, a criminal organization operating in the region.

narrative.html: On 27 December 2022, García Aguilar was kidnapped, along with fellow journalist Jesús Pintor Alegre and website administrator Fernando Moreno. The three were abducted separately but held together. A fourth individual, José Alberto Benítez Santos, a municipal employee, was kidnapped separately after being mistaken for one of the page’s administrators.679 Pintor Alegre later recounted being questioned, beaten, and accused of being the administrator of Escenario Calentano. A video was posted by the perpetrators on the Escenario Calentano Facebook page itself, showing two of the captives, García Aguilar and Moreno, chained hand and foot, with García Aguilar stating: “Escenario Calentano was created five years ago; I was the one who founded the page.”680 The captors’ accompanying message allegedly read: “So you can see that sooner or later we’ll catch the assholes.”681
narrative.text: On 27 December 2022, García Aguilar was kidnapped, along with fellow journalist Jesús Pintor Alegre and website administrator Fernando Moreno. The three were abducted separately but held together. A fourth individual, José Alberto Benítez Santos, a municipal employee, was kidnapped separately after being mistaken for one of the page’s administrators. Pintor Alegre later recounted being questioned, beaten, and accused of being the administrator of Escenario Calentano. A video was posted by the perpetrators on the Escenario Calentano Facebook page itself, showing two of the captives, García Aguilar and Moreno, chained hand and foot, with García Aguilar stating: “Escenario Calentano was created five years ago; I was the one who founded the page.” The captors’ accompanying message allegedly read: “So you can see that sooner or later we’ll catch the assholes.”

narrative.html: On 10 and 11 January 2023, the Guerrero State Attorney General’s office issued two statements that they were investigating the kidnapping.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:682">682</sup> Pintor Alegre and Moreno were released on 11 January 2023. Benítez Santos was released on 22 January 2023. Alan García Aguilar remains forcibly disappeared. Multiple sources attribute responsibility to La Familia Michoacana.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:683">683</sup> No prosecutions have been reported, and no legal follow-up on the cases of the surviving victims has been publicly disclosed.

incidents.heading: Marco Aurelio Ramírez Hernández — Killed, 23 May 2023, Puebla

incidents.identity: Marco Aurelio Ramírez Hernández was a veteran journalist based in Tehuacán, Puebla.
