narrative.html: Marco Aurelio Ramírez Hernández was a veteran journalist based in Tehuacán, Puebla. He was a crime reporter for the news programme Cuarto Poder and hosted a programme on Estéreo Luz FM in which he analyzed aspects of public life in the state of Puebla, including human rights violations and alleged irregularities in the exercise of public office.684 His reporting was notably critical: he had previously covered allegations against the priest Nicolás Aguilar, accused of abusing more than 80 minors.685 Ramírez Hernández had also served as the Director of Public Safety and Government for the Tehuacán City Council for nine months in 2019, during which time he contributed to the dismantling of a criminal organisation involved in fuel smuggling, drug trafficking, and human trafficking.686 During that tenure, members of the “Bigotonas” criminal gang were apprehended, which investigators allegedly identified later as a potential motive for his assassination.687
narrative.text: Marco Aurelio Ramírez Hernández was a veteran journalist based in Tehuacán, Puebla. He was a crime reporter for the news programme Cuarto Poder and hosted a programme on Estéreo Luz FM in which he analyzed aspects of public life in the state of Puebla, including human rights violations and alleged irregularities in the exercise of public office. His reporting was notably critical: he had previously covered allegations against the priest Nicolás Aguilar, accused of abusing more than 80 minors. Ramírez Hernández had also served as the Director of Public Safety and Government for the Tehuacán City Council for nine months in 2019, during which time he contributed to the dismantling of a criminal organisation involved in fuel smuggling, drug trafficking, and human trafficking. During that tenure, members of the “Bigotonas” criminal gang were apprehended, which investigators allegedly identified later as a potential motive for his assassination.

narrative.html: On 23 May 2023, at approximately 1:45 p.m., Ramírez Hernández was leaving a residence and boarding his vehicle in the Fraccionamiento Agua Blanca in Tehuacán when two armed men approached and opened fire, striking him at least five times.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:688">688</sup> His vehicle subsequently struck a tree. Ramírez Hernández died at the scene. ARTICLE 19 reportedly requested protective measures for his family following the killing, as did CNDH, though it is unclear whether such measures were ever implemented.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:689">689</sup>
narrative.text: On 23 May 2023, at approximately 1:45 p.m., Ramírez Hernández was leaving a residence and boarding his vehicle in the Fraccionamiento Agua Blanca in Tehuacán when two armed men approached and opened fire, striking him at least five times. His vehicle subsequently struck a tree. Ramírez Hernández died at the scene. ARTICLE 19 reportedly requested protective measures for his family following the killing, as did CNDH, though it is unclear whether such measures were ever implemented.

narrative.html: The assassination drew immediate and widespread condemnation from international bodies. The OHCHR in Mexico called upon the authorities to redouble efforts for a prompt and effective investigation and to include the victim’s journalistic work as a line of inquiry.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:690">690</sup> The UNESCO Director-General condemned the killing and urged accountability.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:691">691</sup> RSF demanded an exhaustive investigation.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:692">692</sup> On 26 May 2023, CNDH announced it would monitor the state of Puebla’s investigation into Ramírez Hernández’s killing.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:693">693</sup>
narrative.text: The assassination drew immediate and widespread condemnation from international bodies. The OHCHR in Mexico called upon the authorities to redouble efforts for a prompt and effective investigation and to include the victim’s journalistic work as a line of inquiry. The UNESCO Director-General condemned the killing and urged accountability. RSF demanded an exhaustive investigation. On 26 May 2023, CNDH announced it would monitor the state of Puebla’s investigation into Ramírez Hernández’s killing.

narrative.html: On 31 May 2023, José Francisco N. was arrested for drug trafficking, and was charged on 12 July for aggravated homicide in the murder of Ramírez Hernández.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:694">694</sup> In September 2024, Jesús Armando N., alias “El Güero” was arrested by the Attorney General's Office of the State of Puebla and the State Public Security Secretariat for the murder of Ramírez Hernández.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:695">695</sup> After nearly three years of legal proceedings comprising 24 hearings and the presentation of 50 items of evidence, on 16 February 2026, the Tribunal de Enjuiciamiento of the Judicial Branch of Puebla found Jesús Armando N. and José Francisco N. guilty of aggravated intentional homicide. The court determined that the killing was directly related to the victim’s journalistic activity, specifically his investigation into criminal gangs operating in the Tehuacán region.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:696">696</sup> On 26 February 2026, both were sentenced to 46 years and five months of imprisonment.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:697">697</sup> A third implicated individual remains a fugitive, and the intellectual authors of the crime have not been identified.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:698">698</sup>
narrative.text: On 31 May 2023, José Francisco N. was arrested for drug trafficking, and was charged on 12 July for aggravated homicide in the murder of Ramírez Hernández. In September 2024, Jesús Armando N., alias “El Güero” was arrested by the Attorney General's Office of the State of Puebla and the State Public Security Secretariat for the murder of Ramírez Hernández. After nearly three years of legal proceedings comprising 24 hearings and the presentation of 50 items of evidence, on 16 February 2026, the Tribunal de Enjuiciamiento of the Judicial Branch of Puebla found Jesús Armando N. and José Francisco N. guilty of aggravated intentional homicide. The court determined that the killing was directly related to the victim’s journalistic activity, specifically his investigation into criminal gangs operating in the Tehuacán region. On 26 February 2026, both were sentenced to 46 years and five months of imprisonment. A third implicated individual remains a fugitive, and the intellectual authors of the crime have not been identified.

narrative.html: On the morning of 6 July 2023, Hinojosa Viveros was last seen in the Factoría area of Nanchital, in the vicinity of the Pemex complex. He was allegedly intercepted by unknown individuals who abducted him in a white van.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:700">700</sup>

narrative.html: As of the date of this report, no substantive updates on the investigation into his disappearance have been made public.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:701">701</sup> Reporting indicates that the journalist’s family has sought to halt any advocacy or additional investigation not completed by the Veracruz Attorney General’s Office; they have not spoken with any media.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:702">702</sup> They successfully lobbied the Veracruz State Commission for the Attention and Protection of Journalists to stop collaborating with the FGE.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:703">703</sup> This raises the troubling possibility that they have been subjected to threats or intimidation by those responsible for the disappearance. Hinojosa Viveros remains one of Mexico’s disappeared journalists, and his case exemplifies the particular dangers faced by reporters covering sensitive topics in regions where criminal organizations exercise de facto control.

narrative.html: Luis Martín Sánchez Íñiguez, aged 59, was a journalist who served as a correspondent for the national newspaper La Jornada and a contributor to the digital outlet criticadn.mx, both based in Tepic, Nayarit. He was a seasoned crime and public security reporter in one of Mexico’s most violent regions.704
narrative.text: Luis Martín Sánchez Íñiguez, aged 59, was a journalist who served as a correspondent for the national newspaper La Jornada and a contributor to the digital outlet criticadn.mx, both based in Tepic, Nayarit. He was a seasoned crime and public security reporter in one of Mexico’s most violent regions.

narrative.html: Three days prior to his disappearance, Sánchez Íñiguez published an article relaying information from the state prosecutor’s office concerning the recovery of eight bodies from a clandestine grave known as “Devil’s Cave,” situated on the northern slope of San Juan Hill, between the limits of Tepic and the municipality of Xalisco.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:705">705</sup> This article attracted significant public attention and may have constituted the trigger for his abduction.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:706">706</sup>
narrative.text: Three days prior to his disappearance, Sánchez Íñiguez published an article relaying information from the state prosecutor’s office concerning the recovery of eight bodies from a clandestine grave known as “Devil’s Cave,” situated on the northern slope of San Juan Hill, between the limits of Tepic and the municipality of Xalisco. This article attracted significant public attention and may have constituted the trigger for his abduction.

narrative.html: Sánchez Íñiguez’s wife, Cecilia López, last spoke to him on the evening of 5 July 2023 after he returned alone to the family residence in Tepic following a visit to a nearby town. The next day, when he ceased answering his mobile phone, López’s son went to the residence and discovered that his father was gone, along with his laptop computer, mobile phone, and his La Jornada press credential.707 La Jornada subsequently reported that Sánchez Íñiguez’s computer and digital storage devices had been taken from his home, suggesting the perpetrators sought to seize evidence of his investigative work.708
narrative.text: Sánchez Íñiguez’s wife, Cecilia López, last spoke to him on the evening of 5 July 2023 after he returned alone to the family residence in Tepic following a visit to a nearby town. The next day, when he ceased answering his mobile phone, López’s son went to the residence and discovered that his father was gone, along with his laptop computer, mobile phone, and his La Jornada press credential. La Jornada subsequently reported that Sánchez Íñiguez’s computer and digital storage devices had been taken from his home, suggesting the perpetrators sought to seize evidence of his investigative work.

narrative.html: On 8 July 2023, Sánchez Íñiguez’s body was discovered in the village of El Ahuacate near Tepic, bearing clear signs of torture. His body was found bound, with a message affixed to his chest by means of an ice pick, reading: “You can write whatever you want, but don’t mess with the family.”<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:709">709</sup> Authorities estimated that the body had been at the site for 24 to 48 hours before discovery.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:710">710</sup>
narrative.text: On 8 July 2023, Sánchez Íñiguez’s body was discovered in the village of El Ahuacate near Tepic, bearing clear signs of torture. His body was found bound, with a message affixed to his chest by means of an ice pick, reading: “You can write whatever you want, but don’t mess with the family.” Authorities estimated that the body had been at the site for 24 to 48 hours before discovery.

narrative.html: The Nayarit State Attorney General’s office published a statement acknowledging that Sánchez Íñiguez’s work as a journalist was a significant motive for his killing.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:711">711</sup> By 14 July, FEADLE assumed jurisdiction over the case.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:712">712</sup> Notwithstanding, a climate of secrecy surrounded the investigation, with limited information released to the public or to the victim’s family.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:713">713</sup> In May 2025, Juseff Farid “N” was arrested for and charged with Sánchez Íñiguez’s murder. The district judge alleged that Farid “N” participated in the kidnapping and murder of the journalist along with two others. No other updates on the case have since been made public.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:714">714</sup> The method of killing—abduction, torture, and the display of a threatening message—bears the hallmarks of organized crime reprisal against journalists whose reporting threatens criminal interests.

The district judge alleged that Farid “N” participated in the kidnapping and murder of the journalist along with two others. No other updates on the case have since been made public. The method of killing—abduction, torture, and the display of a threatening message—bears the hallmarks of organized crime reprisal against journalists whose reporting threatens criminal interests.

incidents.title: Nelson Matus Peña
incidents.heading: Nelson Matus Peña — Killed, 15 July 2023, Guerrero
incidents.place: the parking lot of a Coppel department store in the Emiliano Zapata neighbourhood on Vicente Guerrero Avenue in Acapulco
incidents.identity: Nelson Matus Peña was the founder and director of the online news outlet Lo Real de Guerrero

narrative.html: Nelson Matus Peña was the founder and director of the online news outlet Lo Real de Guerrero, a platform that focused extensively on coverage of violence and criminal activity in Acapulco, Guerrero.715 Before entering journalism, Matus had served as a member of the Acapulco Fire Department, through which he developed close relationships with members of the security forces, including police and the Red Cross.716 He became deeply trusted within his community and, owing to these relationships, at times received information about criminal incidents before law enforcement agencies, making Lo Real de Guerrero a leading real-time source of information on crime in the Acapulco region.717
narrative.text: Nelson Matus Peña was the founder and director of the online news outlet Lo Real de Guerrero, a platform that focused extensively on coverage of violence and criminal activity in Acapulco, Guerrero. Before entering journalism, Matus had served as a member of the Acapulco Fire Department, through which he developed close relationships with members of the security forces, including police and the Red Cross. He became deeply trusted within his community and, owing to these relationships, at times received information about criminal incidents before law enforcement agencies, making Lo Real de Guerrero a leading real-time source of information on crime in the Acapulco region.

narrative.html: Matus had survived at least two prior assassination attempts. In 2017, he survived an armed attack.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:718">718</sup> In 2019, individuals opened fire on him while he was driving his vehicle; on that occasion he escaped unharmed.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:719">719</sup> In the days immediately preceding his death, his outlet published several stories without bylines covering violent incidents and deadly shootouts in Acapulco, consistent with an environment in which the journalists were aware of the personal risks their reporting entailed.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:720">720</sup>
narrative.text: Matus had survived at least two prior assassination attempts. In 2017, he survived an armed attack. In 2019, individuals opened fire on him while he was driving his vehicle; on that occasion he escaped unharmed. In the days immediately preceding his death, his outlet published several stories without bylines covering violent incidents and deadly shootouts in Acapulco, consistent with an environment in which the journalists were aware of the personal risks their reporting entailed.

narrative.html: On 15 July 2023, at approximately 3:00 p.m., Matus was shot twice—including once in the head—while standing outside his vehicle in the parking lot of a Coppel department store in the Emiliano Zapata neighbourhood on Vicente Guerrero Avenue in Acapulco. He was found beside the driver’s side door and died from the gunshot wound to his head.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:721">721</sup> Some reporting indicates that Matus was alive when he was found, and died en-route to the hospital.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:722">722</sup>
narrative.text: On 15 July 2023, at approximately 3:00 p.m., Matus was shot twice—including once in the head—while standing outside his vehicle in the parking lot of a Coppel department store in the Emiliano Zapata neighbourhood on Vicente Guerrero Avenue in Acapulco. He was found beside the driver’s side door and died from the gunshot wound to his head. Some reporting indicates that Matus was alive when he was found, and died en-route to the hospital.

narrative.html: Authorities in Guerrero sought to distance the killing from Matus’s journalistic work. Officials circulated suggestions that the speed with which Matus arrived at crime scenes indicated he was being tipped off by criminals as early as 2017, and that a rumour was disseminated that the journalist was acting as a spokesman for a cartel.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:723">723</sup> Press freedom organizations identified this as characteristic of the criminalization of journalists by authorities in Mexico at large—whereby officials deflect responsibility by impugning the character of murdered reporters. No arrests have been made in connection with the killing. The case remains unsolved.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:724">724</sup>

incidents.heading: Jesús Gutiérrez Vergara — Killed, 25 September 2023, Sonora
incidents.place: outside his home in the Colonia Aviación neighbourhood
incidents.identity: Jesús Gutiérrez Vergara, aged 47, was the founder and director of Notiface Prensa Digital, an online news platform based in San Luis Río Colorado, Sonora.

narrative.html: Jesús Gutiérrez Vergara, aged 47, was the founder and director of Notiface Prensa Digital, an online news platform based in San Luis Río Colorado, Sonora. He was a known crime reporter who broadcast live police activities on social media and had published material concerning the arrest of an alleged drug trafficker and videos of police vehicles responding to incidents just days before his murder.725 In the early hours of 25 September 2023, Gutiérrez Vergara was outside his home in the Colonia Aviación neighbourhood, speaking with four off-duty municipal police officers, one of whom was his neighbour. A vehicle carrying armed men arrived and opened fire . The attack killed Gutiérrez Vergara and one police officer and wounded three other officers.726
narrative.text: Jesús Gutiérrez Vergara, aged 47, was the founder and director of Notiface Prensa Digital, an online news platform based in San Luis Río Colorado, Sonora. He was a known crime reporter who broadcast live police activities on social media and had published material concerning the arrest of an alleged drug trafficker and videos of police vehicles responding to incidents just days before his murder. In the early hours of 25 September 2023, Gutiérrez Vergara was outside his home in the Colonia Aviación neighbourhood, speaking with four off-duty municipal police officers, one of whom was his neighbour. A vehicle carrying armed men arrived and opened fire . The attack killed Gutiérrez Vergara and one police officer and wounded three other officers.

narrative.html: Officials characterized Gutiérrez Vergara as collateral damage in an attack directed at the police officers rather than at the journalist himself.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:727">727</sup> RSF and ARTICLE 19 publicly challenged this characterization and called upon investigators to consider his journalistic work as a line of inquiry.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:728">728</sup> The UNESCO Director-General condemned the killing, as did Mexico’s OHCHR branch.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:729">729</sup> The National Press Club issued a statement demanding that the perpetrators be brought to justice.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:730">730</sup> Following the killing, Gutiérrez Vergara’s family was enrolled in the federal Protection Mechanism.
narrative.text: Officials characterized Gutiérrez Vergara as collateral damage in an attack directed at the police officers rather than at the journalist himself. RSF and ARTICLE 19 publicly challenged this characterization and called upon investigators to consider his journalistic work as a line of inquiry. The UNESCO Director-General condemned the killing, as did Mexico’s OHCHR branch. The National Press Club issued a statement demanding that the perpetrators be brought to justice. Following the killing, Gutiérrez Vergara’s family was enrolled in the federal Protection Mechanism.

narrative.html: On 25 October 2024, approximately one year after the journalist’s murder, members of SEDENA forced their way into the family home in the same Colonia Aviación neighbourhood. According to family accounts and security footage, soldiers stopped the children as they were closing their gate, forcibly entered the residence and pulled them outside, pushed them to the ground at gunpoint, and detained them.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:731">731</sup> One of the sons, Caleth Jesús Gutiérrez—who had himself become a journalist—activated his panic button. The soldiers withdrew only after a family member informed them the household was under the protection of the Mechanism.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:732">732</sup> This incident constitutes a grave failure of the Mechanism and suggests that state security forces either disregarded or were unaware of the protection measures in place—or, more troublingly, that the family was deliberately targeted. No progress on the investigation into Gutiérrez Vergara’s killing has been reported as of the date of this report.

incidents.place: the Colonia Fronteriza Alta neighbourhood of Ciudad Juárez
incidents.identity: Ismael Villagómez Tapia, known as “El Tiger”, was a photojournalist who had worked for El Heraldo de Juárez for approximately 18 years, covering general assignment stories in Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, including migration, the migrant caravans, and local crime.

narrative.html: Ismael Villagómez Tapia, known as “El Tiger”, was a photojournalist who had worked for El Heraldo de Juárez for approximately 18 years, covering general assignment stories in Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, including migration, the migrant caravans, and local crime.733 His final journalistic assignment was coverage of casualties resulting from a trailer crash at a food stall area.734 To supplement his income as a journalist, Villagómez Tapia also worked as a driver for InDrive, a ride-hailing application.735
narrative.text: Ismael Villagómez Tapia, known as “El Tiger”, was a photojournalist who had worked for El Heraldo de Juárez for approximately 18 years, covering general assignment stories in Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, including migration, the migrant caravans, and local crime. His final journalistic assignment was coverage of casualties resulting from a trailer crash at a food stall area. To supplement his income as a journalist, Villagómez Tapia also worked as a driver for InDrive, a ride-hailing application.

narrative.html: In the early hours of 16 November 2023, Villagómez Tapia was found dead from a gunshot wound to the head while seated in the driver’s seat of his grey Hyundai Elantra in the Colonia Fronteriza Alta neighbourhood of Ciudad Juárez. He had been shot at close range with a 9mm weapon. His mobile phone was missing from the vehicle.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:736">736</sup> It was presumed he was working as a ride-hailing driver at the time; passenger records from the InDrive platform contributed to the investigation.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:737">737</sup>
narrative.text: In the early hours of 16 November 2023, Villagómez Tapia was found dead from a gunshot wound to the head while seated in the driver’s seat of his grey Hyundai Elantra in the Colonia Fronteriza Alta neighbourhood of Ciudad Juárez. He had been shot at close range with a 9mm weapon. His mobile phone was missing from the vehicle. It was presumed he was working as a ride-hailing driver at the time; passenger records from the InDrive platform contributed to the investigation.

narrative.html: Authorities initially arrested three suspects. Jesús Adrián CL (“El Monky”) and Carlos Miguel HH were apprehended in the hours following the killing and found in possession of two mobile phones belonging to Villagómez Tapia.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:738">738</sup> A third suspect, Johan CB, was detained on federal firearms charges.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:739">739</sup> The Chihuahua state prosecutor characterized the killing as likely connected to a robbery rather than to Villagómez Tapia’s journalism, though he stated the journalistic motive was not ruled out.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:740">740</sup>
narrative.text: Authorities initially arrested three suspects. Jesús Adrián CL (“El Monky”) and Carlos Miguel HH were apprehended in the hours following the killing and found in possession of two mobile phones belonging to Villagómez Tapia. A third suspect, Johan CB, was detained on federal firearms charges. The Chihuahua state prosecutor characterized the killing as likely connected to a robbery rather than to Villagómez Tapia’s journalism, though he stated the journalistic motive was not ruled out.

narrative.html: The trial began on 13 November 2024.741 On 28 November 2024, a three-judge tribunal of the Chihuahua Judicial Branch unanimously acquitted CL and HH, finding that the prosecution had failed to present sufficient evidence of their participation in the homicide.742 The presiding judge identified multiple inconsistencies in the investigation, including the handling of key ballistic evidence: the shell casing from the bullet that killed Villagómez Tapia was not discovered until nine hours after the crime, when the vehicle was already in the prosecutor’s compound, and forensic analysts had failed to conduct swabs of the rear door handles to determine whether anyone had been in the back seat at the time of the shooting.743 Villagómez Tapia’s widow told El Heraldo de Juárez she was deeply hurt and outraged by the verdict, stating that her husband’s killers had spent only a year in prison.744 The Chihuahua Attorney General’s Office announced it would appeal.745 According to the latest reporting on 30 November 2024, The third defendant, Johan CB, remains incarcerated at the Cereso No. 3 state prison on federal firearms charges.746 The Asociación de Periodistas de Ciudad Juárez condemned the acquittal, stating that someone in the prosecutorial chain had failed to do their job.747 The case exemplifies the systemic investigative failures that underpin impunity for crimes against journalists in Mexico.
narrative.text: The trial began on 13 November 2024. On 28 November 2024, a three-judge tribunal of the Chihuahua Judicial Branch unanimously acquitted CL and HH, finding that the prosecution had failed to present sufficient evidence of their participation in the homicide. The presiding judge identified multiple inconsistencies in the investigation, including the handling of key ballistic evidence: the shell casing from the bullet that killed Villagómez Tapia was not discovered until nine hours after the crime, when the vehicle was already in the prosecutor’s compound, and forensic analysts had failed to conduct swabs of the rear door handles to determine whether anyone had been in the back seat at the time of the shooting. Villagómez Tapia’s widow told El Heraldo de Juárez she was deeply hurt and outraged by the verdict, stating that her husband’s killers had spent only a year in prison. The Chihuahua Attorney General’s Office announced it would appeal. According to the latest reporting on 30 November 2024, The third defendant, Johan CB, remains incarcerated at the Cereso No. 3 state prison on federal firearms charges. The Asociación de Periodistas de Ciudad Juárez condemned the acquittal, stating that someone in the prosecutorial chain had failed to do their job. The case exemplifies the systemic investigative failures that underpin impunity for crimes against journalists in Mexico.

narrative.html: On 28 November 2023, five journalists were shot in two separate but contemporaneous attacks in the Mexican states of Michoacán and Guerrero, an event that drew international attention and underscored the scale of violence against the press.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:748">748</sup>
narrative.text: On 28 November 2023, five journalists were shot in two separate but contemporaneous attacks in the Mexican states of Michoacán and Guerrero, an event that drew international attention and underscored the scale of violence against the press.

narrative.html: Maynor Ramón Ramírez (“El May”) was a reporter for ABC de Michoacán based in Apatzingán, Michoacán, specialising in crime and security reporting. At approximately 8:30 p.m., Ramírez was standing outside a carpet cleaning business he owned in the Lázaro Cárdenas neighbourhood, near the “El Ahuate” market, when he was attacked with gunfire.749 He sustained multiple gunshot wounds to his abdomen and was transferred by Civil Protection paramedics to the emergency area of the regional hospital of the Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social (Mexican Social Security Institute, “IMSS”).750 A 38-year-old employee of the business, identified only as Juan Manuel, was also injured in the attack. Ramírez survived.751
narrative.text: Maynor Ramón Ramírez (“El May”) was a reporter for ABC de Michoacán based in Apatzingán, Michoacán, specialising in crime and security reporting. At approximately 8:30 p.m., Ramírez was standing outside a carpet cleaning business he owned in the Lázaro Cárdenas neighbourhood, near the “El Ahuate” market, when he was attacked with gunfire. He sustained multiple gunshot wounds to his abdomen and was transferred by Civil Protection paramedics to the emergency area of the regional hospital of the Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social (Mexican Social Security Institute, “IMSS”). A 38-year-old employee of the business, identified only as Juan Manuel, was also injured in the attack. Ramírez survived.

narrative.html: This was the second attempt on Ramírez’s life. On 11 October 2016, he had been shot while at the intersection of Lázaro Cárdenas and Francisco I. Madero avenues in Apatzingán.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:752">752</sup> Reports conflict on whether he was shot in the head or stomach.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:753">753</sup> He recovered from the attack, and continued his journalistic work.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:754">754</sup> The Attorney General’s Office of the State of Michoacán initiated an investigation file.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:755">755</sup> No further information has been made public regarding the status of the investigation or any suspects.
narrative.text: This was the second attempt on Ramírez’s life. On 11 October 2016, he had been shot while at the intersection of Lázaro Cárdenas and Francisco I. Madero avenues in Apatzingán. Reports conflict on whether he was shot in the head or stomach. He recovered from the attack, and continued his journalistic work. The Attorney General’s Office of the State of Michoacán initiated an investigation file. No further information has been made public regarding the status of the investigation or any suspects.

narrative.html: The Chilpancingo Attack. On the same date, four photojournalists in Chilpancingo, Guerrero, came under fire while returning together from covering the murder of a bus driver that had taken place that morning.756 The attack occurred in the vicinity of a military barracks.757 The victims were: Víctor Mateo Francisco, a photojournalist and contributor to ANG, AHORA Guerrero, and Quadratín, who was shot in the face and sustained grave injuries; Jesús de la Cruz, a photojournalist for Noticias Reportes Guerrero, who was shot in the cervical spine, sustaining life-threatening injuries; Óscar Guerrero, a photojournalist for Amapola Periodismo, who suffered a minor injury to his arm from gunfire; and Héctor Camacho, a photojournalist for Interacción Weekly, who escaped physical harm but whose name was frequently withheld from reporting due to safety concerns.758
narrative.text: The Chilpancingo Attack. On the same date, four photojournalists in Chilpancingo, Guerrero, came under fire while returning together from covering the murder of a bus driver that had taken place that morning. The attack occurred in the vicinity of a military barracks. The victims were: Víctor Mateo Francisco, a photojournalist and contributor to ANG, AHORA Guerrero, and Quadratín, who was shot in the face and sustained grave injuries; Jesús de la Cruz, a photojournalist for Noticias Reportes Guerrero, who was shot in the cervical spine, sustaining life-threatening injuries; Óscar Guerrero, a photojournalist for Amapola Periodismo, who suffered a minor injury to his arm from gunfire; and Héctor Camacho, a photojournalist for Interacción Weekly, who escaped physical harm but whose name was frequently withheld from reporting due to safety concerns.

narrative.html: According to RSF, all four journalists targeted in the Chilpancingo shooting primarily covered crime stories—the “nota roja” or “policíaca” beat—in one of Mexico’s most violent states.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:759">759</sup> The Attorney General’s Office stated that a joint operation involving state and local police, the National Guard, and the Army had been initiated to locate the assailant.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:760">760</sup> No subsequent updates have been made public, and no arrests have been reported.

The Attorney General’s Office stated that a joint operation involving state and local police, the National Guard, and the Army had been initiated to locate the assailant. No subsequent updates have been made public, and no arrests have been reported.

narrative.html: The Inter American Press Association condemned the attacks.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:761">761</sup> The fact that five journalists were shot on a single day—in two different states but under strikingly parallel circumstances of crime reporters coming under attack—illustrates both the extraordinary danger confronting members of the press who cover organised crime and public security, and the failure of the Mexican state to provide effective protection. The attacks of 28 November 2023 came just days after three other journalists had been abducted and held for days in Taxco, Guerrero, before being released without explanation.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:762">762</sup>

incidents.place: in Cuernavaca

narrative.html: Roberto Carlos Figueroa Bustos, aged 40, was the founder and editor of Acá en el Show, a digital news outlet based in Cuernavaca, Morelos, that published on Facebook and commanded a following of more than 10,000 users.763 A trained biologist and former state government official, Figueroa transitioned to journalism and online content creation following the 2018 state and federal elections, according to his colleague and friend, the Morelos-based journalist José Montes.764 Through Acá en el Show, Figueroa published news articles, commentary on local politics, and satirical videos critical of local politicians, including Governor Cuauhtémoc Blanco Bravo of Morelos.765 On the day of his abduction and killing, Figueroa posted a short video announcing that he possessed information on corruption involving candidates for the upcoming 2 June state and federal elections.766 He had also recently published a report on the murder of a relative of a candidate for the municipal elections in Tetecala, Morelos.767 The day before his murder, on 25 April, he participated in an event organised by the centre-left political party Movimiento Ciudadano.768
narrative.text: Roberto Carlos Figueroa Bustos, aged 40, was the founder and editor of Acá en el Show, a digital news outlet based in Cuernavaca, Morelos, that published on Facebook and commanded a following of more than 10,000 users. A trained biologist and former state government official, Figueroa transitioned to journalism and online content creation following the 2018 state and federal elections, according to his colleague and friend, the Morelos-based journalist José Montes. Through Acá en el Show, Figueroa published news articles, commentary on local politics, and satirical videos critical of local politicians, including Governor Cuauhtémoc Blanco Bravo of Morelos. On the day of his abduction and killing, Figueroa posted a short video announcing that he possessed information on corruption involving candidates for the upcoming 2 June state and federal elections. He had also recently published a report on the murder of a relative of a candidate for the municipal elections in Tetecala, Morelos. The day before his murder, on 25 April, he participated in an event organised by the centre-left political party Movimiento Ciudadano.

narrative.html: On the morning of 26 April 2024, armed gunmen abducted Figueroa shortly after he dropped off his two daughters at their school in Cuernavaca, approximately 50 miles south of Mexico City.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:769">769</sup> His unidentified captors contacted his wife, Esmeralda, on at least three occasions and demanded a ransom in exchange for his release. During one such call, at approximately 8:00 a.m., Figueroa was put on the telephone and told his wife he needed payment, stating that “it was fine.” In the background, individuals were heard shouting that they would kill her if she called the police.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:770">770</sup> His wife delivered an undisclosed sum at the agreed location near the borders of Cuernavaca, close to the city of Ocuilan.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:771">771</sup> Despite payment of the ransom, after receipt of an anonymous telephone call, Figueroa’s body was discovered later that evening inside a white Ford Ikon on a dirt road in Coajomulco, north of Cuernavaca.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:772">772</sup> He had suffered a fatal gunshot wound to the head.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:773">773</sup> The body of a second, unidentified man was found outside the vehicle.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:774">774</sup>
narrative.text: On the morning of 26 April 2024, armed gunmen abducted Figueroa shortly after he dropped off his two daughters at their school in Cuernavaca, approximately 50 miles south of Mexico City. His unidentified captors contacted his wife, Esmeralda, on at least three occasions and demanded a ransom in exchange for his release. During one such call, at approximately 8:00 a.m., Figueroa was put on the telephone and told his wife he needed payment, stating that “it was fine.” In the background, individuals were heard shouting that they would kill her if she called the police. His wife delivered an undisclosed sum at the agreed location near the borders of Cuernavaca, close to the city of Ocuilan. Despite payment of the ransom, after receipt of an anonymous telephone call, Figueroa’s body was discovered later that evening inside a white Ford Ikon on a dirt road in Coajomulco, north of Cuernavaca. He had suffered a fatal gunshot wound to the head. The body of a second, unidentified man was found outside the vehicle.

narrative.html: Figueroa was not enrolled in the federal Mechanism at the time of his killing. An official of the Mechanism told CPJ on 26 April 2024 that the office had no prior knowledge of any threats against Figueroa.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:775">775</sup> His colleague Montes similarly told CPJ that he was unaware of any specific threats against Figueroa’s life and that the journalist did not appear unusually worried in the days preceding his death. However, Montes noted that the Acá en el Show office had been broken into twice — in November and December 2023 — although nothing was reported stolen.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:776">776</sup>
narrative.text: Figueroa was not enrolled in the federal Mechanism at the time of his killing. An official of the Mechanism told CPJ on 26 April 2024 that the office had no prior knowledge of any threats against Figueroa. His colleague Montes similarly told CPJ that he was unaware of any specific threats against Figueroa’s life and that the journalist did not appear unusually worried in the days preceding his death. However, Montes noted that the Acá en el Show office had been broken into twice — in November and December 2023 — although nothing was reported stolen.

narrative.html: The Morelos state prosecutor’s office opened an investigation. On 29 April 2024, the state attorney general announced at a press conference that Figueroa’s death was “possibly linked to his work as a reporter,” but provided no further details.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:777">777</sup> No arrests have been publicly reported. The killing was condemned by the IACHR Special Rapporteur for Freedom of Expression,<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:778">778</sup> the UNESCO Director-General,<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:779">779</sup> and ARTICLE 19.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:780">780</sup> RSF joined a special commission of journalists and press freedom defenders assisting the Morelos state prosecutor’s office in investigating the murder.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:781">781</sup> As of the date of this report, no person has been charged or convicted in connection with Figueroa’s killing.
narrative.text: The Morelos state prosecutor’s office opened an investigation. On 29 April 2024, the state attorney general announced at a press conference that Figueroa’s death was “possibly linked to his work as a reporter,” but provided no further details. No arrests have been publicly reported. The killing was condemned by the IACHR Special Rapporteur for Freedom of Expression, the UNESCO Director-General, and ARTICLE 19. RSF joined a special commission of journalists and press freedom defenders assisting the Morelos state prosecutor’s office in investigating the murder. As of the date of this report, no person has been charged or convicted in connection with Figueroa’s killing.

narrative.html: Martín Antonio Olivier Rodríguez was a radio broadcaster and announcer for the radio station La que más suena in Ajalpan, Puebla.782 He was reported missing by his relatives on the night of 6 May 2024 after he stopped responding to messages following a local council meeting in the Guadalupe Pantzingo neighborhood.783 His body was found the following day, abandoned in a taxi cab, exhibiting signs of violence. The circumstances of his abduction and the precise cause of death have not been publicly detailed by the authorities. Olivier Rodríguez’s vehicle had been stolen (a completed carjacking) a few days before his murder, though he had recovered it.784 The IACHR Special Rapporteur for Freedom of Expression condemned Olivier Rodríguez’s murder and called on the competent Mexican authorities to conduct a diligent investigation to clarify the facts and identify those responsible.785 As of the date of this report, no person has been publicly reported as charged or convicted in connection with Olivier Rodríguez’s killing.

incidents.title: Alberto Amaro Jordán
incidents.heading: Alberto Amaro Jordán — Death threats, 20 May 2024, Tlaxcala
incidents.place: Apizaco, Tlaxcala
incidents.identity: Alberto Amaro Jordán, aged 35, is the founder and editor of La Prensa de Tlaxcala, a digital news outlet based in the state of Tlaxcala, east of Mexico City

narrative.html: Alberto Amaro Jordán, aged 35, is the founder and editor of La Prensa de Tlaxcala, a digital news outlet based in the state of Tlaxcala, east of Mexico City. He is a third-generation journalist, having followed in the footsteps of his father and grandfather.786 Since founding the outlet in 2018, Amaro has specialised in reporting on local politics, crime, and corruption. Tlaxcala is recognised as a major hub for human trafficking and sexual slavery, home to powerful, family-run criminal networks that traffic girls and young women across Mexico and the U.S.787
narrative.text: Alberto Amaro Jordán, aged 35, is the founder and editor of La Prensa de Tlaxcala, a digital news outlet based in the state of Tlaxcala, east of Mexico City. He is a third-generation journalist, having followed in the footsteps of his father and grandfather. Since founding the outlet in 2018, Amaro has specialised in reporting on local politics, crime, and corruption. Tlaxcala is recognised as a major hub for human trafficking and sexual slavery, home to powerful, family-run criminal networks that traffic girls and young women across Mexico and the U.S.

narrative.html: On 20 May 2024, at approximately 7:00 p.m., unidentified men driving a red truck passed by Amaro’s residence in Apizaco, Tlaxcala, and yelled death threats at the reporter’s bodyguards stationed at the front gate, declaring that they were going to “kill us all.”788 Amaro told CPJ that he believed the threats were possibly related to a reporting trip he had taken five days earlier, on 15 May, to the nearby municipality of Ocotlán, accompanied by human rights activist Viridiana Baena Leyva, a member of Madres Buscadoras (Searching Mothers), a national network that searches for missing family members and demands the Mexican federal government address the crisis of nearly 100,000 forced disappearances. Amaro and Baena had travelled to Ocotlán to investigate rumours of clandestine graves. Upon arrival, they were observed by several individuals in the area, and when they departed, a state police vehicle followed them for more than 10 miles.789
narrative.text: On 20 May 2024, at approximately 7:00 p.m., unidentified men driving a red truck passed by Amaro’s residence in Apizaco, Tlaxcala, and yelled death threats at the reporter’s bodyguards stationed at the front gate, declaring that they were going to “kill us all.” Amaro told CPJ that he believed the threats were possibly related to a reporting trip he had taken five days earlier, on 15 May, to the nearby municipality of Ocotlán, accompanied by human rights activist Viridiana Baena Leyva, a member of Madres Buscadoras (Searching Mothers), a national network that searches for missing family members and demands the Mexican federal government address the crisis of nearly 100,000 forced disappearances. Amaro and Baena had travelled to Ocotlán to investigate rumours of clandestine graves. Upon arrival, they were observed by several individuals in the area, and when they departed, a state police vehicle followed them for more than 10 miles.

narrative.html: The May 2024 threats were part of a sustained and well-documented pattern of violence and intimidation against Amaro dating to 2019. According to his interviews with Amnesty International and CPJ, Amaro has been subjected to a campaign of harassment including physical surveillance of himself, his wife, and his children; hacking of his website; and defamatory posts on Facebook accusing him of criminal activity.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:790">790</sup> On multiple occasions, aggressors attempted to force him off the road while driving. A gunman on a motorbike fired shots at him. Intruders attempted to break into his home and fired shots at his property. One of his pet dogs was fatally poisoned.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:791">791</sup> On 15 April 2020, officers of the Tetla police force allegedly threatened and harassed Amaro while he was reporting on a farmers’ protest, with a commanding officer allegedly telling him, “We are going to kill you.”<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:792">792</sup> In 2021, the mayor of Tetla de la Solidaridad Eleazar Molina Pérez tried to run Amaro off the highway by attempting to ram into his car; no charges were filed against the mayor.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:793">793</sup> In late 2023, three men claiming to be members of the Sinaloa cartel approached Amaro and offered him money to suppress stories about corrupt police officers and to publish defamatory content targeting those who refused the cartel’s demands. Amaro declined.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:794">794</sup> In January 2024, Amaro was chased by an unknown individual in a vehicle who attempted to ram his car; the Mechanism bodyguard driving managed to evade the attacker.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:795">795</sup> In November 2021, Amaro was arrested for filming state police officers extorting citizens.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:796">796</sup> He further reported that Alfredo “N,” the former Secretary of Public Security of Tlaxcala — who is currently a fugitive facing charges of enforced disappearance—ordered state police to photograph Amaro’s family and track his movements.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:797">797</sup>
narrative.text: The May 2024 threats were part of a sustained and well-documented pattern of violence and intimidation against Amaro dating to 2019. According to his interviews with Amnesty International and CPJ, Amaro has been subjected to a campaign of harassment including physical surveillance of himself, his wife, and his children; hacking of his website; and defamatory posts on Facebook accusing him of criminal activity. On multiple occasions, aggressors attempted to force him off the road while driving. A gunman on a motorbike fired shots at him. Intruders attempted to break into his home and fired shots at his property. One of his pet dogs was fatally poisoned. On 15 April 2020, officers of the Tetla police force allegedly threatened and harassed Amaro while he was reporting on a farmers’ protest, with a commanding officer allegedly telling him, “We are going to kill you.” In 2021, the mayor of Tetla de la Solidaridad Eleazar Molina Pérez tried to run Amaro off the highway by attempting to ram into his car; no charges were filed against the mayor. In late 2023, three men claiming to be members of the Sinaloa cartel approached Amaro and offered him money to suppress stories about corrupt police officers and to publish defamatory content targeting those who refused the cartel’s demands. Amaro declined. In January 2024, Amaro was chased by an unknown individual in a vehicle who attempted to ram his car; the Mechanism bodyguard driving managed to evade the attacker. In November 2021, Amaro was arrested for filming state police officers extorting citizens. He further reported that Alfredo “N,” the former Secretary of Public Security of Tlaxcala — who is currently a fugitive facing charges of enforced disappearance—ordered state police to photograph Amaro’s family and track his movements.

narrative.html: Amaro’s case constitutes one of the most extensively documented failures of the federal Mechanism. He enrolled in the Mechanism in 2019 but told Amnesty International and CPJ that it took “months” for the Mechanism to respond to his initial requests for help. Even after enrolment, it took approximately six months for the Mechanism to provide him with a panic button, and bodyguards were not assigned until 2021.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:798">798</sup> One of the vehicles the Mechanism provided for his protection detail had faulty brakes, and the private security company tasked with monitoring his panic button frequently failed to respond to requests for help. Amaro reinforced his property’s perimeter and installed an alarm system and 25 security cameras at his own expense.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:799">799</sup>

He enrolled in the Mechanism in 2019 but told Amnesty International and CPJ that it took “months” for the Mechanism to respond to his initial requests for help. Even after enrolment, it took approximately six months for the Mechanism to provide him with a panic button, and bodyguards were not assigned until 2021. One of the vehicles the Mechanism provided for his protection detail had faulty brakes, and the private security company tasked with monitoring his panic button frequently failed to respond to requests for help. Amaro reinforced his property’s perimeter and installed an alarm system and 25 security cameras at his own expense.

narrative.html: In late July 2023, the Mechanism reassessed Amaro’s security situation and concluded that he was no longer at risk. Upon reviewing the evaluation, Amaro found it contained numerous errors and made no mention of the recent poisoning of his dog.800 Moreover, the evaluation stated that Amaro was no longer in danger because one of the three men who had attempted to bribe him had been arrested — ignoring that the other two remained at large.801 Facing the prospect of losing his bodyguards and being reduced to a panic button and police visits as his sole protective measures, Amaro hired a lawyer and filed an amparo (injunction).802 A judge ruled in his favour in August 2023, blocking the removal of his four bodyguards, although the long-term status of his protection remained uncertain.803

A judge ruled in his favour in August 2023, blocking the removal of his four bodyguards, although the long-term status of his protection remained uncertain.

narrative.html: As a result of the constant attacks and the Mechanism’s failure to guarantee his safety, Amaro reported self-censoring and contemplated abandoning journalism altogether.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:804">804</sup> His case was profiled by Amnesty International and CPJ in their March 2024 joint report, “‘No one guarantees my safety’: The urgent need to strengthen Mexico’s federal policies for the protection of journalists.”<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:805">805</sup>

His case was profiled by Amnesty International and CPJ in their March 2024 joint report, “‘No one guarantees my safety’: The urgent need to strengthen Mexico’s federal policies for the protection of journalists.”

narrative.html: CPJ’s telephone calls to the Tlaxcala State Prosecutor’s Office on 21 and 22 May 2024 regarding the latest threats were not answered. A Mechanism official confirmed to CPJ that the agency was aware of the threats and was investigating, describing Amaro’s protection schedule as “one of the strongest.”<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:806">806</sup> No arrests in connection with the 20 May 2024 threats have been publicly reported. Amaro was threatened with a firearm by a state police officer in relation to his reporting in June 2024.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:807">807</sup> The officer pulled up beside the car Amaro was traveling in at a railroad stop and pulled a gun on him, saying: “This is the damn journalist who published a story against my brother.” Amaro called local police, who refused to arrest the officer.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:808">808</sup>

narrative.html: Víctor Alfonso Culebro Morales, aged 39, was the founder, director, and editor of Realidades, Periodismo con verdad (“Realities, Journalism with truth”), a Facebook-based digital news outlet covering security issues, criminal disputes, and the displacement of families in the state of Chiapas.811 Culebro Morales was married with two children, and was the son of a former Secretary General of Government in Chiapas.812 One day before his disappearance, on 26 June 2024, Realidades published a report stating that the deployment of thousands of soldiers and police officers to Chiapas had failed to stem the violence related to turf wars between criminal gangs — a matter of acute public interest in a state experiencing a dramatic escalation of narco-violence.813
narrative.text: Víctor Alfonso Culebro Morales, aged 39, was the founder, director, and editor of Realidades, Periodismo con verdad (“Realities, Journalism with truth”), a Facebook-based digital news outlet covering security issues, criminal disputes, and the displacement of families in the state of Chiapas. Culebro Morales was married with two children, and was the son of a former Secretary General of Government in Chiapas. One day before his disappearance, on 26 June 2024, Realidades published a report stating that the deployment of thousands of soldiers and police officers to Chiapas had failed to stem the violence related to turf wars between criminal gangs — a matter of acute public interest in a state experiencing a dramatic escalation of narco-violence.

narrative.html: Culebro Morales was reported missing by his relatives on 27 June 2024.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:814">814</sup> The following day, his body was discovered in a roadside ditch at approximately kilometre 20 of the Ocozocoautla-Arriaga toll highway, near the Tierra y Libertad ejido in the municipality of Jiquipilas.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:815">815</sup> His hands were bound, his face was covered with black adhesive tape, and his body bore multiple bullet wounds, including gunshots to the head, as well as signs of severe physical torture and beating.
narrative.text: Culebro Morales was reported missing by his relatives on 27 June 2024. The following day, his body was discovered in a roadside ditch at approximately kilometre 20 of the Ocozocoautla-Arriaga toll highway, near the Tierra y Libertad ejido in the municipality of Jiquipilas. His hands were bound, his face was covered with black adhesive tape, and his body bore multiple bullet wounds, including gunshots to the head, as well as signs of severe physical torture and beating.

incidents.place: Guanajuato

narrative.html: Alejandro Alfredo Martínez Nogués (also spelled Noguéz), aged 57, was a crime reporter based in Celaya, Guanajuato, and the founder and operator of El Hijo del Llanero Solititito (“The Son of the Lone Ranger”), a popular Facebook-based news page with approximately 344,000 followers.823 After decades of working for local radio stations and newspapers, Martínez dedicated his final years to his own digital outlet, reporting on community news and crime in Celaya—one of the most dangerous cities in the state of Guanajuato, a region plagued by violent turf wars between the CJNG and the local Santa Rosa de Lima gang.824 His recent publications included coverage of homicides, vehicle thefts, a disappearance, and the identification of leaders of criminal cells.825
narrative.text: Alejandro Alfredo Martínez Nogués (also spelled Noguéz), aged 57, was a crime reporter based in Celaya, Guanajuato, and the founder and operator of El Hijo del Llanero Solititito (“The Son of the Lone Ranger”), a popular Facebook-based news page with approximately 344,000 followers. After decades of working for local radio stations and newspapers, Martínez dedicated his final years to his own digital outlet, reporting on community news and crime in Celaya—one of the most dangerous cities in the state of Guanajuato, a region plagued by violent turf wars between the CJNG and the local Santa Rosa de Lima gang. His recent publications included coverage of homicides, vehicle thefts, a disappearance, and the identification of leaders of criminal cells.

narrative.html: On the evening of 4 August 2024, Martínez was travelling in the back seat of a municipal police vehicle assigned to him as part of his protection detail. A white pickup truck overtook the vehicle and its occupants opened fire with long-range firearms.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:826">826</sup> Martínez was struck by bullets in the head and body. His two bodyguards, who returned fire at the assailants, were wounded. A woman travelling in another vehicle was also struck by a stray bullet. Martínez was rushed to a hospital in Celaya but did not survive his injuries.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:827">827</sup> Minutes before his death, he had completed a live Facebook broadcast from the scene of a traffic accident, in which he criticised the poor infrastructure at the site.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:828">828</sup>
narrative.text: On the evening of 4 August 2024, Martínez was travelling in the back seat of a municipal police vehicle assigned to him as part of his protection detail. A white pickup truck overtook the vehicle and its occupants opened fire with long-range firearms. Martínez was struck by bullets in the head and body. His two bodyguards, who returned fire at the assailants, were wounded. A woman travelling in another vehicle was also struck by a stray bullet. Martínez was rushed to a hospital in Celaya but did not survive his injuries. Minutes before his death, he had completed a live Facebook broadcast from the scene of a traffic accident, in which he criticised the poor infrastructure at the site.

narrative.html: Several years earlier, in November 2022, Martínez was the victim of an assassination attempt, when an unidentified man arrived at Martínez’s home armed with a firearm and asked for him by name. Martínez managed to close the door before the assailant could fire; some reports indicate the weapon jammed.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:829">829</sup> The assailant fled with an accomplice who was waiting on a motorcycle.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:830">830</sup>
narrative.text: Several years earlier, in November 2022, Martínez was the victim of an assassination attempt, when an unidentified man arrived at Martínez’s home armed with a firearm and asked for him by name. Martínez managed to close the door before the assailant could fire; some reports indicate the weapon jammed. The assailant fled with an accomplice who was waiting on a motorcycle.

narrative.html: At the time of his killing, Martínez was under active police protection provided by the Celaya municipal government  after the first attempt on his life. He reportedly requested protection by traffic officers, explaining that he “trusted” that unit of the Celaya municipal police force.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:831">831</sup> Although Martínez’s preferences are reported in multiple outlets, there are some conflicting reports about the role of his municipal protection versus his state and federal protection, which he was incorporated into on 28 November 2022 and 12 January 2023 respectively.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:832">832</sup> In January 2025, the Guanajuato State Human Rights Commission found Jesús Ignacio Rivera Peralta—Secretary of Security of Celaya at the time of Martínez’s murder—to have failed to safeguard the journalist, by assigning bodyguards that were not consistent with the recommendations of the federal and state Mechanisms that Martínez was already protected by.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:833">833</sup> He was ordered to pay compensation to Martínez’s family, make an apology to the larger journalistic community, show documentation of the decisions made related to Martínez, and establish a formal protection mechanism.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:834">834</sup>As of 5 August 2025, several of these orders had not been complied with.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:835">835</sup> RSF characterised the case as emblematic of the state’s inability to protect journalists even when it has explicitly assumed responsibility for their safety.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:836">836</sup>
narrative.text: At the time of his killing, Martínez was under active police protection provided by the Celaya municipal government  after the first attempt on his life. He reportedly requested protection by traffic officers, explaining that he “trusted” that unit of the Celaya municipal police force. Although Martínez’s preferences are reported in multiple outlets, there are some conflicting reports about the role of his municipal protection versus his state and federal protection, which he was incorporated into on 28 November 2022 and 12 January 2023 respectively. In January 2025, the Guanajuato State Human Rights Commission found Jesús Ignacio Rivera Peralta—Secretary of Security of Celaya at the time of Martínez’s murder—to have failed to safeguard the journalist, by assigning bodyguards that were not consistent with the recommendations of the federal and state Mechanisms that Martínez was already protected by. He was ordered to pay compensation to Martínez’s family, make an apology to the larger journalistic community, show documentation of the decisions made related to Martínez, and establish a formal protection mechanism.As of 5 August 2025, several of these orders had not been complied with. RSF characterised the case as emblematic of the state’s inability to protect journalists even when it has explicitly assumed responsibility for their safety.

narrative.html: The Guanajuato State Attorney General’s Office announced that it had opened an investigation and assigned a forensic and operational team to clarify the facts and identify those responsible.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:837">837</sup> The killing was condemned by CPJ,<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:838">838</sup> RSF,<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:839">839</sup> ARTICLE 19,<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:840">840</sup> and the IACHR Special Rapporteur for Freedom of Expression.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:841">841</sup> At the presidential morning press conference, Deputy Security Minister Luis Rodríguez Bucio confirmed that Martínez was the third journalist murdered in Mexico in 2024.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:842">842</sup> As of the date of this report, no person has been publicly reported as charged or convicted in connection with Martínez’s murder.
narrative.text: The Guanajuato State Attorney General’s Office announced that it had opened an investigation and assigned a forensic and operational team to clarify the facts and identify those responsible. The killing was condemned by CPJ, RSF, ARTICLE 19, and the IACHR Special Rapporteur for Freedom of Expression. At the presidential morning press conference, Deputy Security Minister Luis Rodríguez Bucio confirmed that Martínez was the third journalist murdered in Mexico in 2024. As of the date of this report, no person has been publicly reported as charged or convicted in connection with Martínez’s murder.

narrative.html: Ariel Grajales Rodas, aged 55, is a journalist with more than 30 years of professional experience and the founder and director of the digital news portal Villaflores.com.mx, based in the municipality of Villaflores, Chiapas.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:843">843</sup> He is also the founder of the Unión de Editores y Reporteros de la Frailesca (Union of Editors and Reporters of the Frailesca).<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:844">844</sup> In 2022, he received the Colibrí de Oro prize in recognition of his pioneering work in digital journalism.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:845">845</sup> He covered a broad range of topics, including local politics, security, and crime. He was particularly known for his reporting on the disputes between criminal groups in the Frailesca region of Chiapas, a territory contested by the Sinaloa Cartel and the CJNG.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:846">846</sup>
narrative.text: Ariel Grajales Rodas, aged 55, is a journalist with more than 30 years of professional experience and the founder and director of the digital news portal Villaflores.com.mx, based in the municipality of Villaflores, Chiapas. He is also the founder of the Unión de Editores y Reporteros de la Frailesca (Union of Editors and Reporters of the Frailesca). In 2022, he received the Colibrí de Oro prize in recognition of his pioneering work in digital journalism. He covered a broad range of topics, including local politics, security, and crime. He was particularly known for his reporting on the disputes between criminal groups in the Frailesca region of Chiapas, a territory contested by the Sinaloa Cartel and the CJNG.

narrative.html: At approximately 12:30 a.m. on 21 August 2024, a group of armed men broke down the front door of his home and opened fire on him.847 Grajales sustained multiple gunshot wounds and was transported by his family members to the Hospital General Bicentenario, where his condition was reported as grave.848 The attackers fled the scene before police and investigative units arrived. Hours before the attack, Grajales had published a post on his Facebook page denouncing the widespread extortion of businesses in the Frailesca region through the practice of cobro de piso (protection rackets), writing that the extortion applied equally to all commercial activity in the region.849
narrative.text: At approximately 12:30 a.m. on 21 August 2024, a group of armed men broke down the front door of his home and opened fire on him. Grajales sustained multiple gunshot wounds and was transported by his family members to the Hospital General Bicentenario, where his condition was reported as grave. The attackers fled the scene before police and investigative units arrived. Hours before the attack, Grajales had published a post on his Facebook page denouncing the widespread extortion of businesses in the Frailesca region through the practice of cobro de piso (protection rackets), writing that the extortion applied equally to all commercial activity in the region.

narrative.html: The Chiapas State Attorney General’s Office announced that it had opened an investigation into the shooting.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:850">850</sup> The IFJ condemned the attack and called for an end to impunity for violence against media workers in Mexico.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:851">851</sup> The journalist community in Chiapas collectively condemned the aggression and demanded guarantees for the free exercise of press freedom.<sup class="fn" data-fn="tk:852">852</sup> As of the date of this report, no arrests have been publicly reported in connection with the attack on Grajales.
narrative.text: The Chiapas State Attorney General’s Office announced that it had opened an investigation into the shooting. The IFJ condemned the attack and called for an end to impunity for violence against media workers in Mexico. The journalist community in Chiapas collectively condemned the aggression and demanded guarantees for the free exercise of press freedom. As of the date of this report, no arrests have been publicly reported in connection with the attack on Grajales.
